2cd70993-c8a3-50ff-9205-453f52ff7756.name: Bowl.
2cd70993-c8a3-50ff-9205-453f52ff7756.description:
The development of ceramics painted with metallic lustre was an important advancement in Islamic ceramic art. It was considered luxurious because it gave a metallic sheen, giving the impression of a precious metal. Such ceramics come in various types: normally the lustre is applied on to a transparent glaze; less frequently, it is found on cobalt-blue, manganese and turquoise glaze. This piece is one such example.  
A ceramic bowl with a cylindrical body and a columnar base, the bulk of the body decorated with a double border containing a band of repeating angular pseudo-*kufic* script and curling, stylised vegetal scrolls. Painted semi-circles are arranged around the rim. These designs are executed in dark, reddish-brown metallic lustre underneath a transparent layer of turquoise glaze. While the technique and the designs are familiar in other Fatimid lustre-ware, the shape is somewhat unusual. The emphasis on the decorative quality of calligraphy that this piece exhibits may be evidence of the influence of ceramics derived from the Eastern Samanid Dynasty, which is contemporary to the Fatimid period.
2cd70993-c8a3-50ff-9205-453f52ff7756.short_description: The pseudo-*kufic* calligraphy and semi-circular rim decoration of this lustre-painted and transparent-blue-glazed bowl is most probably the work of Fatimid Egyptian potters who settled in Syria.
2cd70993-c8a3-50ff-9205-453f52ff7756.dates: Hegira late 5th–early 6th century / AD late 11th–early 12th century.
2cd70993-c8a3-50ff-9205-453f52ff7756.method_for_datation: The bowl was dated by comparison with similar pieces found in Tel Minis, a Syrian village near Ma'rrat al-Nu'man. The style was influenced by Egyptian Fatimid pottery of the 5th / 11th century.
2cd70993-c8a3-50ff-9205-453f52ff7756.method_for_provenance: This bowl was found by a resident of Raqqa, but ceramic production in the region did not begin until the early 6th / 12th century. It is thought, therefore, that this piece may be either early Raqqa or Tel Minis ware. Lustre-ware production in Syria was prolific, but the provenance cannot be determined definitively.
2cd70993-c8a3-50ff-9205-453f52ff7756.provenance: Syria; possibly Raqqa or Tel Minis.

2d0ab34f-6c97-5be0-adec-c434b7c0d438.name: Variation of the Basmala
2d0ab34f-6c97-5be0-adec-c434b7c0d438.description: This work is made of patterned light blue-gold silk with mounted calligraphy on paper. The Arabic calligraphy in black ink has been arranged to form the root system of a bouquet of seven spikes, which sprout from the letters themselves. The title of the work appears in black ink on the left, above two red seals. A third red seal appears on the top right.
materials: Ink and red seal colour on rice paper, mounted on silk

2d16dd66-a963-5f6f-b65b-339f7f17148f.name: Carpet
2d16dd66-a963-5f6f-b65b-339f7f17148f.description:
Carpet composed of three cloths joined together with approximately the same width of red and green wool decoration.  
Field: The decorative motifs on the field are formed by a collection of rhombuses that contain palms with small pineapples with a red core lodged in their centre.  
Borders: It consists of five red borders separated by spans. The short sides are extended with green borders.  
The carpet is topped by a woollen fringe of the same colours as the field and borders, with slight wear on its narrow sides.  
The production technique used in this carpet was common throughout the Iberian Peninsula and was known by different names according to the geographical region in which it was utilised; "garbancillo", "caracolillo" or "caramullo". It is more commonly known as the "Alpujarras technique", a term referred to texts and treaties that geographically linked it with historic Andalusia in southern Spain. However, this reference is not wholly correct as this would only be one of several regions in which the technique was used. Furthermore, this association with the Alpujarras region would only occur at the end of the 19th century, despite the technique being considerably older.  
In the Balearic Islands, a similar technique was used for hemp and silk textiles that would adorn walls as well as floor coverings and are more commonly known as *catalufa*.  
Most of the pieces found in the museum, with their decoratively looped wefts, have been produced between the 18th and early 20th centuries. The technique used in this carpet consisted of adding extra wefts, which go from selvedge to selvedge, and are taken out in the form of rings to the surface through the use of an auxiliary needle, whenever the design demands it.  
The design of this carpet evokes the rural countryside and its decoration imitates the Renaissance period carpets known as “of Toledan brocade”. Another inspiration visible in the borders of this carpet is its aesthetic emulation of counted-thread embroidery, a technique common in older Spanish carpets. The calligraphy and style of the borders indicate that this carpet most likely could have been from the 18th century. Similar pieces are preserved in the museum, such as the carpet with inventory number CE00981.

2d3a9974-408a-5de5-bdff-8cfdae9e0b29.name: *Akbarnama*
2d3a9974-408a-5de5-bdff-8cfdae9e0b29.short_description: The Mughal emperors ruled India for more than three centuries. Akbar (r. 1556–1605), the third emperor, was the longest ruling and is considered the greatest of them all. His biography is known as the *Akbarnama* (‘Book of Akbar’) and is an official, imperial biography written by the emperor’s close friend and associate, Abu ’l-Fazl. Begun in 1598, it took almost ten years to complete the text. Two illustrated copies of the text were produced during Akbar’s lifetime, this being the later of the two. In the numerous illustrations that accompany the text, Akbar is portrayed as a powerful, dynamic and highly heroic figure, much as he seems to have been perceived by his contemporaries.
keywords: manuscript; illustration; figural decoration; miniature painting; elephant; Jesuit; religion; ceremony, royal; warfare; battle; court
materials: Coloured pigments and gold on paper

2d7d148e-c180-5cf1-813a-f3b4c6cdb469.name: Prayer book.
2d7d148e-c180-5cf1-813a-f3b4c6cdb469.description:
This small book is a compilation of various religious texts illustrating popular beliefs and customs. Its content is based mainly on the Qur'an to which the first part of the manuscript is dedicated. The text starts with the *fatiha*, the first sura, and ends with the last sura CXIV, but it is not the complete Qur'an. The text was written in a *muhaqqaq* style and in *naskhi* script possibly by two different calligraphers. One of them was Ibrahim Babirbarzadeh, whose signature appears in a later part of the manuscript. On each page the text is framed by a broad gold stripe and lines of black and bright bluish-red ink. The sura headings are illuminated and the verses are marked by golden rosettes. The first part of the manuscript is followed by a selection of suras and Qur'anic verses. According to popular belief, the words of the Qur'an possess supernatural powers because of their divine origin, which help in cases of misfortune. The margins of these pages are also covered with texts. These margin notes might provide explanation of the specific use of the quotations, for example, against disease or poverty. The 99 beautiful names of Allah and the names of the Prophet, which are written on the next pages of the manuscript, are also considered to afford special protection. A common element of books of this kind is prayers of blessing whose recitation was a deserving act of believers. The most impressive part of the manuscript is a series of painted pages showing the names of Allah and Muhammad in golden script against a blue background, the footprint and the sandal of the Prophet, views of Mecca and Medina and powerful quotations, letters and names of God arranged in circles and squares as protection against the evil eye.  
The binding of the book is of dark brownish-red leather ornamented with a central golden rectangle and filled with a rhomb pattern. The inside of the binding is covered with a polished yellow paper showing a design of large leaves.

In addition to the mostly Qur’anic quotations it contains prayers of blessing. Most impressive are its painted pages showing the footprint and the sandal of the Prophet or the views of Mecca and Medina.

2d816e3d-dd49-518b-8af2-f3ada0d2875b.name: "The Story of the Princess of the Blue Pavillion: The Youth of Rum Is Entertained in a Garden by a Fairy and her Maidens"
2d816e3d-dd49-518b-8af2-f3ada0d2875b.alternate_name: Folio from a Khamsa (Quintet) of Amir Khusrau Dihlavi
2d816e3d-dd49-518b-8af2-f3ada0d2875b.description: Approximately one century after the Persian poet Nizami wrote his Khamsa (Quintet), the Indian poet Amir Khusrau Dihlavi composed a response using Nizami’s structure but varying his stories slightly. This painting comes from the Mughal emperor Akbar’s (r. 1550–1605) copy of Amir Khusrau’s verses. It depicts a story told by a princess to the king Bahram Gur, about a youth and the fairy queen he imagines meeting nightly in a lush garden.

2dd5e058-db6d-5ca4-b1c8-b47beedc0811.name: Fragment from a tiraz.
2dd5e058-db6d-5ca4-b1c8-b47beedc0811.description:
This beige-coloured linen fragment is decorated with two horizontal strips of calligraphy embroidered in green silk. The inscription is in *kufic* lettering with split uprights.  
The beginning and end of both inscriptions are missing. In spite of its damaged condition, one can read in the first line; 'May the blessing of God fall on Muhammad the highest of all prophets and on his good and pious ancestors.'  
On the second line is written; '(There is no other divinity) than God in his oneness and may blessings fall on Muhammad the highest of all prophets.'  
The *tiraz* was made using a weaving technique typical of the Egyptian textile industry up to the end of the Fatimid era. Its texture indicates that it was probably part of a *caliph*'s turban. It appears to have been made in a private workshop (*tiraz al-khassa*), reserved for the *caliph* and government dignitaries, rather than in a popular workshop (*tiraz al-amma*). The workshop would have been in the Nile Delta area, one that specialised in linen, and which was probably located in Alexandria, Damiette, Tinnis or Dabiq.
2dd5e058-db6d-5ca4-b1c8-b47beedc0811.short_description: Fragment of beige linen from a *tiraz* made using a needlework technique employed in the Egyptian textile industry during the Fatimid period. The texture of the *tiraz* suggests that it was made in a workshop reserved for use by the caliph and the important dignitaries of the regime.
2dd5e058-db6d-5ca4-b1c8-b47beedc0811.dates: Hegira, last quarter of the 4th–first third of the 5th centuries / AD 10th–11th centuries.
2dd5e058-db6d-5ca4-b1c8-b47beedc0811.method_for_datation: Comparison with other similar pieces of cloth with identical inscriptions referring to the family and good, pious ancestors of the Prophet shows that this piece belonged to an Egyptian Fatimid *caliph*. The absence of exuberant decoration combining geometric, floral and animal motifs would place the date between the last quarter of the 4th and the first third of the 5th century / 10th–11th century.
2dd5e058-db6d-5ca4-b1c8-b47beedc0811.method_for_provenance: The weaving method and the ownership by a Fatimid *caliph* both indicate that the cloth was made in Egypt.
2dd5e058-db6d-5ca4-b1c8-b47beedc0811.obtention: The *tiraz* was bought in 1958 by the late H. H. Abdelwahab, former Director of the National Institute of Art and Archaeology, from an Egyptian antique dealer. He then donated it to the Ribat Museum at Monastir.

keywords: Tiraz; calligraphy; Fatimid textiles; workshop; embroidery
materials: Linen embroidered with silk.

2e402c4d-0004-5e48-84c2-e6f4b24d7d3e.name: Bowl with dark brown slip and white slip decoration
2e402c4d-0004-5e48-84c2-e6f4b24d7d3e.short_description: This earthenware bowl was covered in a dark brown slip before receiving an as yet unread, white floriated *kufic* inscription – possibly containing blessings. 2ed5f331-f245-5701-b5ea-1a6aa1a79c09.name: Qur’an
2ed5f331-f245-5701-b5ea-1a6aa1a79c09.short_description:
This large-scale Qur’an manuscript from India stretches more than one meter in length. Handmade in India, these grand holy books were likely a result of domestic writings of the Qur’an and calligraphy as a form of devotion and worship.  
  
The *ayah* (verses) are composed in black ink in *naskh* script within a black frame refining the border on the delicate paper. Individual *ayah* and decorative elements also appear in liquidized gold for embellishment and emphasis. A selection of pages illustrates segments of *surah* (chapters) in bright colours from pigment in diamond and medallion shapes with floral motifs.

2f8de84c-6136-535a-a12d-f37d60e59baa.name: Column capital.
2f8de84c-6136-535a-a12d-f37d60e59baa.description:
A stone column capital, one of 18 capitals that belong to the water reservoir at the Umayyad palace at al-Muwaqqar, with an inscription that reveals that the reservoir was built by order of the Caliph Yazid II (r. AH 101–5 / AD 720–24). It was found in May 1943 in a yard belonging to a private house located within a few hundred meters of the ruins of the palace. It was broken into two pieces which fit together neatly.  
  
Three sides of the capital are decorated with a row of acanthus leaves separated by paired volutes. One side contains a ten-line Arabic inscription that stands out in relief from a plain background. This inscription reads: 'In the name of the most merciful God. Has ordered the building of this pool the servant of God, Yazid Commander of the Faithful, may God favour him and prolong his life and happiness and bestow upon him blessings and bounties in this world and the next. It has been built by the care of ‘Abdallah the son of Sulaym.' Between the eighth and ninth line of the inscription three words are incised in smaller characters, they read: 'Khamsat Ashara dhira' (15 cubits). The drums of the column, upon which this capital once sat, would have been immersed in the pool; each drum with other incised words indicating the number of cubits; thus forming a water gauge. The highest measurement is on the capital itself, being 15 cubits.  
  
A second inscription in relief runs around the abacus of the three decorated sides, it is interrupted in the middle of each by a circular boss with an inscribed trefoil which reads: 'Allahma salli Ala Abdka Rasul Allah' ('O God bless your servant and messenger Muhammad').
2f8de84c-6136-535a-a12d-f37d60e59baa.short_description: Limestone capital from al-Muwaqqar with a ten-line Arabic inscription in relief mentioning the building of a pool ordered by Yazid II (r. AH 101–5 / AD 720–4). The capital and its drum formed a water gauge and incised words indicate measurements. The last was 15 cubits, recorded within the inscription.
2f8de84c-6136-535a-a12d-f37d60e59baa.owner: Now on display at Jordan Museum
2f8de84c-6136-535a-a12d-f37d60e59baa.method_for_datation: The capital is datable by the inscription which bears the name of the Umayyad Caliph Yazid II (r. 101–5 / 720–24).
2f8de84c-6136-535a-a12d-f37d60e59baa.method_for_provenance: Literary sources indicate that the palatial residence at al-Muwaqqar belonged to the Umayyad Caliph Yazid ibn Abd al-Malik (Yazid II) who reigned from 103–4 / 722–3. Furthermore the capital was found only a few hundred meters from the palace at al-Muwaqqar.
2f8de84c-6136-535a-a12d-f37d60e59baa.obtention: The Museum obtained the capital directly from the owner of the house in which it was found.

2fe554a9-e532-5b15-814f-963ca40c1b1c.name: Small water-basin.
2fe554a9-e532-5b15-814f-963ca40c1b1c.description:
On the broad border of this wide basin there are depicted, between four round medallions, scenes of courtly pleasure hunts. Three riders are shown in every scene, undertaking various hunting practices. The hunters are fighting in tournament, armed with lances, swords, bows and arrows. One rider is accompanied by a hunting cheetah on a horse. These illustrations represent a view of an idealised life. Images of riders and hunters refer not only to the riding abilities of the princes, but also to the courage, strength and perseverance of the rulers. Depictions of hunters with falcons and leopards could be referring to the immense wealth of the rulers. Only rulers such as these could afford to keep and train such expensive hunting animals, only they could hold such lavish hunting parties. This princely lifestyle reached its height during the Mamluk period. The underside of the basin is decorated with plaited bands, and arabesques, vines and birds fill the spaces in between. The decoration is finished in gold and silver inlay. The precious metal decoration gives the brass receptacle a multicoloured appearance and rich tone.  
The coat of arms of Amir Sumul Abu’l-‘Izz, who belonged to the retinue of the ruling Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad bin Qalawun, is set at the centre of each of the round medallions. It can be only guessed that Abu’l-‘Izz commissioned the basin on the basis of a fragment of inscription. Abu’l-‘Izz and his brother Salar, viceroy of Egypt, rebelled against the Sultan and were captured and imprisoned in 1310. At the bottom of the basin, two well-wishing inscriptions are addressed to the person who commissioned it, whose identity remains unclear. Sumul Abu’l-‘Izz’s name could have been inscribed here. If it had, the basin would have been dateable to between AH 693 and 710 / AD 1293 and 1310.
2fe554a9-e532-5b15-814f-963ca40c1b1c.short_description: The design of this brass water-basin with gold and silver inlays shows a frieze with riders hunting or at a tournament. They are separated by four medallions holding a coat of arms typical of the Mamluk nobility. The basin was commissioned for a Mamluk *amir*.
2fe554a9-e532-5b15-814f-963ca40c1b1c.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum
2fe554a9-e532-5b15-814f-963ca40c1b1c.method_for_datation: The coat of arms suggest that the basin belonged to the patron Sumul Abu’l-'Izz. He was in the service of the Mamluk Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad bin Qalawun from 693 to 710 (1293–1310).
2fe554a9-e532-5b15-814f-963ca40c1b1c.method_for_provenance: The Mamluk coat of arms, which establishes the identity of the basin’s patron, points towards Egypt as the country of origin.
2fe554a9-e532-5b15-814f-963ca40c1b1c.obtention: As a donation from the Berlin collector Friedrich Sarre, who bought it in 1897.

310e79cc-ee2c-5e1c-89d1-fcfcb20cf00e.name: Curtain for the door of the Holy Ka‘ba in Makkah al-Mukarramah
310e79cc-ee2c-5e1c-89d1-fcfcb20cf00e.short_description: This curtain, known as *sitara*, *burdah* or *burqa* and embroidered with qur’anic quotations, forms the most elaborate part of the *kiswah* textile cover which encloses the Holy Ka‘ba in Makkah. This example was made under the patronage of King Fahd ibn Abd al-Aziz al-Saud, who ascended the throne in AH 1405 / AD 1985.

320c1324-a266-5d46-8155-00fc3414ae7e.name: Ivory panels.
320c1324-a266-5d46-8155-00fc3414ae7e.description: Two pairs of oblong-shaped ivory panels with carved decoration. Two of the four panels have purely vegetal designs comprising geometric features superimposed on leafy scrolls. The combination of geometric forms with scrolls or arabesques was typical of ivory carvings from the Mamluk period. The remaining pair bears inscriptions carved with a background of vegetal scrolls. The split leaves in all four panels have marked striations. The inscriptions include the name Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun (r. AH 692–741 / AD 1293–1341). These pieces were therefore either set into a door of a building belonging to the sultan, or into a piece of furniture in his possession. Ivory was often used in combination with wood for doors, furniture or caskets in Mamluk architecture and decorative arts.
320c1324-a266-5d46-8155-00fc3414ae7e.short_description: Two pairs of ivory panels with carved decoration. The inscriptions on two of the panels include the name Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun (r. AH 692–741 /AD 1293–1341). The pieces therefore probably came from a door or building belonging to the sultan.
320c1324-a266-5d46-8155-00fc3414ae7e.dimensions: Width 16 cm, height from 5.9 to 7.1 cm.
320c1324-a266-5d46-8155-00fc3414ae7e.method_for_datation: The panels are inscribed with the name Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun who ruled from AH 692 to 741 / AD 1293 to 1341.
320c1324-a266-5d46-8155-00fc3414ae7e.method_for_provenance: The panels are inscribed with the name of Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun who ruled in Cairo, Egypt.

3281a778-30ea-57b8-8d73-b1b6ddf74613.name: Wooden panel.
3281a778-30ea-57b8-8d73-b1b6ddf74613.description: A rectangular wooden panel decorated with two narrow borders flanking a broad central band. The two narrow borders are ornamented with an epigraphic inscription in *kufic* script, which consists of the *bismillah (In the Name of God)* and the 'Throne' verse (2: 255) as well as the expression '*Hasbi Allah*' ('Allah is sufficient for me'). The broad central band is ornamented with geometric motifs, which divide it into seven square-shaped sections. All sections are decorated with vegetal decorations, winged motifs, oval forms and tri-lobed leaf designs. The third and fifth squares hold a lobed arch, within which is vegetal decoration and, flanking the triangular areas between the outer curvature of the arch and the corners of the square-shaped section, are further vegetal motifs. Both the decorative style and the carving of this piece portray a Hellenic stamp, seen in the relief carving of decorative motifs, the oval shapes, the tri-lobed leaves and the vegetal stems. The panel also displays Sassanid influences seen in the winged motifs and lobed arches.
3281a778-30ea-57b8-8d73-b1b6ddf74613.short_description: Islamic art came into being on the shoulders of Hellenistic and Sassanid arts and then developed its own Islamic character. This piece demonstrates the blending of the three artistic styles.
3281a778-30ea-57b8-8d73-b1b6ddf74613.method_for_datation: This panel was dated based on study into the development of *kufic* script, the origins of the decorative motifs, and the technique of manufacture, which included high relief, decorative motifs, winged designs, oval forms and vegetal motifs. Furthermore, during the Abbasid period, entire texts were used as inscriptions on objects; it is possible, therefore, to date this piece to the early part of the Abbasid era.
3281a778-30ea-57b8-8d73-b1b6ddf74613.method_for_provenance: Wooden panels were used to furnish mosques and residences, and embellished tribunes and chairs. Egypt, Fustat in particular, was famous for the production of such panels in the early Islamic period, and production flourished during the Fatimid and Mamluk periods. Many of these panels were discovered in Fustat where they were used to protect the walls of small tombs from the dust and dirt that might fall from the grave onto the deceased.
3281a778-30ea-57b8-8d73-b1b6ddf74613.obtention: The object was discovered during the course of archaeological excavations at Fustat.

32fb3761-3d91-5ac8-b9e9-d93cf46f8c28.name: Lamp from a mosque
32fb3761-3d91-5ac8-b9e9-d93cf46f8c28.short_description: This lamp from a mosque was purchased from a Yemenite from Saana by Franz Steindacher in Aden in 1896. Steindacher was part of an Austrian expedition to explore the Red Sea.

32fdd8a2-bebf-5ad2-bcf2-45ef21b39556.name: Inkwell
32fdd8a2-bebf-5ad2-bcf2-45ef21b39556.short_description: This exquisite inkwell is an exceptional specimen of hardstone carving in medieval Islam. Contemporary accounts of minerals and semi-precious stones all refer to agate, which had been prized for small vessels since classical times but which, compared with rock crystal and jade, has barely survived. The faces of the inkwell bear the *basmala* and a Qur’anic inscription from *sura* *al-Kahf* (XVIII), verse 109, which is charmingly apposite. It reads: ‘If the ocean were ink (wherewith to write out) the words of my Lord, sooner would the ocean be exhausted than would the words of my Lord, even if we added another ocean like it, for its aid.’
32fdd8a2-bebf-5ad2-bcf2-45ef21b39556.holder: Khalili Family Trust – Nasser D. Khalili Collection of Islamic Art
32fdd8a2-bebf-5ad2-bcf2-45ef21b39556.method_for_datation: Exact place of manufacture is impossible to determine with any degree of certainty; dating is based on the style of the calligraphy.
32fdd8a2-bebf-5ad2-bcf2-45ef21b39556.bibliography: Rogers, J.M., *The Arts of Islam. Masterpieces from the Khalili Collection*, London: Thames & Hudson, 2010: no.158, p.132.
keywords: Inkwell; carving; engraving; Kufic; Kufic script; Basmala; Qur’anic inscriptions
materials: Banded agate, carved and engraved

33034cbb-75d9-5619-8b7f-cac29ec681b4.name: Fragment of a basin.
33034cbb-75d9-5619-8b7f-cac29ec681b4.description:
Fragment of a basin sculpted in low relief, triangular in shape, both parts of which have been restored. Two of the sides are flat, the third is curved.  
The scene on the basin, of which only a part has survived, depicts hawking. The torso and part of the thigh of a horse rider can be distinguished, clothed in a pleated tunic belted around the waist by a large belt, and holding a white weapon in the right hand. Behind him, a falconer, whose face is mutilated and whose lower limbs have been amputated, and who is wearing a tunic that is open in front and tightened at the waist by a narrower belt, holds a dead hare. In his left hand, he holds up a falcon, of which only one foot and a bit of the tail can be seen above the horse's rump, the lower part of which is missing. A section of tree trunk, which could belong to a palm tree, appears behind the falconer.  
To the left of this scene lies an inscription consisting of two lines in *kufic* lettering. The first line is rather difficult to interpret ; the second reads as follows: ' …*ine wa arba'ou maya … amal ibn* …' (…four hundred…the work of Ibn…). '*ine*' cannot be translated as it is the last syllable of a number that could just as well be forty as seventy or even ninety.
33034cbb-75d9-5619-8b7f-cac29ec681b4.short_description: Fragment of a sculpted white marble ablutions basin, the two halves of which have been pieced back together. The bas-relief scene shows a falcon hunt. On the left-hand side there is an inscription in *kufic* characters. This object was originally from Andalusian Morocco.
33034cbb-75d9-5619-8b7f-cac29ec681b4.holder: National Museum of Antiquities and Islamic Arts
33034cbb-75d9-5619-8b7f-cac29ec681b4.dimensions: Length 51.5 cm, width 21 cm, thickness 7.5 cm.
33034cbb-75d9-5619-8b7f-cac29ec681b4.method_for_datation: The object features a date which is missing the numerals representing single units and units of tens, and thus can only be placed somewhere between 440 and 489 (1048 and 1096).
33034cbb-75d9-5619-8b7f-cac29ec681b4.method_for_provenance: Through comparing this bas-relief fragment to basins from al-Andalus, Marçais was able to attribute this fragment to a basin, which could have been used for ablutions, of the same origin.
33034cbb-75d9-5619-8b7f-cac29ec681b4.obtention: Gift of Edmond Doutté, who acquired it in Rabat in 1902, during an exploration in Morocco.

333c6f3d-7691-5779-abef-33af94f6d1fb.name: Spherical lamp component
333c6f3d-7691-5779-abef-33af94f6d1fb.short_description: Spherical component of a mosque lamp inscribed in cursive script: “Glory to our Lord the Sultan, the Sultan al-Malik al-Nasir”. It probably refers to al-Nasir al-Hassan, ibn Muhammad, ibn Qalawun, younger brother of Kujuk and of Sha‘ban, who reigned in the middle of the 14th century. These spheres, the so-called ‘eggs’ prevented the lamps’ suspension chains from becoming entangled. Their decoration was usually related to the corresponding lamps and this helps to date them.
keywords: Spherical lamp; Al-Nasir al-Hassan ibn Muhammad ibn Qalawun; Glass
materials: Glass with gilded and enamel decoration

336652f6-ed72-5895-9254-6d9fb253362d.name: Illustrated manuscript of Jami's *Yusuf and Zulaykha*
336652f6-ed72-5895-9254-6d9fb253362d.short_description: This illustrated manuscript was copied by the renowned calligrapher Mir 'Ali al-Katib al-Sultani (c. 1476–1556). He was one of several artists working in the city of Herat (in present-day Afghanistan) when it was captured in 1529. Mir 'Ali and his colleagues were taken to Bukhara where they produced illustrated manuscripts for the Uzbek rulers. Written histories relate that Mir 'Ali was unhappy in his new environment, yet the quality of his work never declined. Purchased at auction, 1962.

materials: Ink, opaque watercolour, and gold on paper; gilded leather binding

33d56671-7bf3-5042-8973-1e88842c1245.name: Carpet
33d56671-7bf3-5042-8973-1e88842c1245.description:
Field: The field is of a reddish hue and depicts motifs of interwoven green ribbons that form elongated hexagons. Inside of these upright pineapples framed on serrated palms are housed.  
Border: The carpet consists of two borders: the interior consists of green and white motifs upon a dark background; The exterior features calligraphic elements and flowers upon a blue background.  
Naturally coloured wool is used for the warp and weft. The wool knots utilise blue, green, red, yellow and white hues.  
The carpet is of a Gothic-Moorish type in which Gothic motifs predominate in the field, while Mudejar styles persist in the valances. The outer border resembles the pseudo-*kufic* inscriptions of the Admiral series, but much more schematic.  
A similar carpet is reproduced in the painting 'The Annunciation' which is currently housed in the Prado museum and dated to around 1500 CE. The painting is composed by the unnamed artist 'Master of the Sisla'.  
The current dimensions do not reflect the original size of the carpet, since it is composed of numerous fragments due to several successive restorations. It is the first in a series that is inspired by contemporaneous fabrics.  
The carpet comes from the Weisberger Collection.
33d56671-7bf3-5042-8973-1e88842c1245.method_for_datation: Through the stylistic and technical analysis of the piece.

33daf898-afb6-58bd-95bf-60b7472151c4.name: Illuminated Qur’an manuscript
33daf898-afb6-58bd-95bf-60b7472151c4.short_description: 19th-century Qur’an manuscripts produced in Istanbul and the Ottoman Empire continued many Islamic art traditions, but could not entirely escape the increasing taste for Western aesthetics.Ssingle-volume Qur’ans like this one became increasingly popular and were completed in large numbers. This example – which appears to have remained unfinished judging by the empty title cartouches above the chapters, begins – as is customary – with a lavishly decorated double page, showing – on the right - the first chapter ‘Al-Fatiha’ and – on the left - the beginning of the second chapter ‘Al-Baqara’. Both texts are contained within broad geometric borders and framed with colourful illuminations with vegetal detailing. The remainder of the all in all 114 chapters of the Holy Qur’an are written in black naskhi and red detailing, with 15 lines to each page. As was customary, the verse markers are rendered as golden circles and each page is confined within delicate gilt borders. Colourful medallions in some of the margins mark important subdivisions of the text.
33daf898-afb6-58bd-95bf-60b7472151c4.holder: Sharjah Museum of Islamic Civilisation / Sharjah Museums Department
33daf898-afb6-58bd-95bf-60b7472151c4.artist: Calligrapher Ali Shukri, known as Nadherzadeh
33daf898-afb6-58bd-95bf-60b7472151c4.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
keywords: naskhi
materials: European paper, black ink, pigments, gilding, pasteboard, leather

3438c1f8-75f5-5936-9cfe-6b8fe4241a2f.name: Qur'an
3438c1f8-75f5-5936-9cfe-6b8fe4241a2f.short_description: This small manuscript is of note for its extensive documentation and equally for its extensive illumination. Its colophon states that it was copied by al-Hasan ibn Juban ibn ‘Abdallah al-Quwani (‘from Konya’) in the *madrasa* (theological school) of Sa‘ad al-Din Kubak in the city of Konya, in eastern Turkey, in AH 678 / AD 1278. Somewhat unusually, the illuminator is also named, one Mukhlis ibn ‘Abdallah al-Hindi (‘from India’). The manuscript now includes seven double-pages and one single page of illumination, all in a palette of mainly blue and gold. (The single-page frontispiece with which the manuscript now opens was probably originally a double-page composition.) Throughout the text, the name of Allah (God) is written in gold ink.
keywords: koran; calligraphy; script; illumination; geometric decoration; palmette; shamsa; religious manuscript
materials: Coloured pigments and gold on paper

343d8541-3a84-5139-8263-7b4033cb1128.name: Footed dish
343d8541-3a84-5139-8263-7b4033cb1128.short_description: Attributed to the “Gurgan hoard” in the past, this rimmed flat dish rests on three feet shaped as crowned sphinxes. The central field shows the depiction of an elephant carrying a palanchin (*hawda*) with a veiled figure, most likely a lady. Such theme is not unusual, and speaks of the intense political and cultural contacts with South Asia at that time. It may be an allusion to the story of Bahram Gur and Sapinud, his Indian bride, from the *Shahnameh*.

34fa4908-e715-5899-b8b5-002b54cad2c5.name: Two dragons entwined on a spray of stylised foliage
34fa4908-e715-5899-b8b5-002b54cad2c5.short_description: Probably executed in the Ottoman court atelier (*naqqashkhana*) in Istanbul, the remarkable intricacy of line and detail of this drawing belies its minute size. It belongs to a distinct style of painting that developed separate from the highly conceptual tradition of manuscript illustration in the second half of the 10th/16th century. Known as the "saz style" after the reed pen employed in its creation, this style highlighted fantastic and dazzling imagery that incorporates chinoiserie motifs and feathery leaves. Here, concealed among the dense, bristly foliage, are two silently slithering dragons, barely visible at first glance. Rather than emphasising pure line, the anonymous artist was caught up with the textural qualities of the dragons' scaly, speckled bodies and the sinuous veins of the serrated leaves. Drawings such as this were evidently reproduced through the aid of pounces or stencils; the LACMA depiction seems to have been made with the identical pounced drawing as a sketch in the Louvre, which was likewise mounted as an album page.
34fa4908-e715-5899-b8b5-002b54cad2c5.holder: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)
34fa4908-e715-5899-b8b5-002b54cad2c5.method_for_datation: While there are no dated works in the “saz style” an album presented to Murad III (Heigra 982-1003 / AD 1574-95) in Hegira 980 / AD 1572-72, now in Vienna, Austrian National Library (Codex Mixtus 313) includes works that closely parallel the drawing in terms of subject and style.
34fa4908-e715-5899-b8b5-002b54cad2c5.method_for_provenance: The calligraphic structure of the drawing and the serrated edges of the leaves and bristly texture of the dragons’ hide are all typical of the Ottoman “saz style”.

350d777a-ce03-5773-a131-b3fa4e4624a8.name: Funerary stele of Ruqayya bint al-Hadj Ahmad ibn Abdallatif.
350d777a-ce03-5773-a131-b3fa4e4624a8.description:
Funerary stele with a rectangular base, whose superior part takes the form of an arch surmounted by a closed crescent. The two sides of this stele are sculpted in relief. On the first side, an inscription in the *thuluth* style is distributed across five cartouches superimposed with the following text: 'Everything, except God the very highest, is perishable / this is the tomb of she to whom God has been merciful, of she who was protected with care, / of the pearl that will receive her pardon and who remained hidden, Ruqayya, the daughter of the deceased al-Hadj Ahmad ibn Abdallatif / may God give him mercy, in the year 1208.'  
The space left by the cartouches at each end are decorated with floral and vegetal motifs, just like the posterior side, which depicts at its centre a vase from which foliage ending in acanthus leaves and palmettes burst forth. A vegetal frieze frames the whole depiction. The rectangular part features a pot at its centre that has the same decoration as the upper part.  
This example, along with another stele that has been preserved in the same museum, belongs to the tomb of one and the same person, as these stelae (*m'chhed*) existed as a pair: the one that professed faith was placed on the tomb on the site of the head of the deceased, and the one featuring the name and date of the person's death was positioned over the feet.  
These stelae are not of particular historical interest, as the two persons mentioned are not referred to by chroniclers, but the finish, execution and design of the decoration cause them to be classified among the most beautiful Muslim funerary stelae of Algeria. The whole attests to the fact that the deceased belonged to a noble family.
350d777a-ce03-5773-a131-b3fa4e4624a8.short_description: Marble funerary stele with a rectangular base bearing an arch crowned with a closed crescent. Both faces of the stele are sculpted, the first with a *thuluth*\-style inscription within five superposed cartouches, and the second with floral motifs.

35453f02-5851-5ed4-841e-211439b842c4.name: Qur’an with box
35453f02-5851-5ed4-841e-211439b842c4.short_description:
The small Qur’an belongs to a group of diminutive holy books intended as a talismanic object. Written in India in the *Turabi* calligraphy style with a single horse hair, the Qur’an represents a devotional book hard to read with the naked eye.  
  
Encased in a silver box, sometimes in textile pouches, the script becomes a pendant for a necklace. While the amulet would guard and empower the wearer, its manufacture was often reserved for sultans and their soldiers for their protection. Furthermore, the silver embellishes the protective power as a lucky metal in Islam. Carried around the neck or attached to ceremonial objects and weapons, good luck charms endure and appear throughout time and place.

3570c6f8-5cc6-5efe-ae6d-f8468dfd121c.name: Set of calligraphers’ tools
3570c6f8-5cc6-5efe-ae6d-f8468dfd121c.short_description:
The desk set comprises paper-scissors, a pen-rest and a penknife. The handles of the scissors are of gold with enamelled ribbons and floral scrolls, lavishly encrusted with diamonds. The gold-damascened ribbed steel blades are hollow-ground. The top of the pen-rest is decorated with a dervish turban on a stand, illustrating the ties between Ottoman calligraphers and sufi brotherhoods.The penknife blade is stamped with the maker's name, Riza.  
Reed pens used by calligraphers had to be trimmed constantly. This was done by placing the pen on the pen-rest and trimming the end using the penknife. The scissors would have been used to trim the paper or the paper-ribbons used in the decorative borders of calligraphic works.  
Many of the Ottoman sultans practised the art of calligraphy, and sets such as this were ordered for use in the court or for for presentation.

359c5242-9309-5cb3-a026-926ac7a00def.name: Album of Ahmed Karahisari.
359c5242-9309-5cb3-a026-926ac7a00def.description:
The Album of Ahmed Karahisari is in two sections and contains the sixth *sura* of the Qur'an (al-An'am), a series of *hadith*s, and a section of the *Qasidat al-Burdah* ('Poem of the Mantle') by the AH 7th- / AD 13th-century poet al-Busiri. The album that contains samples of Ahmed Karahisari's writing including *kufic*, *naskhi*, *thuluth*, and *muhaqqaq* scripts and which expands the boundaries of the art of calligraphy, is carefully pasted together in 15 leaves. The leather binding is not original. This shows that these samples, which were originally written in scroll format, may have been cut down later and brought together in this album.  
  
The album opens with a page featuring the words 'Praise be to God' in square *kufic* script at the top, the *basmala* in the centre, and *sura* 92 in square-*kufic* script at the bottom, all written in black ink and gold. On the other pages, the page layout shows different characteristics according to the style and dimensions of the writing.  
  
In the colophon on the last page Ahmed Karahisari describes himself as a student of his teacher Asadullah Kirmani with whom he studied, rather than with the school of Sheikh Hamdullah, in order to learn to write in the style of the great calligrapher Yaqut al-Musta'simi (AH 7th / AD 13th century). Karahisari breathed new life into 16th-century Ottoman calligraphy and left his mark on it. The school he founded was continued by his student Hasan çelebi (d. AH 1002 / AD 1594) but was abandoned at the end of the 10th / 16th century.  
  
These writings are models of Ottoman calligraphy, and in addition to showing the peak that was achieved in the art of writing their beauty inspires a great many artists even today.
359c5242-9309-5cb3-a026-926ac7a00def.short_description: Calligrapher Ahmed Karahisari left his mark on Ottoman calligraphy of the AH 10th / AD 16th century through the school he founded. This album contains samples of his works which expand the boundaries of calligraphy in the 'layering' of letters.
359c5242-9309-5cb3-a026-926ac7a00def.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts.
359c5242-9309-5cb3-a026-926ac7a00def.initial_owner: The original owner is unknown. The work bears a seal of Sultan Mahmud I (AH 1143–68 / AD 1730–54), as it was given by him as a pious endowment (*waqf*) to the library he founded in his own name.
359c5242-9309-5cb3-a026-926ac7a00def.method_for_datation: Although the colophon does not include a date, the dates of the calligrapher Ahmed Karahisari (AH 875–963 / AD 1470–1556) are known with certainty, and so the work can be dated to the period of his life.
359c5242-9309-5cb3-a026-926ac7a00def.method_for_provenance: The calligrapher Ahmed Karahisari is known to have lived in Istanbul and thus the work is thought to have been made there.
359c5242-9309-5cb3-a026-926ac7a00def.obtention: The album was transferred to the Museum in 1914 from the Library of Sultan Mahmud I at Ayasofya Museum.

35d28d2d-69ab-5ec0-a006-32f2135420d3.name: Textile with prayer niche (*mihrab*).
35d28d2d-69ab-5ec0-a006-32f2135420d3.description: The fabric, made of red, black and yellow-brown silk, is decorated with motifs embroidered with silver- and gold-plated copper wire woven into a cotton base. The basic decorative element consists of a large prayer niche (*mihrab*), at the centre of which, at the top, there hangs a mosque lamp. Above and beside it there are scrolls containing decorative epigraphic motifs. The background of the fabric, with the exclusion of the inside of the niche where there are naturalistic floral motifs, is decorated with arabesque elements consisting of intertwined palmettes of various shapes or half-palmettes surrounded by spirals.
35d28d2d-69ab-5ec0-a006-32f2135420d3.short_description: This fabric, embroidered with metal thread and decorated with a prayer niche (*mihrab*), a large mosque lamp and epigraphic motifs, is typical of late Ottoman textile production.

35dafca1-8ab1-5d22-8ffd-d39248a402df.name: *A Ferry Crossing the Gagos River*
35dafca1-8ab1-5d22-8ffd-d39248a402df.short_description:
This is one of the both unnecessary and revolutionary illustrations in Abdallah ibn al-Fadl’s copy of Dioscorides’s medical treatise.  
The text states that on the shores of the Gagos River, jet can be found effective against pain in the uterus, but the artist took the opportunity to depict a ferry with a helmsman, two rowers, and eight passengers looking out of a porthole.
35dafca1-8ab1-5d22-8ffd-d39248a402df.type: Miniature from a copy of *Kitab al-hashaish*, a translation of Dioscorides’s *De Materia Medica*, scientific manuscript, miniature

366838a9-73be-5d88-a818-531e4ee3e0d0.name: Genealogical chart of Jahangir
366838a9-73be-5d88-a818-531e4ee3e0d0.short_description: This is a painted genealogy of selected male figures from the house of Jahangir, the fourth emperor of Mughal India (r. 1605–1627). For the Mughals, history and genealogy played an important role in establishing their legitimacy to rule, as well as their prestigious pedigree and culture. In the portraits, Jahangir and his descendants display similar idealized facial features, robes and turbans, adorned with rich fabrics and precious jewellery, as if adhering to a specific dynastic standard.

36b1f585-6689-57a6-af25-716c209224fe.name: Funerary stele ‘with ears’.
36b1f585-6689-57a6-af25-716c209224fe.description:
Fired-clay moulded funerary stele with a rectangular lower and rounded upper part and two appendages. It has been treated with an opaque, shiny tin glaze on to which the geometrical decoration and inscription in *kufic* characters has been applied using the metallic highlighting technique.  
The piece may have been mounted on the cresting of a funerary monument or fixed directly into the ground at the head of a grave.  
In al-Andalus, in accordance with Islam's sense of equality, tombs were characterised by their great simplicity. Nonetheless, we still find different types of burial. The most modest graves were usually marked with a single rough, unworked headstone, while stelae of a different type were used for people of higher social standing.  
Pieces of glazed and gilded clay were also produced for burials. Some are simple rectangular bricks, but the most important are the ones known as 'stelae with ears', which are made up of a rectangular part, the unglazed base of which was fixed into the ground, and a rounded part with two appendages, or 'ears', on top, hence the name. Some are tin glazed with an inscription in gold or cobalt on the front and a plant motif or 'hand of Fatima' (*hamza*) on the back.
36b1f585-6689-57a6-af25-716c209224fe.short_description: Funerary stele typical of the Kingdom of Granada said to have ‘ears’ due to the two appendages sticking out of the upper part. Sadly, some of its rich lustre decoration on a white base has been lost.
36b1f585-6689-57a6-af25-716c209224fe.dimensions: Height 30 cm, width 14 cm, depth 5 cm.
36b1f585-6689-57a6-af25-716c209224fe.method_for_datation: Parallels with similar pieces, kept in Huelva and the Institute of Valencia de Don Juan (Madrid), catalogued by Martínez Caviro as Nasrid from the 9th / 15th century.
36b1f585-6689-57a6-af25-716c209224fe.method_for_provenance: The piece is from Gibralfaro (Malaga), whose castle, built in the 8th / 14th century by Yusuf I (r. 734–55 / 1333–54), was built on top of an existing building erected by Badis al-Muzaffar (reign AH ?–465 / AD ?–1073) of the Zirid dynasty of Granada. From the 7th / 13th century, Malaga is mentioned in Arab sources as an important centre for the production of gold highlights.
36b1f585-6689-57a6-af25-716c209224fe.obtention: The piece was donated to the National Archaeological Museum in 1894.

36b43269-5ffd-5b5e-bb6b-ea170ad7ed06.name: Facing Pages from a Manuscript of the Qur'an
36b43269-5ffd-5b5e-bb6b-ea170ad7ed06.short_description: In the second half of the sixteenth century especially, Shiraz was an important hub for the creation of large-format luxury manuscripts of the Qur’an, some of which were intended for export to the Ottoman Empire. This pair of facing pages from the closing section of a dispersed manuscript includes the *du‘a al-khatm*, or prayer said at the conclusion of a reading of the Qur’an; it is preceded by the closing verses of the Qur’an, and followed by a *falnama*, (a Persian versified form of divination). The beautiful decoration framing the gold calligraphy of the khatm prayer epitomizes the Shiraz style of illumination in its colorful exuberance. The recto of the right-hand page is comprised of Suras 113-114 indicating that the full text must have similarly composed of large lines of blue *muhaqqaq* and gold *thuluth* alternating with blocks of smaller *naskh* in black on gold-sprinkled paper, framed by panels of scrolling floral illumination, the sura headings in white on gold and polychrome illuminated panels, marginal roundels marking various points in the text. Numerous similarly decorated manuscripts of the Qur’an are preserved in Istanbul collections, demonstrating a distinct Turkish affinity for the Shiraz style.
36b43269-5ffd-5b5e-bb6b-ea170ad7ed06.holder: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)
36b43269-5ffd-5b5e-bb6b-ea170ad7ed06.dates: Hegira c. third quarter 10th century / AD c. third quarter 16th century
36b43269-5ffd-5b5e-bb6b-ea170ad7ed06.method_for_datation: The pages relate to the standard program of illumination and calligraphy associated with Shiraz qur’ans from the mid –second half of the 16th century, the most famous of which is the so-called Ruzbihan Qur’an (Chester Beatty Library, Dublin, Is 1558), after its calligrapher Ruzbihan Muhammad al-Tab‘i al-Shirazi.
36b43269-5ffd-5b5e-bb6b-ea170ad7ed06.method_for_provenance: The pages relate to the standard program of illumination and calligraphy associated with Shiraz Qur’ans of the Safavid period.

372e3810-b18e-5d0c-b107-9bd837cefb1e.name: Hijaz Railway Medal
372e3810-b18e-5d0c-b107-9bd837cefb1e.description: Medal of the Hijaz Railway fund. In September 1900, (the 25th anniversary of Sultan Abdul Hamid’s accession to throne) he addressed a call for all the Muslims all over the world to collect donations for establishing a railway between Damascus and the holy places to facilitate transporting the pilgrims. The call was responded to enthusiastically and with great support from all Muslims. Sultan Abdul Hamid II began the donations with 300,000 Ottoman gold lira, then kings and heads of Islamic world donated money or materials for setting the railway. The donations continued till 1907. On this occasion the sultan issued gold, silver and nickel medals to donors – for instance a nickel medal given to whoever donated 5-50 Lira, a silver medal for whoever donated 50-100 Lira and named them bey, and for donations of more than 100 Lira a gold medal and the title of Pasha. After that the donation become compulsory in which the officials disclaim a one month salary. This is a gilt nickel medal issued AH 1318 / AD 1900. On its obverse, within a wreath: tuğra of sultan Abdul Hamid II with "al-Ghazi" and form of locomotive and the date ١٣١۸ (AH 1318) below. On reverse, حميديه حجاز تيمور يولنه خدمت ايدن حميتمندانه مخصوص مدالية در ("Medal reserved to patriots who have served the Hamidiye Hijaz Railway") written in Divan script.

keywords: Railway; pilgrimage; 'Abd al-Hamid; Ottoman; Germany; Hijaz; Makka al-Mukarrama; Mecca; al-Madina al-Munawwara; Medina; sharif; railway; route; numismatics
materials: Nickel

374a32ae-e579-53c0-bfce-25a5e5c80764.name: *Tuğra* of Sultan Osman III.
374a32ae-e579-53c0-bfce-25a5e5c80764.description:
The Sultan's official monogram or *tuğra* (tughra) is drawn in gold outlined with black ink on a blue ground. The areas between the letters in the lower part of the *tuğra*, the 'arms' of the *tuğra*, and its flaring bow are filled with floral decoration. These floral compositions show two different styles: one following the Chinese influence *hatayi*\-style, and the other reflecting the appearance of baroque designs in Ottoman illumination under European influence. In the upper right-hand corner are depictions of the Ka'ba in Mecca and of Medina rendered in an oval frame. The paintings of Mecca and Medina resemble similar compositions in AH 11th–12th- / AD 17th–18th- century decorative arts, manuscript painting and tiles. In the lower left-hand corner is a medallion containing the signature of the artist who drew the *tuğra*, Karabağlı Kaptan-ı Derya Süleyman Pasha, phrased thus: 'The slave of the court, Süleyman Pasha, made the *tuğra* of the Sultan of the world'. The date AH 1270 (AD 1854) is also given. This is surprising and possibly incorrect for Kaptan-ı Derya (Grand Admiral) Süleyman Pasha does not appear in the historical sources for that year. He was promoted to that rank by Sultan Osman III in AH 1168 / AD 1754 and remained in that position until he was removed from it in AH 1171 / AD 1757. In the same year he was restored to his post by Sultan Mustafa III (r. AH 1171–87 / AD 1757–74) and remained in it until AH 1172 / AD 1759. Since the work has undergone much restoration in various periods, the date must be AH 1170 / AD 1756–7 rather than AH 1270 / 1853–4.  
  
Sultan Osman III, who ascended the throne at age fifty-five, was the oldest Ottoman prince to become sultan, and his reign lasted only three years. The *tuğra* reads 'Osman Khan, son of Mustafa, ever-victorious'. The *tuğra* was a kind of signature of the Ottoman sultans, drawn by a special official of the Imperial Chancery (*Divan-ı Hümayun*) or under his instruction. Because of its size and the fact that it is executed so as to display in detail all the aspects of a *tuğra*, this example must have been made in the Imperial Chancery as a model with the aim of ensuring that *tuğra* copies could be made without any mistakes.
374a32ae-e579-53c0-bfce-25a5e5c80764.short_description: *Tughras*, official monograms of the sultans, are one the first things to come to mind when Ottoman art or history is mentioned. The size of this *tughra* of Sultan Osman III makes it an interesting example and it has features peculiar to the art of the AH 12th / AD 18th century.
374a32ae-e579-53c0-bfce-25a5e5c80764.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts.
374a32ae-e579-53c0-bfce-25a5e5c80764.method_for_datation: Dated according to the signature, in which the name of the Grand Admiral Süleyman Pasha appears; he was Grand Admiral during the reign of Sultan Osman III. (No other Grand Admiral by that name was found in the historical sources for reigns other than that of Osman III).
374a32ae-e579-53c0-bfce-25a5e5c80764.method_for_provenance: Only the Imperial Chancery (*Divan-ı Hümayun*) was allowed to print the sultan's *tuğra*. Large examples like this one were prepared as models to ensure that the *tuğra* was drawn correctly when added to official documents. Thus, it must have been produced in the Topkapı Palace, Istanbul.
374a32ae-e579-53c0-bfce-25a5e5c80764.obtention: Transferred to the Museum in 1916 from the library of Kılıç Ali Paşa in Istanbul.
374a32ae-e579-53c0-bfce-25a5e5c80764.bibliography: Ölçer, N., *et al, In Pursuit of Excellence: The Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts*, Istanbul, 1993, p.43, pl. 22, 61.

377425e8-db47-571b-85e2-27702d394d1d.name: Scroll with views of Mecca and Medina
377425e8-db47-571b-85e2-27702d394d1d.short_description: The text consists of Qur’anic verses, short prayers, invocations and numerous repetitions of the *basmala* and the *shahada*, the latter arranged into decorative shapes such as vases, flowers, a pagoda and *Dhu’l-faqar*, the bifurcated sword given by the Prophet to ‘Ali. In addition, there are depictions of the Masjid al-Haram at Mecca and the Prophet’s mosque at Medina (where the domed tomb is depicted on the wrong side). The last panel encloses the *hilya* of the Prophet Muhammad.

37a27989-a571-558d-8e53-62ed28c07f4f.name: Chandelier.
37a27989-a571-558d-8e53-62ed28c07f4f.description:
This copper object consists of a six-segment ring on a cylindrical drum supported by six consoles.  
The ring acts as a plate to which were fixed the metallic supports that held the oil jars that were used as lamps. It is decorated with inscriptions and plant motifs, both combined with and independent of the inscriptions.  
The inscriptions are engraved on two circular bands that delimit its surface. On the outer band, the inscription in cursive characters includes pious formulas and eulogies, as well as the date the chandelier was made.  
The inner band, engraved in *kufic* characters, combines a eulogy and floral decoration.  
Between the two bands there is a wide section of openwork and carved plant decoration, including palms on foliage (single or asymmetrical palms with calyxes and double palms with axillary buds).  
The same decorative scheme can be found on the surface of the drum. Between two bands containing votive inscriptions in cursive characters, a wide openwork band bears a votive inscription in *kufic* characters and floral motifs emerging from foliage.  
The flower-shaped consoles are decorated with plant motifs engraved in the spandrels and votive inscriptions in the rectangular frame.  
This light is a simplified prototype of the plate chandeliers used since the Almohad period until the beginning of the 20th century to light mosques and prayer rooms in *madrasas*. These chandeliers, which belonged to sanctuaries, were carefully decorated, particularly under the Marinids. The chandelier of the Taza mosque and Al-'Attarin Madrasa in Fez are two of the best examples.
37a27989-a571-558d-8e53-62ed28c07f4f.short_description: This lamp, decorated with inscriptions and plant motifs, is a simplified prototype of the plate chandelier, which had metal supports for the oil jars. They were used to decorate and light prayer rooms as late as the beginning of the 20th century.
37a27989-a571-558d-8e53-62ed28c07f4f.dimensions: Upper diameter 67 cm, base diameter 24.3 cm.
37a27989-a571-558d-8e53-62ed28c07f4f.method_for_datation: The inscription engraved on the outer band of the plate finishes by mentioning the date of manufacture: 'Made on 11 Dhu'l Qa'dah 690' (4 November 1291).
37a27989-a571-558d-8e53-62ed28c07f4f.method_for_provenance: The object was bought in Fez and resembles chandeliers from the Marinid mosques and *madrasas* of that town.

37c7ac1e-311b-504e-b4d9-c3f7173a7125.name: Candlestick.
37c7ac1e-311b-504e-b4d9-c3f7173a7125.description:
A candlestick with a truncated, conical body and double ridges around the lower edge and below the shoulder. The shoulder is flattened and has been damaged and repaired. From the centre of the shoulder a cylindrical neck rises into a projecting candle socket, echoing the shape of the body in the double ridges around its base and mouth; damage and deformation affect the aperture of the socket. The candlestick is embellished with incised decoration, much of which was originally inlaid with silver. On the socket there is a cursive inscription band, interrupted by roundels with whirling rosettes and enclosed by a continuous plain border. The inscription gives the official titles of the owner. The two ridges of the socket are enhanced by hatching.  
On the neck are three bands: the two outer bands comprising latticework with individual four-leaf motifs, interrupted by two roundels with whirls. The broad band in between has a tall *thuluth*\- script inscription set against a stylised leaf-scroll background that is interrupted by two large roundels with individual lotus blossoms, five-petalled flower heads and floral scrolling. The base of the neck is enhanced by obliquely set leaf shapes and a stylised scroll band. On the shoulder two elongated cartouches alternate with two roundels; they are filled with individual lotus blossoms, the cartouches further enhanced with secondary motifs such as five-petalled flower heads.  
The two ridges below the shoulder have an oblique-leaf decoration similar to that seen on the base of the neck, above and below this is a narrow interlacing leaf scroll. On the body of the candlestick, two elongated epigraphic cartouches alternate with two epigraphic roundels. The remaining background is filled with a geometric T-fret pattern. The cartouches give the titles and name of Sultan Muhammad ibn Qalawun, who was twice deposed, reigning three times between AH 693 and 741 / AD 1293 and 1340. At the centre of the roundels the titles are repeated: ‘al-sultan al-nasir’, with further titles radiating from it with tall, slim and densely set *hastae* (spears). The decoration on the body is completed at the base by oblique leaf designs on the ridges, between which is a leaf scroll guilloche.
37c7ac1e-311b-504e-b4d9-c3f7173a7125.short_description: In Mamluk times splendid silver- and gold-inlaid utensils were commissioned by officials and rulers. Most show proud large-scale inscriptions with the patron’s name or titles, some are radial sun-like compositions around the owner’s emblem, attesting to his self-confidence and spiritual aspirations.
37c7ac1e-311b-504e-b4d9-c3f7173a7125.initial_owner: Sultan al-Nasir Nasir al-Din Muhammad ibn Qalawun.
37c7ac1e-311b-504e-b4d9-c3f7173a7125.method_for_datation: Produced for Sultan al-Nasir Nasir al-Din Muhammad ibn Qalawun who was twice deposed, reigning three times: 693–4/698–708/709–741 / AD 741 / 1293–4/1299–1309/1310–1340.
37c7ac1e-311b-504e-b4d9-c3f7173a7125.method_for_provenance: The style of this candlestick is consistent with Mamluk metalwork executed during the 8th / 14th century in both Egypt and Syria, characterized in particular by the large and emphatic titular inscriptions, highlighted by silver inlay. There is also a notable tendency to display inscriptions in radial compositions around the blazon of the owner like sun rays; a device that probably held symbolic significance and attests to the self-confidence and spiritual aspirations of Mamluk patrons. Lotus blossoms are also in evidence during this period, coupled on occasion with peonies and other minor chinoiserie motifs.
37c7ac1e-311b-504e-b4d9-c3f7173a7125.obtention: Purchased by NMS from Bluett and Sons, London, in 1966.
37c7ac1e-311b-504e-b4d9-c3f7173a7125.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
keywords: Thuluth; al-Nasir Nasir al-Din Muhammad ibn Qalawun; calligraphy; inscription
materials: Hammered and incised sheet-brass with remains of silver inlay.

37ddf905-ac01-5a2a-b943-6617e2945431.name: *Rustam at the Fort near Mount Sepand* (folio from a *Shahnama* manuscript)
37ddf905-ac01-5a2a-b943-6617e2945431.short_description: A folio from the manuscript of the *Shahnama* (Book of Kings) epic poem by Ferdowsi tells the story of Rustam's military campaign to Mount Sepand to destroy the impregnable fortress city. The painting illustrates an episode when Rustam and his army approached the walls of a fortress. The warriors resorted to treachery, pretending to be salt merchants. The fortress guards believed the “merchants” and opened the gates to them. According to the content of the episode, Rustam is portrayed as a merchant, without his traditional attributes of a hero: tiger skin, helmet and weapons. Shabby figures of people, types of their headdresses and Chinese-style clouds may suggest the painter’s affiliation with a Shiraz school of miniature.
37ddf905-ac01-5a2a-b943-6617e2945431.dates: Second half of the AD 15th century
37ddf905-ac01-5a2a-b943-6617e2945431.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis and inscription reading by V. Krachkovskaya (publication, 1926, origin and date), A. Ivanov (examination, 1966, date specified, school suggested).
37ddf905-ac01-5a2a-b943-6617e2945431.method_for_provenance: Publication of Vera Krachkovskaya (1927). Old Museum Inventory Register (1925-1946).
37ddf905-ac01-5a2a-b943-6617e2945431.obtention: Purchased by Bohdan and Varvara Khanenko in Paris, 1914, presumably from Fredrik Robert Martin's collection. Donated by Varvara Khanenko in 1918, nationalised by Bolshevik regime in 1919.

37f27206-1cef-5263-96db-efb6c241eb7f.name: Holy Qur’an manuscript
37f27206-1cef-5263-96db-efb6c241eb7f.short_description: This single-volume Qur’an appears to be unfinished judging by the empty title cartouches above the chapters. The ornate opening double page is followed by folios covered with 15 lines of black *naskhi*, enhanced by red detailing, golden verse markers, gilt borders and lavish margin medallions. The calligrapher is \`Ali Shukri, known as Nadherzadeh.
keywords: Naskhi; Ottoman religious manuscripts; religious manuscript

3820f22f-64c5-54c7-80da-20ed18f8af7b.name:
The constellations Andromeda and Pisces  
Folio from a dispersed *Kitab Suwar al-Kawakib* (Images of the Fixed Stars)
3820f22f-64c5-54c7-80da-20ed18f8af7b.short_description: The lady in this saffron-coloured robe and crown-like helmet is a personification of the constellation Andromeda, which was identified by the second-century CE astronomer Ptolemy and continues to be considered a major constellation. With the translation of Ptolemy’s *Almagest* in the court of the ninth-century Caliph al-Ma’mun in Baghdad, astronomers working under the patronage of the Muslim rulers in modern-day Iraq and Iran adopted the Greco-Roman astronomical knowledge and expanded on it from the indigenous Arab (*Anwa’*) and Indian astronomical traditions, in this illustration combining Andromeda with Pisces. The most prominent example of this tradition is 'Images of the Fixed Stars' written by the Iranian astronomer ‘Abd al-Rahman al-Sufi (died 986), which contained two representations of each constellation, one looking up at the constellation from Earth and the other looking down on it from above. Al-Sufi’s work continued to be in broad circulation, and various copies exist in major museum collections.
3820f22f-64c5-54c7-80da-20ed18f8af7b.obtention: Former Prince Saddrudin Aga Khan Collection
keywords: Folio; work-on-paper; works-on-paper; figure; female-figure; constellations; science; space; astronomy; astronomical; stars
materials: Opaque watercolour, ink, gold, and silver on paper

38408d83-304f-5d3b-ba1f-3b4dc4fb028b.name: Curtain for the *minbar* of the Meccan sanctuary, with the name of King Faruq I of Egypt
38408d83-304f-5d3b-ba1f-3b4dc4fb028b.short_description:
This is an exceptionally fine example of the high quality of embroidery produced by the craftsmen of Dar al-Kiswa in the mid 20th century. Very few curtains for the Meccan *minbar* survive, and none of the known examples predates the early 20th century. This is probably one of the last ones made, as Egypt stopped sending curtains for the Meccan *minbar* around that time.  
  
The top panel is inscribed, ‘God Almightly said in his revered book’. The three lines below have *sura al-Jumu‘a* (LXII), verse 9, which appropriately mentions the call to prayer on Fridays. The last panel states that ‘This sitara for the minbar of the sacred House of God was ordered by him who depends on God, the king of Egypt Faruq I, may God grant him succor, in the year 1365’.
38408d83-304f-5d3b-ba1f-3b4dc4fb028b.type: Textile; Mecca *minbar* curtain; *sitara*; *kiswa*; Dar al-Kiswa; wire embroidery
38408d83-304f-5d3b-ba1f-3b4dc4fb028b.holder: Khalili Family Trust – Hajj and the Arts of Pilgrimage Collection
38408d83-304f-5d3b-ba1f-3b4dc4fb028b.method_for_datation: The date is embroidered on the curtain.

384dcfe8-dbaa-5658-9b1b-12f3a00fa9a4.name: Frieze tile
384dcfe8-dbaa-5658-9b1b-12f3a00fa9a4.short_description: The tile modelled in the form of a rectangle (almost a square) is adorned with a large cobalt-blue inscription in Persian standing out against a background of dense lustre-painted decor of floral curls, leaves, arabesques, birds and hares. At the top runs a border of relief palmette-patterned band. The tile once formed a part of a gorgeous frieze on walls of some early 14th century Ilkhanid palace. The art of lustre painting on ceramics was mastered by Iranian potters of Kashan in late 12th century. The technique involved application of metal-based pigment over already glazed and fired vessel.

389ca57a-de31-5831-9a59-bb851adbe95e.short_description: Umar is one of the spies (*Ayyar*), who support the continuous fights of Hamza.

38bee4ad-cee4-5177-b8e7-dff8c1f903a8.name: Inscribed reed floor mat
38bee4ad-cee4-5177-b8e7-dff8c1f903a8.short_description: A fine floor mat, woven on the loom, with sparse decoration, self-patterned borders with interlocking lozenge pattern and pairs of brown brocaded bands. The inscriptions, written in a *kufic* script, have benedictory content with details about the work's creation, as naming *Tabariya* the place of production. Such floor coverings were made for domestic and religious interiors and were possibly used during prayers.
keywords: Floor mat; Kufic; Prayers; Tabby weave
materials: Tabby weave with brocaded decoration, hemp and bast fibre

38c49d86-1f30-5ebd-a391-a533a976b571.name: Bowl.
38c49d86-1f30-5ebd-a391-a533a976b571.description: A deep-sided brass bowl engraved and inlaid with silver; the bottom has been hammered (repoussé) into a radiating palmette design. The major element of the bowl's decoration are the large cartouches which carry majestic calligraphic inscriptions reading, 'Glory to our lord, the Sultan, the just ruler, the holy warrior, the guardian of the frontiers, the aided [by God], the victorious, sultan of Islam and the Muslims, al-Malik al-Ashraf Abu'l-Nasr Qaytbay'. Smaller roundels between these cartouches also praise Qaytbay and add the phrase 'may his victory be glorious', implying that he is still alive. It seems likely that this exquisite bowl was made as a basin for hand-washing for the personal use of Sultan Qaytbay. The style and quality of the decoration are characteristic of the revival of the arts under the relatively peaceful and prosperous reign of Qaytbay.
38c49d86-1f30-5ebd-a391-a533a976b571.short_description: A deep-sided brass bowl, hammered and engraved with decoration including the name and titles of Sultan Qaytbay. Since the inscriptions imply that he is still alive, the bowl may well have been made for his personal use as a hand-washing basin.
38c49d86-1f30-5ebd-a391-a533a976b571.method_for_datation: The inscription names Sultan Qaytbay and implies that he is still ruling ('may his victory be glorious'). Thus the bowl is dated to his reign between 872–901 / 1468–96.
38c49d86-1f30-5ebd-a391-a533a976b571.method_for_provenance: Cairo was the Mamluk capital and thus the likeliest place that an object of such quality would have been made.
38c49d86-1f30-5ebd-a391-a533a976b571.bibliography: Stanley, T., with Rosser-Owen, M. and Vernoit, S., Palace and Mosque: Islamic Art from the Middle East, London, 2004, p.56, p.98, p.134 and plate 112.
38c49d86-1f30-5ebd-a391-a533a976b571.author: Barry Wood
keywords: floral decoration; water; calligraphy; inscription
materials: Inlaid brass.

38e4904d-c574-52b6-a1e1-5202c0c6e8ba.name: Pilgrimage certificate
38e4904d-c574-52b6-a1e1-5202c0c6e8ba.short_description: This certificate was made for a pilgrim named Sayyid Yusuf bin Sayyid Shihab al-Din Mawara al-Nahri for his ‘umra, illustrating significant locations in Mecca, Medina, and other religious locations. Beside these illustrations are inscriptions from the Quran and texts written in Arabic and Persian related to pilgrimage, with the name of the pilgrim and his six witnesses featured at the end. Pilgrimage certificates are considered legal documents acquired by the pilgrim at the end of the journey.

39548f51-03b2-558c-9e39-2e9427feaf5c.name: Basin.
39548f51-03b2-558c-9e39-2e9427feaf5c.description: A large marble fountain-basin. The basin is basically a large hemisphere supported on a short foot and topped with a 12-sided rim, one side of which is blank and another of which has a section cut out to support the channel which brought water. Eleven of the sides carry an inscription giving the name and titles of the Ayyubid governor of Hama, al-Malik al-Mansur Muhammad ibn al-Muzaffar Mahmud ibn Muhammad ibn ‘Umar ibn Shahanshah ibn ‘Ayyub (also known by his shorter title of Mansur II Muhammad), who ruled from AH 641–83 / AD 1244–84. The exterior of the basin is carved with a bold design of two interlacing arabesque designs, each repeated six times in alternation and set off against a background of smaller floral decoration. Such a fine basin would probably have been placed in a prominent public mosque to serve the needs of congregants and to proclaim the glory of the ruler.
39548f51-03b2-558c-9e39-2e9427feaf5c.short_description: A large marble basin for ablutions, carved on the exterior with prominent interlacing arabesque designs. The 12-sided rim is inscribed with the name and titles of the patron, the governor of Hama. Thus the basin served both the ritual needs of the community and the governor’s public image.
39548f51-03b2-558c-9e39-2e9427feaf5c.method_for_provenance: The basin is inscribed with the name and titles of the Ayyubid governor in whose honour this object was made (see description above).
39548f51-03b2-558c-9e39-2e9427feaf5c.bibliography: Ayers, J., Oriental Art in the Victoria and Albert Museum, London, 1983, p.111.
39548f51-03b2-558c-9e39-2e9427feaf5c.author: Barry Wood
keywords: floral decoration; religious objects; water; inscription
materials: Carved marble.

39ae7c13-54bb-57fc-9069-e9898933a6cc.name: Fragment of marble funerary stele with Arabic inscription in *kufic* characters.
39ae7c13-54bb-57fc-9069-e9898933a6cc.description: Fragment of the top right corner of a rectangular marble slab. The inscription ran along the edge of the slab, delimited by an upper and a lower fillet, according to V. Grassi, who recently published the inscription. Comparison with similar stelae from Malta suggest that the lower part of this piece is missing. The inscribed area would have been crowned by a horseshoe arch, evoking the *mihrab* niche. The space between the extrados of the arch and the top right corner of the stele (the only part to have survived) is decorated with a three-petal flower and a central almond motif similar to that of stele no.1, but in a more divided and schematic style. The *kufic* characters are adapted to this style and can be attributed to the first half of the AH 5th / AD 11th century. The inscription in the inscribed area has been lost, but some of the one that ran around the sides has survived (ascending section on the right-hand side and the top section) which must have reproduced a passage from the Qur’an (Sura 3 verse 185) often used in sepulchral inscriptions: ‘…then you receive your recompense on the Day of Resurrection …’.
39ae7c13-54bb-57fc-9069-e9898933a6cc.short_description: Fragment of funerary stele. Stelae usually contain inscriptions of typical formulas taken from the Qur’an, sometimes accompanied by professions of the faith, devotion and virtues of the deceased.
39ae7c13-54bb-57fc-9069-e9898933a6cc.dates: First half of the Hegira 5th / AD 11th century.
39ae7c13-54bb-57fc-9069-e9898933a6cc.dimensions: Max. height 20 cm, max. width 16 cm, depth 6.3 cm.
39ae7c13-54bb-57fc-9069-e9898933a6cc.method_for_datation: On the basis of the style of the characters and the decoration.
39ae7c13-54bb-57fc-9069-e9898933a6cc.method_for_provenance: It was one of ten inscriptions found in the Di Ferro collection, first given to the Fardelliana Library and then to the Pepoli Museum. In this case, however, it is not possible to show that it comes from Trapani; indeed comparisons take it away from Sicily, to Malta.
39ae7c13-54bb-57fc-9069-e9898933a6cc.obtention: Transferred from the Fardelliana Library in Trapani.

3a0d9391-5934-5a05-a66d-5b570463ddec.name: Coin.
3a0d9391-5934-5a05-a66d-5b570463ddec.description:
The object is an Islamic gold *dinar* of the Almoravid Amir Ali bin Yusuf (r. AH 500–37 / AD 1106–43). The inscription within the obverse central field consists of several Qur'anic quotations and the name of the ruler: 'There is no deity but God alone (XLVII, 19). He has no peer (VI, 163). Muhammad is God's apostle (XLVIII, 29). Commander of the Muslims, Ali bin Yusuf.' The obverse circular legend is also a quotation from the Qur’an: 'He who chooses a religion other than Islam, it will not be accepted from him and in the world to come he will surely be among the losers (III, 85).'  
The reverse circular legend contains the place and date: 'In the name of God! This gold coin was struck in Ishbiliya in the year five hundred and sixteen.' The inscription of the reverse central field refers to the Abbasid caliph in Baghdad, calling him Imam ‘Abdallah, who was al-Mustarshid (r. AH 512–29/ AD 1118–35) at that time.
3a0d9391-5934-5a05-a66d-5b570463ddec.short_description: Islamic gold *dinar* of the Almoravid Amir ‘Ali bin Yusuf. The inscriptions consist of Qur’anic quotations and the name of the amir. The reverse circular legend refers to the place and the date where and when the coin was struck: in Ishbiliya in the year AH 516 / AD 1123.
3a0d9391-5934-5a05-a66d-5b570463ddec.method_for_datation: The coin is dated on the reverse.
3a0d9391-5934-5a05-a66d-5b570463ddec.method_for_provenance: The inscription on the reverse names the place Ishbiliya (Seville).
3a0d9391-5934-5a05-a66d-5b570463ddec.obtention: This coin was part of a treasure found in Gotland, in the parish of Visby, Sweden, and allotted to the museum in 1844.

3a8f4926-8bbd-5e0d-af9c-239cc5185d26.name: Marble inscription panel.
3a8f4926-8bbd-5e0d-af9c-239cc5185d26.description:
A large, marble inscription panel produced to mark the foundation of the trench around the fortification wall of the old city of Jerusalem during the Ayyubid period. Produced four years after the Battle of Hattin, the panel was made with the aim that it would protect the city from new incursions launched by the Crusaders. Al-Asfahsalar Ali bin Ahmad al-Hikkari (d. AH 588 / AD 1192) supervised the digging of the trench.  
It is probable that the inscription panel was taken to the Haram al-Sharif while repairs to the city walls were being carried out during the reign of the Ottoman Sultan, Sulayman al-Qanuni (known in the West as Sulayman the Magnificent; r. AH 926–74 / AD 1520–66). The inscription is laid out in six lines of cursive Ayyubid *naskhi* script carved in high relief. The text offers an insight into the period of Salah al-Din Ayyubi (Saladin), founder of the Ayyubid Dynasty, and the defensive techniques employed in order to protect the city from the Crusaders, such as the ditch that was excavated around the citadel following the successful liberation of the city. The inscription reads as follows:  
“In the Name of God the most Beneficent, the most Merciful  
And Blessings be upon Muhammad, the Prophet and his household.  
The order to build this and to dig the trench was given by our master, the Victorious Sovereign, the Salvation of this world and religion, Sultan of Islam and the Muslims,  
Servant of the two holy sanctuaries and this holy abode, Abu al-Muzaffar Yusuf bin Ayyub,  
Reviver of the State, Commander of the Faithful, May God lengthen his days and support his star in the days of the great Amir, al-Asfahasalar Sayf al-Din Ali bin Ahmad, may God strengthen him in AH 587 \[c. 1191\]”.
3a8f4926-8bbd-5e0d-af9c-239cc5185d26.short_description: After Salah al-Din Ayyubi (Saladin) reconquered Jerusalem from the Crusaders, he renovated its citadel and dug a trench to improve the city’s defences against fresh attack from the Crusaders. This inscription affirms these works and mentions the sultan and a commander of his troops. The panel is now in the plaza of the Dome of the Rock.
3a8f4926-8bbd-5e0d-af9c-239cc5185d26.holder: Islamic Museum, al-Aqsa Mosque / Al-Haram al-Sharif.
3a8f4926-8bbd-5e0d-af9c-239cc5185d26.initial_owner: Sultan Salah al-Din Ayyubi (r. AH 564–89 / AD 1169–93).
3a8f4926-8bbd-5e0d-af9c-239cc5185d26.dimensions: Length 190 cm, width 100 cm, depth 6 cm.
3a8f4926-8bbd-5e0d-af9c-239cc5185d26.method_for_datation: The panel bears a reliable date.
3a8f4926-8bbd-5e0d-af9c-239cc5185d26.method_for_provenance: Jerusalem was narrowed down as the place of production supported by the inscription on the panel.
3a8f4926-8bbd-5e0d-af9c-239cc5185d26.obtention: The piece was found at the Dome of Yusuf Agha on southern side of the plaza of the Dome of the Rock, and then transferred to the Islamic Museum.
