materials: Marble; carved.

54f861aa-1d28-5c1b-b3c3-07e65ff10862.name: 'Picture of the Tents of the Turks'. Photographer: H. A. Mirza & Sons
54f861aa-1d28-5c1b-b3c3-07e65ff10862.description:
This image shows the tents of the Ottoman Turkish troops at their camp at Medina. Despite the apparently secular nature of the subject, and the fact that the camp does not depict a stopping-off point on the hadj, the laudatory poetry and prose makes clear the relevance of the image to the experience of the hadj – that is, that the Turks, as ‘military people of the highest rank’ serve Islam by defending and enabling the passage to Mecca and Medina for other Muslims.  
  
As with the other photographs in this album (Photo 174/1-13), whose subjects are architectural and landscape, the figures are not the subject of the image. However, a detailed examination of the image shows the soldiers going about their day-to-day activities, such as cooking and eating. The method by which the ground would have been prepared before a tent was erected is indicated by the empty low circular foundation in the lower left corner of the image. In the distance, in the right-hand background of the image, beyond the dry-stone wall delineating the camp, palm groves and permanent dwellings can be identified.
54f861aa-1d28-5c1b-b3c3-07e65ff10862.dimensions: Mount (external): 35 x 44,6 cm; Mount (internal): 20,2 x 27,3 cm [landscape]
keywords: Travel; Hijaz; Medina; Mecca
materials: Mottled blue-tinted window mount, card, gelatin silver print, indigo ink (printed), red ink (hand-painted)

55152a48-4ea9-5d88-b3d1-c71ba5a5a61a.name: *Panj Ganj* (‘Five Treasures’) of Jami
55152a48-4ea9-5d88-b3d1-c71ba5a5a61a.short_description: The *Panj Ganj* (‘Five Treasures’) is a collection of five poems written by the Persian poet ‘Abd al-Rahman Jami‘ (d. AD 1492). The manuscript was produced in Iran but was not finished until it ended up in India, in the possession of ‘Abd al-Rahim, commander-in-chief of the Mughal army for both Akbar and Jahangir. The specific manner in which the text has been laid out results in three small triangular spaces on each page. ‘Abd al-Rahim’s artists completed the decoration of the manuscript by filling these spaces with decoration, usually figures of animals and birds (several examples from various folios are included here). They also added new, boldly decorated margins to each folio and added a painting on the final, colophon page of the manuscript.
55152a48-4ea9-5d88-b3d1-c71ba5a5a61a.dates:
Calligraphy: Hegira 926 / AD 1520  
Painting and illumination: Hegira 1015 / AD 1606-07

552161b5-1f28-593b-b0d4-243b48261076.name: Perfume sprinkler '*qumqum*'
552161b5-1f28-593b-b0d4-243b48261076.short_description:
The body of this perfume flask or sprinkler was created by flattening a blown glass ball, from which a thin long neck was then drawn. On both sides of the body there are large relief inscriptions in Arabic, applied in blue enamel on a gold background: “The sovereign is fair, glory to his victory”. The inscriptions are bordered with an ornament of green trefoils.  
The shape of the vessel is believed to have originated in Syria in the 12th century. The 13th and 14th centuries witnessed flourishing of new décor, namely enamelling and gilding. As leading centres historians mention Aleppo and Damascus.  
At the same time, the tradition of using fragrances and aromatic substances as well as preserving them in glass vessels came to the Islamic world long before - from the Late Antiquity.  
In medieval Islamic culture, substances such as musk, amber, sandalwood or aloe were used not only as perfume but also as culinary ingredients, medicines and aphrodisiacs. In terms of concentration and value, these substances formed the basis of a mixture when dissolved in water in similar flasks or sprinklers.  
Although the sprinkler could contain a whole spectrum of different substances, most likely it was rose water. Obviously, the invention of Islamic civilization, rose water was made by heating fresh rose petals in a water bath, resulting in aromatic vapor condensing. In addition to being used in gastronomy, rose water was also used at certain stages in the process of serving and consuming food. For example, when guests were finishing their meal, they were offered to wash their hands and mouths with saline, flavoured with rose water. Or servants might walk around guests spraying their clothes with refreshing aromatic liquid.

55612a5e-2511-58ed-bb67-272440566fbb.name: Imperial decree (*Ferman*)
55612a5e-2511-58ed-bb67-272440566fbb.description:
This imperial edict (*ferman*), bearing the hand-drawn *tughra* (imperial monogram) of Sultan Abdülmecid, concerns the schedule of water distribution days among the villages of Eşeközü hamlet in the Kayseri district.  
The *ferman* is black in color and originates from the Kayseri region.

5599db05-ed21-5635-bc98-8d9bcd6907e1.name:
Album page  
Front, Emperor Jahangir at the *jharoka* window  
Back, calligraphy
5599db05-ed21-5635-bc98-8d9bcd6907e1.short_description: This double-sided page, intended for an album, is likely the product of two masters: Abu‘l-Hasan, one of the most famous artists of the Mughal court, and Muhammad Husayn al-Kashmiri, honoured by the emperor Akbar (r. 1556–1605) with the title of 'Zarin Qalam' (Golden Pen). \[1\] The painting depicts Emperor Jahangir (r. 1605–27) in a balcony window (called a *jharoka*) and looking down to Agra Fort. His top-ranking officials stand on the marble terrace just below him. Beneath the terrace, lower-ranking officials and the public gather in a courtyard. Near the red canopy at the left is suspended a golden chain with golden bells.
5599db05-ed21-5635-bc98-8d9bcd6907e1.obtention: Former Prince Saddrudin Aga Khan Collection

55d49521-1b28-5354-afd2-875a445cde61.name: Fly Whisk
55d49521-1b28-5354-afd2-875a445cde61.short_description:
This conical, tubular object is made of a cast copper alloy. It combines various metalworking techniques. Engraved bands with copper and silver inlaid inscriptions mark off the top and the bottom end. The *naskhi* script has elongated ends bearing faces engraved into the silver inlay. Openwork characterizes the main section of the shaft. Representations of 12 animals arranged in four rows of three animals of a kind on a background of scroll tendrils. The bottom is surrounded by the representation of a sitting dove in profile. On the next level we see a griffin, followed by a flying falcon, topped by a hunting animal, probably a cheetah attacking an ibex. Apart from the griffin, which can be interpreted as a symbol of sovereignty, the animals belong to the sphere of the royal hunt and courtly pastimes.  
The fragile openwork design also suggests that the object was not meant to be handled with physical force but rather served as a ceremonial device. The conical shape is suitable to hold a bundle of peacock or ostrich feathers and to serve as a handle for a fly whisk. Apart from their practical use, fly whisks belonged to the iconography of the kings of ancient Persia, as shown on reliefs of the palace of Xerxes in Persepolis. Throughout Islamic times, flabella were used in royal ceremonial rites. Here, especially during official ceremonies, an attendant was standing behind the ruler to fan fresh air and keep flies away.
55d49521-1b28-5354-afd2-875a445cde61.holder: University Museum of Islamic Art | The Bumiller Collection
55d49521-1b28-5354-afd2-875a445cde61.method_for_datation: The casting technique with openwork is typical of eleventh- to twelfth-century bronzes from Khorasan, such as incense-burner, lampstands and oil lamps.
55d49521-1b28-5354-afd2-875a445cde61.method_for_provenance: The design of the epigraphic bands shows characteristic features of Khurasanian metalwork.
55d49521-1b28-5354-afd2-875a445cde61.bibliography: Korn, Lorenz, “A Tubular Bronze Object from Eastern Iran”, in V. Porter and M. Rosser-Owen (eds), *Metalwork and Material Culture in the Islamic World: Art, Craft and Text*, Essays presented to James W. Allan, London: I.B. Tauris, 2012: 143-154.

keywords: Metalwork; Ceremonial device
materials: Bronze caste, engraved, inlaid, openwork

566f599e-0817-50e5-8d87-c71e445f657b.name: Qur’an fragment
566f599e-0817-50e5-8d87-c71e445f657b.short_description: This Qur’an fragment was copied in 12th-century Iran or Iraq and its text includes sura 15, 44, 16:1-85, which is penned in monumental and geometric-ornamental angular (*kufic*) script in five lines per page. This is fully vocalised in red and blue with diacritical marks appearing in the form of golden dots. Individual verses are separated by gold rosettes with blue dots containing *kufic* counting letters. The circular medallions in the margins contain the verse count written and ornamented in gold, with a blue frame and ray-like extensions.
566f599e-0817-50e5-8d87-c71e445f657b.dimensions: 248 x 190mm (185 x 120mm). ff. I, II*, 36 folios.
566f599e-0817-50e5-8d87-c71e445f657b.method_for_provenance: On fol. 1a, the owner's note by Darwish Muhammad Saza'i (or Sazali or Magali?) b. Ahmad Rifaat is visible. A restoration note of the Austrian National Library can be dated to 1931.
566f599e-0817-50e5-8d87-c71e445f657b.bibliography: Duda, Dorothea, *Islamische Handschriften II. Persische Handschriften, Die illuminierten Handschriften und Inkunabeln der Österreichischen Nationalbibliothek*, vol. 5, Vienna: Verlag der Österreichischen Akademie der Wissenschaften, 1992: 231-233.
566f599e-0817-50e5-8d87-c71e445f657b.binding_desc: This black leather flap binding has a differing front and back cover. Both covers contain borders across the edges of the cover as well as a braided band and stylised leafy vine in blind print. However, the front doublures are made of European marbled paper while the back is made of red leather. The binding was probably assembled and restored in Europe in the 20th century from older oriental pieces.

567ac179-c89c-5f43-a912-af9c71a221ec.name: Collection of Mughal miniatures
567ac179-c89c-5f43-a912-af9c71a221ec.short_description:
This album contains 70 miniature paintings realised using the courtly Mughal style, arranged on 66 folios. As the miniatures were composed by different artists they vary greatly in size and execution. It is assumed that these miniatures constituted a part of a large collection of miniatures that Maria Theresia had purchased to decorate the so-called "Millionenzimmer" (Millions Room), one of her private reception rooms in Schönbrunn Palace. Most likely, only part of the overall collection was used for the decoration resulting in the remaining miniatures then being gathered into two albums, Min. 44 and this one, Min 64. This thesis is supported by the contemporaneous renovations of the Millions Room, which we know for a fact that Maria Teresia undertook around the 1760's AD, and the arrival of the two albums into the collection of the Imperial Court Library in 1762 AD.  
The themes of the miniatures range from intricate courtly portraits and illustrations of Persian epics to classical scenes from Hindu-mythology.
567ac179-c89c-5f43-a912-af9c71a221ec.dates: 10th to 11th century AH / 17th to 18th cenutry AD
567ac179-c89c-5f43-a912-af9c71a221ec.method_for_datation: The date and origins of the miniatures were establish based on the artistic style of the paintings.
567ac179-c89c-5f43-a912-af9c71a221ec.method_for_provenance: There are many Dutch marginalia throughout the album, mainly providing the titles of miniatures. It is likely that the miniatures in this album came to Amsterdam through the Dutch East India Company, from where they made their way to Vienna.
567ac179-c89c-5f43-a912-af9c71a221ec.obtention: A written record of the album appears in the card catalogue of the Imperial Court Library in the 19th century. Despite this, there is no information on how the miniatures and the album were obtained initially. It appears to have entered the collection at the same time as a similar album of Mughal miniatures (Min. 44), around 1762 AD.

5691ad24-fe0c-597d-8ca1-206be34877d4.name: Panel of tiles.
5691ad24-fe0c-597d-8ca1-206be34877d4.description:
A comprehensive group of ceramic tile panels in the form of a pointed arch. Apple-green is used for the background of the peripheral panels while a dark-blue dominates the central panels. Both the floral ornamentation and the calligraphic inscriptions are coloured white and carefully stencilled in black. The technique used to apply the colours is underglaze painting.  
These fine Damascene Ottoman tiles were found in the tomb chamber of the Mustafa Lala Pasha mosque, located above the window that overlooks the cemetery. The three lines of *thuluth* script translate as follows:  
(1) Protector  
(2) May the mercy of the Lord be upon him in every moment  
(3) Everything is mortal except for the countenance of God, He has the power of rule, to Him you will all return.  
The year AH 998 / AD 1590 was written in numerals in two locations between these lines. The spaces surrounding the inscription, as well as the space between the words, are filled with finely executed stylised vegetal motifs. The depiction of multiple flower varieties swaying in the breeze recalls the extent to which Chinese styles influenced the repertoire of Islamic ceramics. The choice of *thuluth* script for the calligraphy is a favoured ornamental script in tile work because of its monumental letter proportions and its curvaceous painterly quality.
5691ad24-fe0c-597d-8ca1-206be34877d4.short_description: Ottoman style underglaze painted tiles made in Damascus display the painterly quality of *thuluth* calligraphy on a background of spiralling floral motifs.
5691ad24-fe0c-597d-8ca1-206be34877d4.initial_owner: Probably a governor of Damascus during the reign of Sultan Murad III (r. AH 981–1003 / AD 1574–95).
5691ad24-fe0c-597d-8ca1-206be34877d4.method_for_datation: The inscription on the panel includes the date of its completion, 998 (1590).
5691ad24-fe0c-597d-8ca1-206be34877d4.method_for_provenance: The underglaze technique is consistent with local Syrian techniques of ceramics manufacture and distinctive from the Ottoman overglaze method. During this period, Damascus was a flourishing tile-production centre. It is therefore likely that the tiles were produced in Damascus.
5691ad24-fe0c-597d-8ca1-206be34877d4.provenance: Mosque of Mustafa Lala Pasha, Damascus, Syria.
5691ad24-fe0c-597d-8ca1-206be34877d4.obtention: The tile panels entered the Museum in 1919 when the mosque in which these tiles were originally located was demolished to make room for the Suq al-Hal, the Cardamom Market.

56be57e8-2f07-5969-a236-a5ddc30a31cd.name: Lamp.
56be57e8-2f07-5969-a236-a5ddc30a31cd.description:
Bronze lamp consisting of various elements supported by a central rod. First, four spherical parts arranged in ascending order of size with a central fretwork border and *naskhi* inscription. Next, an eight-sided prismatic element with vegetal fretwork decoration. The lamp is completed by a truncated pyramid in the shape of a four-sided bell, decorated with plant motifs and two inscribed cartouches, one at the top and one at the bottom, with the emblem of Muhammad III: 'There is no conqueror but God. The Most Exalted'. There is another inscription in the bronze on the border, with a series and blessings and titles, as well as the date of manufacture.  
There is a convincing hypothesis as to the placement of the holders for the lights: the lamp arrived at the Museum with its hinged arms badly damaged; these arms would open out around the truncated pyramid section into a circle, some of which has survived. There were two arms per side, making a total of 16 arms and between 48 and 64 glasses that produced light without being obscured by the body of the object.  
We know that the Royal Alhambra Mosque was constructed at the behest of Muhammad III, and therefore the lamp would have hung in the central nave before the *mihrab* (prayer niche), the appropriate place for an object bearing the sovereign's emblem. It is logical to assume that the founding sovereign would have also provided the fixtures.
56be57e8-2f07-5969-a236-a5ddc30a31cd.short_description: A masterpiece of Andalusian metalwork for the exquisite fretwork decoration on the body, this lamp was commissioned by Muhammad III for the mosque in the Alhambra, according to its inscription. The body still bears the hooks for the arms that would have held the glass bowls for the lights.
56be57e8-2f07-5969-a236-a5ddc30a31cd.initial_owner: Following the conquest of Granada in AH 898 / AD 1492, the lamp was removed from its fixing and taken to Oran. Eventually it became part of the collection of Cardinal Cisneros, who deposited it with San Ildefonso College in Alcala de Henares, from where it passed to the University.
56be57e8-2f07-5969-a236-a5ddc30a31cd.dimensions: Total height 230 cm, height of truncated pyramid 54 cm, diameter 79 cm.
56be57e8-2f07-5969-a236-a5ddc30a31cd.method_for_datation: The lower edge of the lamp bears a *naskhi* inscription with the year 705 / 1305.
56be57e8-2f07-5969-a236-a5ddc30a31cd.method_for_provenance: Despite the damage to the lower part of the lamp, the titles that appear in the inscription around the edge allow us to attribute it to Muhammad III (r. 702–9 / 1302–9), who would have commissioned it for the Alhambra mosque.
56be57e8-2f07-5969-a236-a5ddc30a31cd.provenance: Mosque of the Alhambra, Granada, Spain.
56be57e8-2f07-5969-a236-a5ddc30a31cd.obtention: The piece was assigned to the National Archaeological Museum as part of the organisation of the State collection on 20 March 1868.

5702c937-55b7-5f65-adc4-2d6ddc8a7f83.name: *Dinar* (gold coin).
5702c937-55b7-5f65-adc4-2d6ddc8a7f83.description:
The *dinar* is one of the types of coins that Muslims circulated. It was, by definition, made from gold and was the type of coin with the highest value in compared to the *dirham*, which was made of silver, and the *fils*, which was made of copper. It weighed about four grams.  
This piece is an Ayyubid *dinar* of the Fatimid type, meaning that the inscription is arranged in concentric circles around the middle. This style was first used by the Fatimids in the AH 4th / AD 10th century and is very different from the *kufic* style used previously, in which the text is distributed between one circle around the rim and three or four horizontal lines in the centre. The choice on the part of the Shi'a Fatimid dynasty to make such a radical change can be seen as an attempt to differentiate themselves from the Sunni Umayyad, Abbasid and Central Asian rulers who used the *kufic* style before them. Subsequent rulers, like Salah al-Din, also chose to use this design.  
This coin is attributed to the reigns of 'Abbasid Caliph al-Mustadi' (r. AH 566–75 / AD 1170–80) and the Ayyubid ruler Saladin. It was minted in Cairo in AH 574 / AD 1178. An Arabic inscription in *naskhi* script is recorded on both of its faces, and may be translated as follows:  
Obverse  
Band 1 – “In the name of God, the Merciful and Compassionate, this *dinar* was minted in Cairo in the year five hundred seventy-four”  
Band 2 – “There is no God except God, who is without partner. Abu Muhammad” (where Abu Muhammad indicates the Abbasid Caliph al-Mustadi).  
Band 3 – “al-Mustadi' bi-amr Allah, Commander of the Faithful”  
Band 4 – “al-Imam al-Hasan”  
Reverse  
Band 1 – “Muhammad the Messenger of God has been sent with guidance and the religion of truth, to proclaim to all religion”  
Band 2 – “even if the polytheists despise it. May God bless him \[the Prophet Muhammad\] and his family”  
Band 3 – “al-Malik 'al al-Nasir 'Alim”  
Band 4 – “Yusuf bin Ayyub”.
5702c937-55b7-5f65-adc4-2d6ddc8a7f83.short_description: This gold coin, known as a *dinar*, was minted by the Ayyubids in Cairo following a Fatimid style with inscriptions arranged in three concentric circles around the centre.
5702c937-55b7-5f65-adc4-2d6ddc8a7f83.initial_owner: Al-Malik al-Nasir Salah al-Din Yusuf bin Ayyub (Saladin, r. AH 569–89 / AD 1174–93).
5702c937-55b7-5f65-adc4-2d6ddc8a7f83.method_for_datation: The inscription on the coin specifies the date of minting as 574 (1178).
5702c937-55b7-5f65-adc4-2d6ddc8a7f83.method_for_provenance: The inscription on the coin states that it was minted in Cairo, Egypt.
5702c937-55b7-5f65-adc4-2d6ddc8a7f83.obtention: The coin was confiscated by the security forces and registered at the Museum in 1992.
5702c937-55b7-5f65-adc4-2d6ddc8a7f83.bibliography: Delpont, E. (ed), *L'Orient de Saladin: l'art des Ayyoubides*, Paris, 2001, p.36.
5702c937-55b7-5f65-adc4-2d6ddc8a7f83.author: Mona al-Moadin
keywords: Coin; gold; Cairo; Damascus; coinage; dinar; Saladin; Caliph al-Mustadi'; numismatics; Salah al-Din
materials: Minted gold.

576b29fe-1757-5d8f-b8d8-aa0a86493db6.name: Carpet
576b29fe-1757-5d8f-b8d8-aa0a86493db6.description:
Carpet of rectangular format with a continuous field decoration.  
Field: On a dark blue background, two zigzagging white parallel ribbons, depicting alternating spaces, which contain stars separated by rhombuses. The different colours of these elements show diagonal bands, producing a false transverse decoration effect.  
Border: Composed of multiple borders. The long sides alternate four narrow and wide borders with motifs similar to the field as well as the decoration of other carpets of this same series. The short sides contain a very wide border, with pseudo-*kufic* writing of a purely aesthetic nature, including similar motifs. The perimeter is topped by a single border with a double zigzag motif in the same colours as the field.  
The knots consist of wool in navy blue, yellow, red, white and brown.  
The border is composed of multiple borders, something characteristic of a series identified as "carpets of a honeycomb field and multiple borders", as Sánchez Ferrer calls them. This series is named by some scholars as a heraldic series or "of the Admirals", since in some of the preserved specimens there are heraldic motifs of various aristocratic families inserted in the field.  
The decoration of this carpet is in the Mudejar style.  
Whilst the carpet does not retain its original size, decoratively speaking, it has been very well reconstructed.

576b29fe-1757-5d8f-b8d8-aa0a86493db6.method_for_provenance: Through the stylistic and technical analysis of the piece.

577527f6-207f-54b6-8eee-af77d7cc4100.name:
Shah Faridun spurning the peace envoys of Salm and Tur  
Folio detached from a *Shahnameh* (Book of Kings) by Abu’l-Qasim Firdausi (d. 1010)
577527f6-207f-54b6-8eee-af77d7cc4100.short_description: Recounting the legendary history of Iran’s shahs (kings) up to the Arab conquest in 642 AD and the country’s adoption of Islam, Firdausi’s epic poem the *Shahnameh* (Book of Kings), completed in 1010, inspired many illustrated copies. The present folio depicting Shah Faridun spurning the peace envoys of Salm and Tur was detached from a copy that is known as the “Big Head” *Shahnameh*. This name refers to the characteristic feature of the majority of its paintings: the large heads of its human figures.
577527f6-207f-54b6-8eee-af77d7cc4100.obtention: Former Prince Saddrudin Aga Khan Collection

materials: Opaque watercolour, gold and ink on paper

57952ce7-c1d9-5593-a21a-cd6480d6eec9.name: Illuminated Qur’an manuscript
57952ce7-c1d9-5593-a21a-cd6480d6eec9.short_description: 19th-century Qur’an manuscripts produced in Istanbul and the Ottoman Empire continued many Islamic art traditions, but could not entirely escape the increasing taste for Western aesthetics. The quality of this Qur’an manuscript suggests that it might have been executed for a member of the Imperial household. The radiant opening double-page shows two delicate cartouches with ‘Al Fatiha’ and the beginning of ‘Al Baqara’ set into a majestic framework of gilt floral arabesque cartouches. The main body of the text is executed in finest black naskh, 15 lines to the page, the sura headings written in white riqa' on a solid golden ground. Beyond the gold margins, delicated medallions mark important subdivisions in the text. The last double page shows the end of sura 113 and sura 114 on the right and the dedication page on the left. Both texts are embedded in rectangular panels accentuated with richly gilt and blue ornamentation. Beyond, the entire page is covered with delicate sprays and leaves painted in solid gold.

57952ce7-c1d9-5593-a21a-cd6480d6eec9.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
keywords: sura; riqa'
materials: European paper, black ink, pigments, gilding, pasteboard, leather

580df60c-19a7-5ac3-bbe6-d83553b95b42.name: *Bustan* of Sa'di
580df60c-19a7-5ac3-bbe6-d83553b95b42.short_description: These folios are from a copy of the *Bustan* (‘Orchard’), a didactic poem consisting of moralizing stories and anecdotes written in the mid thirteenth century by the Persian poet Sa‘di. The manuscript was produced in Iran in 1649 for the ruler of Bukhara, ‘Abd al-Aziz ibn Nasr Muhammad. However, the decorations that fill the margins of almost every page may have been added later. Oddly, they are positioned perpendicular to the text and none appear to relate to the text in any way. Some are scenes of animals (often mythical Chinese creatures) set amongst vegetation, while other are scenes of sensitively rendered people engaged in various activities, such as purchasing goods at a market.
keywords: illustration; miniature painting; calligraphy; script; illumination; border decoration; simurgh; imaginary animal; zoomorphic imagery; Chinese motifs
materials: Coloured pigments and gold on paper

58b704d2-eb03-5537-a131-1e943e19c77a.name: First Small *Shahnama*
58b704d2-eb03-5537-a131-1e943e19c77a.short_description: The poet Firdausi completed the writing of his *Shahnama* (‘Book of Kings’) in AD 1010. It is considered the national epic of Iran and in some sixty-thousand verses relates the tales of the heroes and kings of Iran, from the dawn of time until the Islamic conquest of the country in the mid seventh century. These folios belong to one of three manuscripts known collectively as the Small *Shahnama*s. None are dated, but they are generally thought to have been produced in about AD 1300, making them the earliest illustrated *Shahnama* manuscripts in existence. (Three thirteenth-century, unillustrated *Shahnama*s also exist.) There are, however, earlier objects (mainly ceramics) decorated with scenes from the various stories that make up the *Shahnama*.
keywords: illustration; miniature painting; calligraphy; script; illumination
materials: Coloured pigments and gold on paper

5956a116-f2da-52fd-9a46-aa5a243e3598.name: Coin (*dinar*).
5956a116-f2da-52fd-9a46-aa5a243e3598.description:
The coin, produced at the Egyptian mint, can be dated to the reign of Abu ‘Ali al-Hakim bi-‘amr Allah (AH 386–411 / AD 996–1021). The coin has a four-line inscription with *kufic* characters on both sides. The inscription on the front reads ‘*‘Alî lâ ilâ illâ Allâh wahda-hu lâ sarik la-hu Muhammad rasûl Allâh wâli Allâh*’ (‘There is no God but Allah, the One, there is none like unto him. Muhammad is the Messenger of God’) and the inscription around the edge reads ‘*Muhammad rasûl Allâh arsala-hu bi-l-hudâ wa al-haqq li-yuzhira-hu alâ al-dîn kulli-hi wa la-hu kariha al-musrikûn*’ (‘Muhammad is the messenger of God. He has sent His messenger with the guidance and the true religion, and will make it dominate all religions, in spite of the idol worshipers’).  
The inscription ‘*Abd Allâh wûliya al-Mansûr Abû Ali al-imâm al-Hakîm bi-amr Allâh amir al-mu’ minîn*’ appears in the middle of the front side, and the edge bears the inscription ‘*bismi-llâh duriba hadâ-l-l-dînâr bi-Mis'r sana talat wa arba maya*’ (‘This coin was minted in the name of God in Egypt in the year three and four hundred’).
5956a116-f2da-52fd-9a46-aa5a243e3598.short_description: The *dinar*, which takes its name from its Byzantine predecessor the *denarius*, is decorated with an inscription in *kufic* characters. This coin was minted during the reign of the Caliph al-Hakim.

5956a116-f2da-52fd-9a46-aa5a243e3598.method_for_datation: From the inscription on the edge of the obverse.
5956a116-f2da-52fd-9a46-aa5a243e3598.method_for_provenance: From the inscription on the edge of the obverse.

materials: Gold / minting.

59a7e631-51cd-5c00-96df-73c23c2e673f.name: Frieze with calligraphy.
59a7e631-51cd-5c00-96df-73c23c2e673f.description:
This frieze was set into the wall of the *qibla* of the central court of the Zawiya al-Gharianiya, above the outside *mihrab*. The large *kufic* characters stand out in strong relief from the background. Thin grooves outline their contours. The letters are designed to look monumental but have richly ornamented motifs attached to them.  
The *kufic* writing on this frieze is extremely sophisticated. The shaping of the letters shows a concern for composition and the overall design is skilfully worked out to fill the whole space harmoniously. Particularly remarkable is a highly complex foliated scroll, which emerges from the letter *nun* and terminates in a three-lobed fleuron touching the preceding letter. This scroll motif contains a stylised five-lobed leaf of a type found in the Ifriqiyan decorative repertoire from the AH 3rd / AD 9th century. The carver's skill in choosing this elaborate decoration has resolved the problem of the letter *mim* falling between two letters with tall uprights (*lam* and *nun*). Notice also the heart-shaped motif suspended from the letter 'as- S*alam*' (peace), the symbol of love and affection.  
The inscription is unfinished and says: 'Enter into here in peace, into the shelter from all fear and …'
59a7e631-51cd-5c00-96df-73c23c2e673f.short_description: Set in the *qibla* wall of the central courtyard of the Zawiya al-Gharianiya above the external *mihrab*, this frieze has an incomplete inscription in *kufic* script of great palaeographic value. Its style and decoration have marked similarities with dozens of Kairouanese funerary steles.
59a7e631-51cd-5c00-96df-73c23c2e673f.dates: Hegira, first half of the 5th century / AD 11th century
59a7e631-51cd-5c00-96df-73c23c2e673f.dimensions: Length 141 cm; height (total) 37 cm, (carved strip) 32 cm, (letters) 31 cm; thickness 0.5 cm.
59a7e631-51cd-5c00-96df-73c23c2e673f.method_for_datation: The calligraphy in this frieze is very similar in style and decoration to dozens of Kairouanese funerary stelae which date from the first half of the 4th / 10th century. Furthermore, similar types of lettering have been found at Kairouan dating from the same era; for example, the lettering carved in wood on the frieze at the *maqsura* of the Great Mosque and the inscription on the two piers re-used as uprights in the Bab Tunis itself (437 / 1046).
59a7e631-51cd-5c00-96df-73c23c2e673f.method_for_provenance:
All the evidence suggests that this frieze was taken from the site at Sabra al-Mansuriyya. This view is corroborated by the presence of various pieces of material such as capitols, columns, with inscriptions, and crossbeams used in the construction of the monument in the 8th / 14th century and which date from the Fatimid–Zirid era.  
In fact, the Sabra site was used as a quarry by the Kairouanese during the reconstruction of their town after the Hilalian invasion, and is the only one with such an abundance of these materials.
59a7e631-51cd-5c00-96df-73c23c2e673f.obtention: During the restoration work on the Sidi Abid al-Ghariani Mausoleum this frieze was acquired by the National Institute of the Patrimony of Tunis. It has been on display since 1986 at the Museum of Islamic Art at Raqqada.

5afb9d0a-a173-5509-83ce-e5ce7f4da179.name: Page from a manuscript on horsemanship.
5afb9d0a-a173-5509-83ce-e5ce7f4da179.description:
A page from a manuscript on horsemanship, written in the *naskhi* script in black ink. The main titles indicating the subject matter are written in red. On this page the sub-title reads: 'the section on how to break the pole and avoid it'. At the top of the page, three Mamluk horsemen are portrayed, two of which are engaged in combat with poles. Each of them is wearing a knee-length tunic and a skull-cap, known in historical sources as *a zomt.* The third man is wearing a turban and a longer garment with narrow sleeves. He leans on the stick in a stance that suggests that he is observing the contenders and is possibly their trainer. The men's clothing has been painted in red, black and violet, appearing to be patterned with coloured threads, going in different directions in a haphazard fashion. This illustration clearly reflects the distinguishing features of the Arab school of painting that was widespread from the AH 9th / 15th century in the area encompassing Iran, Iraq, Syria, Egypt and North Africa. The school was, however, differentiated by specific local characteristics in each region, although collectively it did reflect some general trends, the most important of which were: the small number of people depicted; the lack of a pictorial frame or background; the use of vivid colours; the absence of realism; a lack of regard to the fundamentals of perspective and the third dimension; an emphasis on the depiction of animals, especially horses. The Museum of Islamic Art in Cairo has acquired three pages from this manuscript.  
The whereabouts of the remaining pages may suggest that the dealer of antiquities, Isa Ma'aluf, who had the manuscript in his possession until the year 1928 set about selling the book by the page to a number of countries. The manuscript was originally made up of 184 pages and contained 16 drawings depicting the mobilisation of armies. It included 46 colour illustrations to elucidate the subject matter. Unfortunately, the name of this manuscript and its author are unknown since the first and the last pages are lost. The manuscript contains a number of sections on the arts of war and horsemanship including: horsemanship and teaching it; drawing a bow; manoeuvres with a sword; knowledge on the different forms of a bow; raising and carrying a lance; manoeuvres with a shield on the ground and on a horse; javelin-throwing and casting a spear and shooting arrows. The manuscript also deals with cannons and gun-powder.
5afb9d0a-a173-5509-83ce-e5ce7f4da179.short_description: The Mamluk period saw a renaissance of all the arts, especially book illustration. Iraqi artisans migrated to Egypt and Syria after the Mogul invasion of Baghdad and revived there the tradition of that art. This illustration from a book on horsemanship is a fine example of the Arab school of painting.
5afb9d0a-a173-5509-83ce-e5ce7f4da179.method_for_datation:
A number of technical terms and words appear in the text of this manuscript which are seen also in the works of historians who were writing about Egypt in the latter half of the Mamluk period. It also appears that the linguistic style, which includes words from the colloquial dialect, resembles that of the historian Ibn Iyas, who died in 930 / 1524.  
Furthermore, the illustrator was intent on painting the clothing and head coverings of the characters in costumes true to those worn in the Mamluk period, reproducing the colours and styles as described in contemporary literary accounts. Sources also report that the Mamluks used to wear a loose outer garment called a *Kabr* during military training, and a red *zomt* on their heads. It is known that the red *zomt* was confined to the heads of Mamluks from the middle of the 9th / 15th century, by order of Sultan al-Ashraf Barsbay in the year 841 / 1437. Likewise, Ibn Iyas mentioned in his book, *Bada'i -Zuhur fi Waqa'i al-Duhur \[The Wonders of Flowers in Encounters Through the Ages\]* that the general public, the peasants, were forbidden to wear the *zomt* on their heads for it was restricted solely to the Mamluks. The *zomt* was usually red in colour and fluffy as seen in the manuscript paintings.
5afb9d0a-a173-5509-83ce-e5ce7f4da179.method_for_provenance: This illustration clearly reflects the distinguishing features of the Arab school of painting that was widespread from the 9th / 15th century in the area encompassing Iran, Iraq, Syria, Egypt and North Africa. The school was, however, differentiated by specific local characteristics in each region and this particular manuscript depicts the Mamluk hierarchy in Egypt some time after the 9th / 15th century.
5afb9d0a-a173-5509-83ce-e5ce7f4da179.obtention: This manuscript was bought in 1955 from the antiquities dealer, Asherof.

5b111959-0e06-5d73-9d98-5177f4d07663.name: Mamluk armour
5b111959-0e06-5d73-9d98-5177f4d07663.short_description: In the AD 1559 inventory of the collection of Archduke Ferdinand II of Tyrol (AD 1529–95) this helmet and cuirassier armour were wrongly attributed to "N. König zu Cuba in India“ (a king of Cuba in India). In AD 1788 the shield was correctly added and the ensemble, for no apparent reason, identified as belonging to the North African maritime hero, Dragut Reis, King of Kairun (died AD 1565). Modern attribution to a Mamluk prince is based on the artefact's similarity to the *morion* (open helmet) of Khairbak, the Mamluk governor of Aleppo (Istanbul, Topkapı Sarayı Museum) who handed over Syria to the Ottoman Sultan Selim I in AD 1517. It is the most sumptuous example of this type of Oriental armour.
5b111959-0e06-5d73-9d98-5177f4d07663.dates: Hegira 10th century / AD 1st quarter of the 16th century

5b1c8043-09cd-5175-9295-722ec38d28a3.name: Ewer
5b1c8043-09cd-5175-9295-722ec38d28a3.short_description:
The ewer gives a peculiar example of the late 12th–early 13th century inlaid brassware from Khorassan (Northeastern Iran). It has a cylindrical 12-faceted body with a flat bottom (probably later remade), a high cylindrical neck with two repoussé lions on both sides of the spout and a simple loop handle.  
On the shoulders of the ewer there is a large relief 12-pointed rosette with fish between ends. The surface of the body facets are decorated with three bands of ornament. On the top there is a row of medallions with human figures, probably musicians (significantly erased). Beneath runs a *naskh* inscription of traditional blessings addressed to the owner of the vessel: “Glory, success, lordship, happiness, patronage, care…”. In the lower part a large band of figural medallions depicting the 12 signs of the Zodiac is placed. Elements of the décor, which includes floral arabesque background, are articulated with silver inlay (partially lost) and contrasting black filler. There is also a *kufic* inscription on the neck, not read.

5b81d47f-3acf-5855-8fa6-e5ebc2df14f4.short_description: The shape, size, and decoration of this bowl demonstrate an affinity between lustre‑painted glass and ceramic lustreware, as the division of its walls into panels and the use of stylised palmette‑tree motifs also frequently appear on ceramic lustre‑painted bowls made in Fatimid Egypt. 5b990d35-bcaf-52cf-a880-52eebc5cded0.name: *Zulaikha Seizing the Skirt of Yusuf's Robe* Folio from an album (or manuscript) with ghazals by Sa'adi
5b990d35-bcaf-52cf-a880-52eebc5cded0.short_description:
The miniature on the folio illustrates one of the key episodes of the poem "Yusuf and Zuleikha" by Jami. Zuleikha invites Yusuf (pictured with a “flame of the prophet" around his head) to a magnificent palace where he declares love. However, the virtuous Yusuf tries to escape. Zuleikha catches up to him at the door and grabs the edge of his robe. The man in the golden crown watching the scene from behind the open door on the left is probably the husband of Zulayaha, the Egyptian nobleman. He holds a "finger of surprise" at his mouth - a conditional gesture in Persian miniature signifying great astonishment.  
The composition and style of the painting follow a famous miniature of AD 1640, attributed to the brush of Muin Musavvir (1617–1702), an outstanding master of the Isfahan painting school.  
Interestingly, the miniature is painted on a folio from a poetic album (or a manuscript) of the late 16th century, containing poems by Sa’adi Shirazi (1203 / 1210–1291), a great Persian poet.
5b990d35-bcaf-52cf-a880-52eebc5cded0.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis by L. Guzalian (1953, date, origin) and H. Rudyk (2017, origin specified). Sa'adi ghazal identified by N. Vyshnevska (2016).

5b990d35-bcaf-52cf-a880-52eebc5cded0.obtention: Purchased in 1940s in Kyiv from a private owner.

5ba1e422-156b-52c9-b178-d1de57501788.name: Piri Reis b. Hajji Mehmed, *Bahriye* (Navigation or Sailing Manual)
5ba1e422-156b-52c9-b178-d1de57501788.short_description: The important manual on navigation and sailing called “*Bahriye*” was authored by Piri Re’is b. Hajji Mehmed (died 962 AH / 1554–55), an Ottoman navigator and cartographer. This 17th-century copy was penned in large *naskh* script, possibly in Ottoman Istanbul. Piri Re’is, a Turkish captain and later admiral of the Ottoman fleet, is credited with the creation of two famous world maps as well as this sailing manual for the entire Mediterranean. While the latter is relatable to Catalan and Italian *Portolane* and *Isolarii* (Sea Atlases or Naval Manuals, and Island Books respectively), the work of Piri Re’is is considered quite independent and original as it contains detailed descriptions of the coasts and islands of the Mediterranean, starting from the Bosporus and the Dardanelles. Interestingly, this manuscript is a late copy of his first version of 1521, while a separate second version, which included a longer and more detailed text, was made five years later and was dedicated to Suleyman the Magnificent. The earlier text consists of 132 chapters with descriptive texts of historical, geographical, and navigational content. Moreover, this copy contains 133 half– to full-page map sketches that accompany the text, of which most feature a black compass rose in the centre. Like the other more than 20 surviving copies, it likely served primarily practical purposes. In contrast, the second version of the text is extant in about ten surviving copies which reflect a representative courtly quality both in their elaborate calligraphy and illustration. This suggests that these manuals were rather intended for the education of the nobility. It has been postulated that the Vienna copy, with its schematic, rather inconsistently oriented sketches that sometimes even extend into the text block, was produced by sailors or members of the Ottoman Navy in the arsenal or in cartographic workshops. The map sketches show port cities and fortresses identified by toponyms and other representational details added in bright colours. These representations seem to follow a fixed compositional formula with stylised landscape depictions. Small offshore islands or reefs, for example, are usually highlighted in red. Judging from the illustrations, this manual is stylistically comparable to the copy kept in the University Library of Bologna (MS 3613, dated 977 AH / 1569 AD), and it has been argued that the Vienna manuscript may be a copy of the Bologna manuscript from the second half of the 17th-century. The owners’ notes and stamps on fol. 1a reveal that the manual was part of the collections of a certain Zeynül'Abidin Evliyazade as well as of Joseph von Hammer-Purgstall.

5c505fce-a478-511a-be3a-4ccea6c65fe1.name: An illustrated copy of the *Shahnamah* of Firdawsi
5c505fce-a478-511a-be3a-4ccea6c65fe1.short_description:
This copy of Firdawsi’s epic is richly illustrated with 62 paintings, most extending well beyond the rulings. Stylistically, the paintings are the work of at least four artists, but only three of them are signed by Kazim Quli, who is otherwise unrecorded.  
According to the colophon on folio 541a, the copying of the text was completed on 14 September 1602. No patron is mentioned, but a note on folio 1a, written by the Mughal emperor Jahangir, mentions that the manuscript entered the Mughal royal library on 21 March 1609. The manuscript remained there until at least 25 April 1686, as attested by a number of inspection and transfer notes on folios 1a and 541b, written by librarians during the reigns of emperors Jahangir, Shah Jahan and Awrangzeb. A note on folio 1a, accompanied by the names of 3 witnesses, mentions that the manuscript was in Shikarpur on 10 September 1739, when it was given to a certain Haji ‘Abbas who was to hand it over to Sardar Mir Afdal Khan in Qandahar.
5c505fce-a478-511a-be3a-4ccea6c65fe1.holder: Khalili Family Trust – Nasser D. Khalili Collection of Islamic Art
5c505fce-a478-511a-be3a-4ccea6c65fe1.dates: Dated Friday, 27 Rabi‘ al-Awwal 1011 / AD 14 September 1602
5c505fce-a478-511a-be3a-4ccea6c65fe1.method_for_datation: Date and provenance are based on the colophon and the notes written by Mughal emperors and officials within the Mughal royal library.
5c505fce-a478-511a-be3a-4ccea6c65fe1.obtention:

5cb50de2-2586-516f-843e-945e72d7f294.name: Miniature
5cb50de2-2586-516f-843e-945e72d7f294.description:
In this miniature, an entire world of living beings—mothers and children, animals, plants, and all forms of life—is depicted within a single drop of water. Beneath the drop appears an Arabic inscription from the Qur’an, Surat al-Anbiya (21:30):  
"*Ve ce‘alnā min al-mā’i kulla shay’in ḥayy*" —  
“We created every living thing from water.”  
  
The work symbolises the idea that all beings are bound together through water, sharing a common origin and interdependence. Reflecting this message, the Istanbul Water Museum has embraced the motto “Su Kardeşliği” — "The Brotherhood of Water."
5cb50de2-2586-516f-843e-945e72d7f294.holder: İstanbul Su Müzesi / Istanbul Water Museum
5cb50de2-2586-516f-843e-945e72d7f294.method_for_datation: Date and origin are written on the piece.
5cb50de2-2586-516f-843e-945e72d7f294.author: Ercan Topçu, Barış Topçu
keywords: Water; Qur'an; Miniature
materials: Paper, ink

5cf968b5-3058-5930-a6d0-15159faf8517.name: Bowl with Epigraphic and Vegetal Decoration
5cf968b5-3058-5930-a6d0-15159faf8517.short_description: This strikingly modern bowl is made from humble earthenware, disguised and beautified through the application of a white slip, a semifluid colored clay. Its interior is decorated with an encircling black inscription, and the spaces between the letters are filled by abstract decoration that is augmented by the color red, all covered by a transparent glaze. Read by turning the bowl counterclockwise, the Arabic inscription presents a proverb that retains some resonance even today: “Greed is a sign of poverty.” This proverb, which is inscribed on a number of Samanid bowls, is one of the sayings of the Shi’ite Imam ‘Ali ibn Abu Talib.
5cf968b5-3058-5930-a6d0-15159faf8517.holder: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)
5cf968b5-3058-5930-a6d0-15159faf8517.method_for_datation: The inscribed bowl exemplifies the elegant "black-on-white wares" excavated in the cities of Nishapur and Samarqand, both of which were governed by the Samanid dynasty beginning in Hegira 289 / AD 900.
5cf968b5-3058-5930-a6d0-15159faf8517.method_for_provenance: The material, technique and decoration are all consonant with Samanid epigraphic pottery.
5cf968b5-3058-5930-a6d0-15159faf8517.obtention: Collection of Nasli M. Heeramaneck (1902-1971), New York, until 1973 (sold to); LACMA, The Nasli M. Heeramaneck collection, gift of Joan Palevsky.

5d100163-7783-5d0b-b8a8-5ee5feece0df.name: Candlestick
5d100163-7783-5d0b-b8a8-5ee5feece0df.short_description: The candlestick was dedicated by the Mamluk sultan Qaytbay to the shrine at Medina in 1482. Monumental inscriptions whose letter-ends curve to form tongs enclosing small palmettes, occupy almost the entire height of the base. The sultan Qaytbay had the mosque of the Prophet restored in 1480 and offered to it at least five candlesticks, of which another two have survived and are now in Cairo.
keywords: Candlestick; Sultan Qaytbay; Metalwork
materials: Brass inlaid with black organic material

5d425d12-049a-5704-9607-305414bcdb67.name: Beaker
5d425d12-049a-5704-9607-305414bcdb67.short_description: Mamluk beakers are one of the most prolific types of enamelled glass vessels with a wide variety of forms and decorations. This tubular glass beaker has a flared top and a rounded foot. The overall composition of enamelled and polychrome decorations is divided into two main registers outlined by narrow red bands. The first register shows a scene with two figures depicted using thin red lines, each with an enamel, red and blue robe and turban. One of the figures is holding a small beaker while the other sits with his legs crossed. Above them an inscription outlined in red on a blue background reads: “al-malik al-sultan" (The King, the Sultan). These beakers were used as drinking vessels as often depicted in other media from that time.
5d425d12-049a-5704-9607-305414bcdb67.dates: AH late 7th century AH / AD late 13th century

5d9c4672-e793-561a-835c-cda69931fe09.name: *Hamsat al-Jami* (Five poems by Jami)
5d9c4672-e793-561a-835c-cda69931fe09.short_description:
This manuscript contains the *Hamsat al-Jami* ("Five poems of Jami") from 951 AH / 1544 AD. Maulana Nur ad-Din ʿAbd ar-Rahman was born in 817 AH / 1414 AD in Torbat-e Jam, which is why he is mostly referred to as Jami. During his roughly fifty years as a poet, Jami wrote countless famous works including the collection of poems in this manuscript as well as the *Haft Awrang* ("Seven Thrones"). Most of his poetic works are allegories to spirituality and religion, as Jami was a devout scholar of Sufism.  
As the name suggests the Hamsat al-Jami contains five poems by the name of Tuhfat al-ahrar ("Gift of the Free"), Subhat al-abrar ("Rosary of the Pious"), Yusuf u Zulaikha ("Yusuf and Zulaikha"), Laila wa Magnun ("Layla and Majnun"), and Iskandar-nama ("History of Alexander the Great").
5d9c4672-e793-561a-835c-cda69931fe09.dates: 5th of Muharram 951 AH / 29th of March 1544 AD
5d9c4672-e793-561a-835c-cda69931fe09.method_for_datation: The colophon (fol. 30a) indicates that the copying of the text was completed on the 5th of Muharram 951 AH / 29th of March 1544 AD.
5d9c4672-e793-561a-835c-cda69931fe09.method_for_provenance: Duda compared the illustrations in the manuscript with other miniature paintings and came to the conclusion that the manuscript most likely originated from Bukhara. This hypothesis is based on the stylistic attributes of the illustrations which closely align with those known to have been produced by the Bukhara school of miniature painting.
5d9c4672-e793-561a-835c-cda69931fe09.obtention: There is a stamp of a previous owner that dates back to 1080 AH / 1669 AD. Due to the poor conditions of this stamp, the owner’s name could only partially be deciphered by Duda. Based on an older shelf mark, she suggests that the manuscript has been in Vienna since the 18th century. Joseph von Hammer-Purgstall first mentions the manuscript being in Vienna in 1811 and was most likely bought by him for the Imperial Court Library.
5d9c4672-e793-561a-835c-cda69931fe09.bibliography:
Duda, Dorothea, *Islamische Handschriften I. Persische Handschriften, Die illuminierten Handschriften und Inkunabeln der Österreichischen Nationalbibliothek*, vol. 4, Vienna: Verlag der Österreichischen Akademie der Wissenschaften, 1983: 22-25.  
Flügel, Gustav, *Die arabischen, persischen und türkischen Handschriften der Kaiserlich-Königlichen Hofbibliothek zu Wien*, vol. 1, Vienna: Verlag der K. K. Hof- und Staatsdruckerei, 1865: 565-567.
5d9c4672-e793-561a-835c-cda69931fe09.binding_desc:
The black lacquer binding on this manuscript closes with a flap. On the spine of the flap there are verses written in gold starting with the words "in hamsa", therefore relating directly to the text of the manuscript. Because of this relation between the text and the binding it can safely be assumed that the binding was manufactured explicitly for this manuscript.  
The binding is decorated with floral motifs and golden ornamental medallions. The doublures of the manuscript are made out of brown leather and decorated with blue medallions.  
The binding is rather fragile and parts of the painted lacquer have chipped off.

5e053a64-1076-5c13-b2f5-a260eeae41de.name:
The court of Kayumars  
Folio from the *Shahnameh* (Book of Kings) of Shah Tahmasp
5e053a64-1076-5c13-b2f5-a260eeae41de.short_description: Firdausi’s epic poem the *Shahnameh* (Book of Kings), completed in 1010, recounts the history of all of Iran’s shahs (kings) up to the Arab conquest in 642 AD and the country’s adoption of Islam. A large part of the poem focuses on prehistoric, legendary kings, some of whom ruled for hundreds of years and established man’s knowledge of everything from fire to weaving. According to Firdausi, the very idea of kingship originated with King Kayumars, who ruled for thirty years, overseeing a peaceable kingdom in which men wore leopard-skin robes and wild animals grew tame. In this utopia Kayumars had one secret enemy, the evil Ahriman, whose envy drove him to incite his own son, the Black Div, to murder Siyamak, the son of Kayumars. Before the assassination took place, the angel Surush warned Kayumars of Ahriman’s plot.
5e053a64-1076-5c13-b2f5-a260eeae41de.obtention: Former Prince Saddrudin Aga Khan Collection
5e053a64-1076-5c13-b2f5-a260eeae41de.bibliography: Welch, Stuart Cary, *A King’s Book of King’s: The Shah-Nameh of Shah Tahmasp*, New York: Metropolitan Museum of Art, 1972. ISBN: 9780300192650.
5e053a64-1076-5c13-b2f5-a260eeae41de.artist: Attributed to Safavid master Sultan Muhammad
keywords: Kayumars; Guymars; Shahnameh; Shanama; kings; book-of-kings; folio; painting; work-on-paper; works-on-paper
materials: Opaque watercolour, ink, and gold on paper

5ea5b8ab-9f07-5718-8f32-a6c53d04b318.name: Tunic.
5ea5b8ab-9f07-5718-8f32-a6c53d04b318.description:
This tunic is dyed black. It has a rounded collar and half-length sleeves. The garment opens at the back and can only be donned by first putting the hand into the sleeves. It was probably made for a child and is similar in design to contemporary Coptic clothing. The embroidery occurs where the sleeves join the body and is different on each side.  
The right-hand band has a red background on which yellow lines form geometric shapes. These are interspersed with medallion shapes containing stylised vegetable, floral and animal motifs, some could be hares.  
In the left-hand band the colours are more varied and the motifs are animal; mainly hares and dogs in blue, green and black. The background is yellow. The two bands are framed with pious inscriptions in angular *kufic* lettering embroidered in silk. Although they are damaged and almost illegible, we can read;  
'Lasting blessings \[…\] sovereignty is with God'.
5ea5b8ab-9f07-5718-8f32-a6c53d04b318.short_description: The shape of this linen tunic, dyed black and undoubtedly intended for a child, is reminiscent of Coptic clothes. Each sleeve is decorated around the shoulders slightly differently from the other with plant and floral elements mixed with stylised zoomorphic motifs.
5ea5b8ab-9f07-5718-8f32-a6c53d04b318.dimensions: Length 70 cm, width 50 cm to 70 cm; 120 cm (with sleeves).
5ea5b8ab-9f07-5718-8f32-a6c53d04b318.method_for_datation: Tunics dating from the High Muslim era are rare, and this limits our dating criteria. However, based on the decoration and the type of script, we can date this object fairly accurately from the 3rd–4th / 9th–10th centuries.
5ea5b8ab-9f07-5718-8f32-a6c53d04b318.obtention: This garment was bought from an antique dealership in Cairo in 1958 by H. H. Abdelwahab, former Director of the National Institute of Art and Archaeology. He donated it to the Bardo Museum in 1962.
5ea5b8ab-9f07-5718-8f32-a6c53d04b318.bibliography: Skik, K., *Musée du Bardo, département musulman*, Tunis, 1974, p.16, fig. 6.
5ea5b8ab-9f07-5718-8f32-a6c53d04b318.author: Mourad Rammah
keywords: Textiles; figurative decoration; costume
materials: Linen embroidered in wool.

5eacbf30-4e9e-5c27-a757-04efcf633b45.name: Wooden frieze.
5eacbf30-4e9e-5c27-a757-04efcf633b45.description:
An almost complete frieze that would undoubtedly have come from a religious monument. Its surface is decorated with a flowery and twisted *kufic* inscription repeating the end of Qur'anic verse 73 of Sura 22 ('Pilgrimage'). The *kufic* characters are embellished with vegetal elements in the form of tri-lobed demi-fleurons and five-lobed fleurons that prolong the angle of the bevel.  
The text is carved on a plant background consisting of a dense floral composition with absolutely no empty spaces. This decorative element uses pinecones and palms carried by foliage or decorating the involutions: asymmetric smooth palms with calyxes and branches stretching into loops and veined double palms with acanthus leaves whose offshoot, which separates the veins into twos, assumes an oval shape reminiscent of a pinecone scale.  
This frieze, with its low-relief decoration covering the entire surface and where a taste for abundance and ornamental opulence has supplanted Almohad rigour and simplicity, well illustrates the aesthetic choices of Marinid art, which adopts some elements of Almoravid art.
5eacbf30-4e9e-5c27-a757-04efcf633b45.short_description: This incomplete frieze would almost certainly have come from a religious monument. It is decorated with a Qur'anic inscription in flowery, twisted *kufic* characters on an unbroken background of plant decoration in low relief, a good illustration of aesthetic choices in Marinid art.
5eacbf30-4e9e-5c27-a757-04efcf633b45.dimensions: Height 21.6 cm, length 107 cm, depth 3.5 cm.
5eacbf30-4e9e-5c27-a757-04efcf633b45.method_for_datation: From stylistic analysis. The rendering of the letters and the floral forms, which can also be seen in the decoration of the Bab Mrissa gateway in Salé dating from the second half of the 7th / 13th century, as well as its decoration suggests the style of the beginning of the Marinid era.
5eacbf30-4e9e-5c27-a757-04efcf633b45.method_for_provenance: Information taken from the inventory register.

5f89dbe5-9c2a-5bd5-873c-3b29fca4dd90.name: Coronation mantle
5f89dbe5-9c2a-5bd5-873c-3b29fca4dd90.short_description:
The precious mantle embroidered with gold, pearls and cloisonné-enamelled plaques was part of the set of robes used at the coronations of the kings and emperors of the Holy Roman Empire. The semicircular edge of the mantle is decorated with a gold-embroidered *kufic* inscription. It reveals that the mantle was produced in AH 528/ AD 1133/34 during the reign of the Norman king Roger II of Sicily (AD 1095–1154) in the royal workshops in Palermo where among others Arabic artisans worked.  
Ancient motifs are depicted on the surface of the semicircular mantle: to both sides of a palm-tree (representing the tree of life) a lion triumph over a camel, which has a saddle and bridle and has thus been domesticated.
5f89dbe5-9c2a-5bd5-873c-3b29fca4dd90.method_for_datation: Art historical and historical analysis (style criticism, archive and inventory research)
5f89dbe5-9c2a-5bd5-873c-3b29fca4dd90.obtention: Made for king Roger II of Sicily as part of the Norman treasure transferred by heritage to the Hohenstaufen and finally used as coronation mantle of the kings and emperors of the Holy Roman Empire.

5fb9df90-7b26-5354-a02b-04f0411593be.name: Ka`ba tile
5fb9df90-7b26-5354-a02b-04f0411593be.short_description: This rectangular tile depicts a stylised view of Mecca, with the black-shrouded Ka‘ba in the centre of the *Masjid al-Haram*. It is part of a larger material corpus related to the Hajj, the pilgrimage to Mecca and sites in the vicinity, which was a favoured theme in Ottoman workshops. Although this tile is painted in the traditional colour palette used by seventeenth century Iznik workshops, the bird’s-eye view, inspired by the European pictorial tradition, is a characteristic of later examples made at Tekfur Sarayı in Istanbul, a less well-known Ottoman ceramic workshop.

5ff2f6bf-6eef-590b-81ac-758e18790131.name: Calligraphy
5ff2f6bf-6eef-590b-81ac-758e18790131.description:
This artwork blends modern calligraphy with classical Islamic *sülüs*– and *tuğra*–inspired forms. The central inscription features the Qur’anic verse from Surah Al-Anbiyā’ (21:30): “And We created every living thing from water.” The phrase emphasises the essential and sacred nature of water as the origin of life, reflecting a cosmological theme deeply rooted in Islamic thought.  
  
On the right side, the intricate calligraphic motif expresses a devotional invocation, rendered in fluid, interwoven lines that echo the movement and vitality of water. The turquoise background reinforces the symbolism of purity, creation, and continuity. Together, these elements merge spiritual meaning with visual harmony, inviting viewers to contemplate the relationship between nature, divine creation, and artistic expression.

5ff60937-5e79-50fd-9f4b-b979480be0f5.name: *A Youth with a Lion* Folio from an album
5ff60937-5e79-50fd-9f4b-b979480be0f5.short_description:
The depicted scene takes place in a garden of a Persian Shah or a lord. Only the upper elite of Iranian society could afford keeping large predatory felines in their gardens. The young man's headdress fits the AD mid-17th century Safavid fashion.  
The author of the painting is Afzal al-Husayni (also named Mir Afzal Tuni, Afzal), a younger contemporary and follower of Reza Abbasi. Known primarily as the master of erotic drawing, Afzal preferred to depict the leisure of the Persian aristocracy: young men or love scenes in the garden. In addition to the artistic manner, the author is also indicated by an inscription in the bottom right of the folio that reads: “He! On the first day of the month of Jumat the Second of year 1056, the drawing of the most humble Afzal al-Husayni was completed”.  
Since the late 16th century the Iranian miniature has acquired the role of an independent piece of art. The prestige of the artist's work and his creative and economic freedom was growing, and it became much easier to make a living on producing single page works than on illustrating a whole book. Separate paintings as well as calligraphic folios with poems constituted *murakka* albums, reflecting the aesthetic and intellectual demand of wealthy collectors.

603d37ce-f178-5cd4-9e44-f5656d6bd87a.name: Ten-*dinar* coin.
603d37ce-f178-5cd4-9e44-f5656d6bd87a.description:
While being a rarity in Almohad coinage, this ten-*dinar* gold medal features the characteristics of the coins from that period. Immediately after the capture of Marrakesh in AH 540 / AD 1146, 'Abd al-Mu'min minted a new coin distinct from that of his predecessors. He introduced the square shape, codified the text and its location on the coin, and modified the written style. Thus on the obverse square of the coin we can read the profession of faith of the unity of God and Mohamed's prophetic mission after the *basmala* and the salutation to the prophet and his companions. The name of the reigning prince who issued the coin, followed by his father's name, appear on the segments. Inside the reverse square, the *imamat* of the *mahdi* (the messenger) is announced, followed by the name of 'Abd al-Mu'min ibn 'Ali, Caliph commander of the faithful, first Almohad monarch. The segments contain the name of the ancestors of the king who commissioned this coin along with their titles: the Caliph, commander of the faithful, Abu Hafs al-Murtada, son of Ibn Ibrahim, grandson of Abu Ya'qub, great-grandson of 'Abd al-Mu'min. As was common in this type of minting, there is no mention of the date. In accordance with the new code, the texts are written in cursive script with a linear clarity and sobriety typical in Almohad art.  
In the squares, the letters are embellished with annulets whereas the segments display fleurons, tendrils and smooth palmettes. All these features make this coin a beautiful, elegant object. It is not surprising that it has been mounted for use as jewellery. These gold coins, called *masmudia*, were much sought-after throughout the Spanish Catholic states for their weight and the purity of the gold. They continued to be used in exchanges even after the fall of the Almohads.
603d37ce-f178-5cd4-9e44-f5656d6bd87a.short_description: This ten-*dinar* gold coin medallion bears the hallmarks of the coins minted by the dynasty that introduced square coins, codified the content and placement of the text and changed the writing style. It was converted into jewellery because of its rarity and elegance.

60d42b24-3acf-5ae0-ab4f-e3aae453f313.name: *Still-life with Calligraphic Panel*
60d42b24-3acf-5ae0-ab4f-e3aae453f313.short_description: Feyhaman Duran was particularly interested in portrait painting and went to Paris in 1910 through the patronage of the Egyptian Prince Abbas Halim Pasha to further his studies in this genre. He greatly profited from the teaching of Paul Richet, professor of anatomy in the School of Fine Arts in Paris. He also attended the Julian Academy where he learned a great deal from Jean-Paul and Albert Laurens. In 1913-14 he worked in the Cormon studio in the School of Fine Arts. Although devoting most of his time to portrait painting, Feyhaman Duran also did paintings of flowers and nudes, but he was definitely most interested in the portrayal of people, and he had very little time for non-figurative painting.

materials: Oil on canvas

618bc97a-0543-5e59-aeff-839fc23ec12e.name: *Sitara* for the *rawda* of the Prophet’s mosque in Medina
618bc97a-0543-5e59-aeff-839fc23ec12e.short_description:
That this curtain was intended for the *rawda* is suggested by the text in the large medallion at the top. It consists of a *hadith* of the Prophet, *ma bayna qabri wa minbari rawda min riyad al-janna* (‘Between my tomb and my minbar is one of the gardens of Paradise’). The same text appears above the *mihrab* in the *rawda*.  
Sultan Mahmud II is known to have practised the art of calligraphy and a number of *sitara*s commissioned by him for the Prophet’s mosque bear his pear-shaped signature cartouche which reads, *katabahu al-‘abd Mahmud bin ‘Abdulhamid khan* (‘written by the servant \[of God\] Mahmud, the son of ‘Abdulhamid Khan’).

6199aa8d-fb08-53d5-bf97-2267cb49f32d.name: Incense Burner
6199aa8d-fb08-53d5-bf97-2267cb49f32d.short_description:
This hollow cast incense burner in the shape of a bird is hinged and consists of two parts, which allows the object to be fully opened to insert the incense.  
The whole surface is engraved. Perforated decoration can be found on the chest, wings, back and tail. The eyes are highlighted by studs and engraved feathers cover the neck. An angular inscription runs chain-like around the neck and reaches the middle of the chest. A pierced, interwoven motif is placed in between. The wings contain a medallion with an elevated centre and spiralling tendrils and knots. The wingtips are ribbed and framed by an interlaced band which widens below them. The area between hinge and tail tip contains an ornament band with interwoven patterns. The legs are covered in engraved feathers and the claws are shaped in a detailed manner.  
The hinged body is different to most other bird-shaped incense burners, which either have a square drawer or an opening for the incense.

61e3f563-8d0b-554f-837e-efc244795bf1.name: Qur’anic illumination.
61e3f563-8d0b-554f-837e-efc244795bf1.description:
The right-hand page has the illumination, which is framed inside a gilt rectangle. The central decoration has two concave diamond shapes with a gilt background marked with brown lines framing stylised multi-lobed fleurons. The decoration is surrounded on each side by six triangles containing similar floral motifs. The whole illumination is separated by strips on a white background dotted with brown markings and divided by gilt segments.  
The left-hand page contains black *kufic* script. Vowels are marked by red dots and the *hamza* is shown with a green dot, as in the Abi al-Aswad system. The end of the verse is indicated by a triangle of three gilt dots. The end of the fifth verse is marked by a gilt medallion.  
The title of the *sura*, with the number of its verses, is indicated on the same line by a gilt *kufic* inscription with brown edges which terminates in a palm-leaf motif pointing towards the left-hand margin.
61e3f563-8d0b-554f-837e-efc244795bf1.short_description:
The illumination, in a gold rectangular frame on the right-hand page, has two concave lozenges in its centre, gilded at the bottom and peppered with brown lines.  
The left-hand page is written in black *kufic* script with the title of the *sura* and the number of verses given in golden *kufic* script.
61e3f563-8d0b-554f-837e-efc244795bf1.initial_owner: The Qur’an was part of a legacy (*habus*) left to the Great Mosque of Kairouan by Fadhl Mawlat Abi Ayub.
61e3f563-8d0b-554f-837e-efc244795bf1.method_for_datation: The colophon of the Qur'an includes the Act of Mortmain (*Tahbis*) dated 295 / 907.
61e3f563-8d0b-554f-837e-efc244795bf1.method_for_provenance: This Qur'an was copied and left to the Great Mosque of Kairouan by a woman who appears to be Kairouanese. It was probably copied in Kairouan itself which was a great centre of book production at the time.
61e3f563-8d0b-554f-837e-efc244795bf1.obtention: After the abolition of the *habus* foundation in Tunisia, the National Library obtained this Qur'an in 1967. In 1983 it went back to Kairouan, to the Centre of the Islamic Arts and Civilisation of Raqqada. It has been displayed at the Raqqada Museum of Islamic Art since 1986.

620147b9-073c-55b0-9874-1ee32624af18.name: Qur’an.
620147b9-073c-55b0-9874-1ee32624af18.description:
Two books of this multi-volume Qur'an, of which pages 100 and 101 of book II are shown here, are the only ones kept in the Rabat National Library. On almost square pages, they are both in Maghrebi *kufic* script in brown ink on parchment. Although in the same style, the calligraphy in the two volumes is not the same, suggesting the work of two copyists. However, judging from the thickness of the lines, the roundness in the angles of the letters and the depth of the curves, the two styles belong to the same period and to the same Qur'an. *Kufic* script in the West started to differ from the oriental style in the second half of the AH 3rd / AD 9th century, evolving towards a style known as Maghrebi, which reached maturity two centuries later. This type of writing, which continued to obey Abu al-Aswad's archaic system of vocalisation, has no diacritical marks. Only the short vowels are represented (*fatha*, the letter A ; *damma*, the letter O, red dots over the line), *kasra* (the letter I, red dot under the line), and *shedda* (indicating the duplication of the letter) which today is written like a lower case *w*. The yellow and green round dots denote the vocal attack.  
In this Qur'an, the titles of the suras lack any specific decoration. Only small golden rosettes framed by little dots, alternately blue and red, mark the separation between the verses, whereas the big rosettes, delicately adorned, embellish the verses in groups of ten. The written forms found in this specimen could link it to Zirid Qur'ans. Some very regular small punched holes in the upper margin of every page, where the word *habus* appears, prove that this book was brought as a pious offering to a shrine, probably in Fez.
620147b9-073c-55b0-9874-1ee32624af18.short_description: This Qur'an transcribed on parchment was offered as a pious gift to a shrine. The square format and the archaic *kufic* script with its rounded angles are characteristic of the Maghrebi calligraphy of the period. The red dots and golden rosettes mark the vowels and the separation of the verses.
620147b9-073c-55b0-9874-1ee32624af18.method_for_datation: Format and stylistic analysis of the script: archaic *kufic* style, codified for the system of vocalisation devised by Abu al-Aswad ad Du'ali (68 / 688) and adopted in the Muslim world from the 2nd–3rd / 8th–9th centuries. The calligraphy in these two volumes of the Qur'an is similar to the Western variant, known as Maghrebi.
620147b9-073c-55b0-9874-1ee32624af18.method_for_provenance: This Qur'an is thought to be from Fez, as the town was the Idrisid capital and home of the Qarawiyyin university.

6392fda5-b738-5dec-9a45-71733b02404b.name: Tent panel
6392fda5-b738-5dec-9a45-71733b02404b.short_description: This appliqué is one of a set of six featuring designs that echo the bold geometry of Egypt’s period of Mamluk rule (1250–1517). The format of calligraphy above a central roundel with trefoils is similar to other works of art created during the Mamluk Revival period. This particular textile features the following verse from the Qur’an: “That man can have nothing but what he strives for...” (53:39). Appliqués of this type were often used to embellish tents.

63a0f023-76ca-5378-a69c-036e6ca9862e.name: *Divan-ı Hafız* by Şemşeddin Muhammed Hafız Şirazi
63a0f023-76ca-5378-a69c-036e6ca9862e.description: The miniature depicts a social gathering for entertainment. A servant offers a plate of pomegranates to the individual seated on the carpet in the centre, who is accompanied by a beautiful young boy clapping his hands and reciting a *ghazal* (love poem) to the accompaniment of musicians.

63d7eb6d-8326-5395-9279-d48a47c2abba.name: Pair of *mihrab* candlesticks.
63d7eb6d-8326-5395-9279-d48a47c2abba.description: Each candlestick has a round base, a bell-shaped body, a cylindrical neck with a ring, and a wide candleholder. At the top and bottom of the body is a band of heart-shaped motifs with palmettes at their centres, a border repeated at the bottom of the neck. On the ring of the neck are large leaf motifs in relief. The neck itself is decorated with wavy lozenges featuring *hatayi*\-style (peony) motifs shown both frontally and in profile. The candleholder is decorated with interlacing cartouches with inscriptions. The main part of the body is decorated with a wide inscription band on a background of peonies and spiralling tendrils. The inscription in Persian is a poem praising the light of the candlestick; the Arabic inscription reads: 'May Sultan Bayezid be preserved from calamities'; the inscription in Ottoman Turkish informs us that the candlesticks were made for the mosque of Sultan Bayezid II in Edirne. Both candlesticks are entirely gilded. The forms of these candlesticks recall Mamluk candlesticks.
63d7eb6d-8326-5395-9279-d48a47c2abba.short_description: When Ottoman sultans commissioned the construction of their mosques, they also ordered the production of candlesticks to be placed on both sides of the *mihrab*. These candlesticks were made for the Mosque of Bayezid II in Edirne and the inscriptions offer good wishes for the sultan.
63d7eb6d-8326-5395-9279-d48a47c2abba.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts.
63d7eb6d-8326-5395-9279-d48a47c2abba.method_for_datation: The mosque of Bayezid II in Edirne, named on the inscriptions of the candlesticks, was completed in 894 / 1488. Thus the candlesticks must have been produced at about the same time.
63d7eb6d-8326-5395-9279-d48a47c2abba.obtention: The candlesticks were transferred to the Museum in 1911 from the Selimiye Mosque in Edirne.

63db5c62-6d08-59c2-901b-88672c5ff510.name: Candlestick.
63db5c62-6d08-59c2-901b-88672c5ff510.description:
A brass candlestick of a standard shape. Most surface areas, including the neck, shoulder and body, are decorated with inlaid silver. The main ornament of the body is a superb inscription in a grandly flowing script which reads: 'Made for His Highness, the exalted personage, the man of lordly rank, the officer in the service of Rukn al-Din, Rukn al-Din Muhammad Ibn Qaratay al-Baghdadi'. Dividing the large inscription are three medallions with scalloped borders which extend the full height of the body. Within these medallions are curious designs in which a series of spiralling branches coil outward from a small face-like motif and sprout birds, animals and masks from their ends. Both these medallions and the large inscription they punctuate are set against a background of dense leafy arabesques. The neck is decorated with smaller versions of the medallions on the body, and the collar repeats in smaller letters the dedicatory inscription.  
  
At some point in its history the candlestick was re-silvered, giving it a brighter and newer appearance than most candlesticks of this age. Also, a later owner engraved an inscription in Armenian into the top of the candlestick's body; the reading is uncertain but it seems to say, 'This candlestick is in memory of Temar, valiant son of Mkrtich \[sic\], who gave it to the Mother of God'. Although the identity of Temar and the church or monastery to which the candlestick was donated are unknown, this inscription is a fascinating glimpse into the life of a beautiful object.
63db5c62-6d08-59c2-901b-88672c5ff510.short_description: A brass candlestick inlaid in silver with ornament whose main feature is a superb inscription naming the patron. Candlesticks of this shape are common in Islamic art of the medieval period. Later in its history this candlestick was also inscribed with a dedication in Armenian.
63db5c62-6d08-59c2-901b-88672c5ff510.initial_owner: Rukn al-Din Muhammad Ibn Qaratay al-Baghdadi.
63db5c62-6d08-59c2-901b-88672c5ff510.method_for_datation: The patron is described as in the service of Rukn al-Din. This can refer either to Sultan Rukn al-Din Baybars I al-Bunduqdari, (r. 658–76 / 1260–77), or to Sultan Rukn al-Din Baybars II al-Jashankir, who reigned only briefly (708–9 / 1309).
63db5c62-6d08-59c2-901b-88672c5ff510.method_for_provenance: Cairo and Damascus were the two most important centres of art production under the Mamluks.

63db5c62-6d08-59c2-901b-88672c5ff510.author: Barry Wood
keywords: floral decoration; figurative decoration; inscription; calligraphy
materials: Brass inlaid with silver.

647040db-954c-553c-b7b9-c7c2901d4516.name: Album of calligraphies including poetry and prophetic traditions (*hadith*)
647040db-954c-553c-b7b9-c7c2901d4516.short_description: This album contains samples written by one of the most celebrated Turkish calligraphers, Shaikh Hamdullah (d. 1519), who developed the *naskhi* and *thuluth* styles from masters of the past to suit Ottoman taste. These pages, which show control, exactitude, and gentle flow, but also exaggeration of some letters to create a lively rhythmic pattern, demonstrate the calligrapher’s mature phase. The text comes from the hadith, the compilation of the Prophet Muhammad's words and deeds that is an important source for moral and legal guidance in the Islamic tradition. On each page, several lines of a small script (*naskhi*) are framed by one or two lines in a larger script (*thuluth* or *muhaqqaq*) and then pasted onto sheets of marbleized paper, which developed in Turkey and came to be much favored for calligraphic works.

649d4fc6-efad-5c54-848f-c9739373ad0f.name: *The Elephant Clock*, folio from a *Book of the Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices* by al-Jazari
649d4fc6-efad-5c54-848f-c9739373ad0f.short_description: This folio comes from a treatise on fantastic devices invented by the author Isma‘il al-Jazari. His elephant clock was especially intricate: every half hour, the bird on the dome whistled, the man below dropped a ball into the dragon’s mouth, and the driver hit the elephant with his goad. This automaton is reminiscent of the elaborate clocks found on medieval town halls in Europe, which made the passage of time more entertaining through the performance of the moving figures. The folio is a rare survival from Syria, where few such manuscripts from this date are known.
