64a752d6-b788-5de5-9e6e-354842dbf466.name: Gravestone.
64a752d6-b788-5de5-9e6e-354842dbf466.description: This rectangular marble slab is carved with an 11-line inscription that is framed within a carved, horseshoe-shaped, pillared arch. Palmettes decorate the spandrels of the arch, and the frieze that forms the decorative border incorporates undulating half-palmette tendrils. The execution of the gravestone reveals that it was designed to include a *mihrab* (prayer niche). Gravestones such as these were typical in Andalusia, particularly in the town of Almería. The inscription is composed in a not very accomplished *kufic* script, the characteristic script of the Maghreb. A classic feature of this script was the subtle inclusion of small leaves or decorative dots within the text. The meaning of the inscription can be outlined as follows: after the *basmala*, the Islamic profession of faith, verses from the Qur’an are quoted (Sura 3 verse 182 and Sura 38 verses 67–8). The name of the deceased follows: ‘This is the grave of Djabir, son of Mohammed al-Khashab, the trader of wood \[?\], who is known under the name of Ibn al-Qallal. He died on the *youm al-Itnine* \[Monday\] of the first decade of the month of Ramadan in the year 435 \[2 April 1044\], at which time he witnessed that there is no God other than God and that Mohammed is God’s Prophet, and that Paradise and Hell, the Resurrection and the Hour of Judgement, all truly exist.’ The profession of faith is referred to in Sura 22 verses 3–7. At the time of the named person’s death, the Banu Sumadih ruled in the important port of Almería. The fact that this type of gravestone, with its typically Andalusian horseshoe arch, has frequently been found around Almería, could suggest that it originated from around there.
64a752d6-b788-5de5-9e6e-354842dbf466.short_description: Horseshoe-arched marble gravestones were typically found in the city of Almería near Malaga in al-Andalus. This example, with its compact *kufic* script completely filling the space and very typical arabesque borders and spandrel fillings, was made for a man who died in AH 435 (AD 1044).
64a752d6-b788-5de5-9e6e-354842dbf466.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum
64a752d6-b788-5de5-9e6e-354842dbf466.method_for_datation: The inscription dates the gravestone to 435 / 1044.
64a752d6-b788-5de5-9e6e-354842dbf466.method_for_provenance: There are markings on the gravestone itself which were made when it was constructed and which are characteristic of gravestones from Almería, Spain.

65973130-c1da-546d-85a1-c58354b8bdfe.name: Bowl fragment.
65973130-c1da-546d-85a1-c58354b8bdfe.description:
An earthenware fragment that formed the centre and part of the rim of a footed and steep-sided bowl, showing a roundel embellished with an incised arabesque decoration; on the rim can be seen fragments of a band of Arabic calligraphic text. The technique, known as *sgraffito* (an Italian word meaning to scratch), involves dipping the vessel into a lighter coloured liquefied clay, known as a slip. With the aid of a pointed tool, the pattern is scratched into the slip, revealing parts of the clay as the design is drawn. The vessel is then glazed and fired. The incised pattern creates contrast; it reveals the colour of the darker clay, while the spaces between the lines show the lighter slip. The glaze on this bowl is a transparent ochre-yellow colour. This type of vessel was less costly to make than coloured ceramics, and therefore fulfilled the demands of the less affluent customers, who had just as much aspiration and taste for glazed wares with decorative texts and patterns, as did the wealthier customers.  
  
The city of Fustat continued to be an active commercial city during the Mamluk period (AH 647–922 / AD 1250–1517), although it had lost some of its fame to Cairo, which was established by the Mamluks and subsequently subsumed by her.
65973130-c1da-546d-85a1-c58354b8bdfe.short_description: This was once part of an impressive steep-sided bowl, decorated using an incising method called *sgraffito* – to scratch. It was less costly to make such monochrome ceramics in comparison to multicoloured ceramics, which made them more affordable to comparatively less-affluent people.
65973130-c1da-546d-85a1-c58354b8bdfe.holder: Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum, Glasgow Museums.

65a53b99-07d5-5553-b2ed-33b6de70f6c6.name: Covered Vessel with Relief Design of Arabic Inscription in *Kufic* Script
65a53b99-07d5-5553-b2ed-33b6de70f6c6.short_description:
A circular steatite vessel with a thin, flat lid with a vertical, eared wing handle that has a mushroom-shaped cut-out in the center. Around the exterior of the lid is a band of cross-hatching, and another band of the same width crossing the diameter of the lid. This band is also cross-hatched on one half, up to where it intersects with the handle, then becomes "transparent," filled only with the raised relief inscription beneath that covers the remaining surface of the lid.  
The vessel has straight sides with an upper and lower border of cross-hatching, enclosing a relief band of inscription. The stone is carved to form an Arabic inscription in relief, in an angular script style known as *Kufic*. The tops of the taller letters end in leaves and flowers, a popular calligraphic device in the 10th century. On opposing sides of the vessel are bar-like handles with deep gouges on their outer edges. The area where each handle attaches to the vessel is bordered by cross-hatching.
65a53b99-07d5-5553-b2ed-33b6de70f6c6.dates: Hegira Late 2nd to late 4th / AD 10th century

65a53b99-07d5-5553-b2ed-33b6de70f6c6.method_for_provenance: Steatite vessels such as this one were used for cooking in the 9th–10th centuries in the northeastern Iranian city of Nishapur. Many small steatite objects have been excavated, but this is the largest complete vessel known.

65b8349d-08ce-503c-b05b-efd23a69c645.name: Box and cover
65b8349d-08ce-503c-b05b-efd23a69c645.short_description: Cast bronze and brass objects displaying religious messages as the Basmala or the Shahada in *Sini* script were popular during the Xuande and Zhengde periods of the Ming Dynasty. 65d47d8e-ddfc-5e73-9b72-7398f5e3072b.name: Amorous couple observed by a wet nurse
65d47d8e-ddfc-5e73-9b72-7398f5e3072b.short_description:
The brush drawing of a pair of lovers in close embrace is by Muʿin Musavvir, one of the most famous and prolific Iranian painters of the 17th century. Young amorous couples were a fairly popular subject in his time and they exist in countless variations. The present version is erotically charged, portraying a young Georgian man (distinguished by his fur cap) embracing a young Persian woman. Self-confident, she stops the demanding gesture of his left hand. Further dating evidence is provided by the swelling calligraphic line, characteristic of 17th century drawings. About a dozen brush drawings by Muʿin are known to exist; quite often, they show a similar palette consisting of red, green and ochre in addition to black ink  
  
Muʿin is known for his rather conservative style, remaining true, during his entire 60 year career, to the style established by Riza ʿAbbasi at the beginning of the 17th century. Therefore, Europeanising motifs are very rare in his oeuvre. However, in this piece he not only integrated a set piece probably stemming from European portraits and prints - the symmetrically divided and high-bound curtain - but also an old woman peering in through the door. The theme of the uninvited observer was to enjoy great popularity in Iran, especially in the 19th century, making it one of the earliest representations of this specific iconography.

65d60827-50d1-52dc-867b-96169525d2f1.name: Brass box.
65d60827-50d1-52dc-867b-96169525d2f1.description: A cylindrical brass box with a hinged lid, inlaid with silver decoration. The lid has a plait design around the edge and four ducks with their necks bent backwards in a knot pattern in the centre. A series of quatrefoil medallions with alternating arabesques and figures, surrounded by a geometric pattern, decorate the body of the box. An Arabic inscription around the lid reads: 'Glory to our master, the clement King, all wise, just, aided by God, victorious, having the support of the Deity, who combats infidels, who practices devotion, Badr al-din Lu'lu', the sword of the commander of the faithful'. Badr al-Din Lu'lu' was appointed Atabeg (Turkish 'father-lord') for three Zangid princes from AH 615–31 / AD 1218–33. Atabegs, initially guardians or tutors for princes of the Seljuq dynasty, grew more powerful while the authority of the Seljuqs waned. In AH 631 / AD 1233 Badr al-Din Lu'lu' became an independent ruler and took sovereign title of Malik al-Rahim after obtaining an investiture from the Abbasid Caliph, al-Mustansir. Badr al-Din Lu'lu' was an active patron of the metalwork industry; no fewer than five extant inlaid metal objects bear his name. Although the inlaid technique was borrowed from the East, the decorative motifs and vessel forms were from local models.
65d60827-50d1-52dc-867b-96169525d2f1.short_description: Mosul was renowned for its metalwork industry in the early AH 7th / AD 13th century. This brass box, inlaid with silver, is particularly interesting as it is inscribed with the name Badr al-din Lu’lu’, who was ruler of Mosul and a keen patron of inlaid metalwork.
65d60827-50d1-52dc-867b-96169525d2f1.dimensions: Height 10.2 cm, diameter (of base) 11 cm; upper diameter (of lid) 8.5 cm.
65d60827-50d1-52dc-867b-96169525d2f1.method_for_datation: The inscription contains the name of Badr al-Din Lu'lu' and his sovereign title; the box would have been produced, therefore, when Badr al-Din was ruler of Mosul between AH 631–59 / AD 1233–59.
65d60827-50d1-52dc-867b-96169525d2f1.method_for_provenance: The inscription mentions the ruler of Mosul, Badr al-Din Lu'lu'. Mosul was a prosperous city on the banks of the Tigris in northern Iraq with a thriving metalwork industry.
65d60827-50d1-52dc-867b-96169525d2f1.bibliography:
Rice, D. S., "The Brasses of Badr al-Din Lulu", in *Bulletin of School of Oriental and African Studies* 13, 1951, pp.627–34.  
  
Ward, R., *Islamic Metalwork*, London, 1993, p.80.
65d60827-50d1-52dc-867b-96169525d2f1.author: Emily Shovelton
keywords: Geometric decoration; figurative decoration; figurative representation; Zangids; inlay; inscription; calligraphy, geometric pattern; geometric decoration; engraving; arabesque
materials: Engraved and silver inlaid brass.

65d727fa-f4a0-5ab9-9f61-747c086b56f5.name: God
65d727fa-f4a0-5ab9-9f61-747c086b56f5.description: In his practice, Haji Noor Deen employs, develops and further interprets Sini calligraphy. The Sini style, which emerged in the 14th century AD, fuses Chinese and Arabic calligraphic traditions. Born in 1963 in Shangdong province, China, Haji Noor Deen graduated from Egypt Sadat Calligraphy School and obtained his calligraphy *ijaza* in Istanbul. This work is made of patterned light blue-gold silk with mounted calligraphy on paper. The central calligraphy in black ink depicts the word "God" in both Chinese and Arabic letters in thick, opaque brush strokes. The title of the work appears in black ink on the left, above two red seals. A third red seal appears on the top right.
materials: Ink and red seal colour on rice paper, mounted on silk

665aed9d-195b-51b5-8961-06a52dfd6aab.name: Piece of the *kiswa* (cover) of the Ka’ba.
665aed9d-195b-51b5-8961-06a52dfd6aab.description:
A piece of the Ka'ba *kiswa* (cover) which was probably produced in Syria, and was sent as part of the *Shami mahmal* (the Syrian Caravan carrying gifts for the Ka'ba) to Mecca to re-adorn the Ka'ba. Such a ritual occurred every year before the season of the Hajj, and included a venerated ceremony at which the commencement of the Hajj season was officially announced. It was and still is the case that the Ka'ba is washed, perfumed and purified every year and is then covered with a new *kiswa*. The fragmentexhibited here is made from red silk and embroidered with silver silken thread. The design includes two undulating bands which assume the form of a continuous chain made up of number “7”s. Both bands run from the beginning to the end of the cloth. Small, dispersed decorative elements are scattered between the two borders, as well as between the two undulating bands. Written inscriptions appear, the most prominent being: “There is no God but God and Muhammad is his Prophet”, repeating in the middle of the *kiswa* between the two zigzag bands. The two expressions, “Ya Mannan” (“Oh Merciful”) and “Ya Hannan” (“Oh Compassionate”) are also repeated, and consist of flowery forms running along both edges. On the upper undulating band, there is a verse from the Qur'an, “al-Baqara” (“the Cow”, 2: 144). The lower undulating band holds another chapter from the Qur'an: Surat Al 'Imran “the Family of Imran” (3:96). At the top and the bottom of the piece there are two expressions: “Dhu al-Jalal” (“Possessor of Majesty”) and “Dhu al-Ikram” (“Possessor of Honour”). One can conceptualise the size of the complete *kiswa* by bringing to mind the enormous scale of the Ka'ba. It is likely that the forms and inscriptions on this piece were repeated on the *kiswa* in its entirety. The name of the donor, the date of production and the emporium where it was produced is not recorded; the evidence has probably been cut off.  
It is worth mentioning that once used to cover the Ka'ba, the *kiswa* was cut into small pieces and sent as gifts to different capitals and cities in the Islamic world to bestow blessing on them. Ruling palaces and councils contained pieces of the *kiswa*, which were used to confer legality and sanctity.
665aed9d-195b-51b5-8961-06a52dfd6aab.short_description: Every year the Ka’ba is washed and covered with a *kiswa* (cover) marking the beginning of the Hajj season. This piece is of red silk and embroidered with silver silk forming fragmented zigzags that repeat from the beginning of the piece to its end. Small forms are scattered in different places within inscription bands.
665aed9d-195b-51b5-8961-06a52dfd6aab.holder: Islamic Museum, al-Aqsa Mosque / al-Haram al-Sharif.
665aed9d-195b-51b5-8961-06a52dfd6aab.method_for_datation: This fragment was dated based on comparison with similar pieces in the museums of Istanbul, whose dates had been narrowed down to around the 13th / 19th century.
665aed9d-195b-51b5-8961-06a52dfd6aab.method_for_provenance: It is likely that this piece was made in Syria, since it is reminiscent of other pieces in the museums of Istanbul known to have been produced in the region.
665aed9d-195b-51b5-8961-06a52dfd6aab.obtention: Al-Sayyid Tahir Sayf al-Din, about whom nothing is known, donated the *kiswa* fragment to the Islamic Museum in 1937.
665aed9d-195b-51b5-8961-06a52dfd6aab.author: Nazmi Al-Ju'beh
keywords: Embroidery; silk; cloth; kiswa of the Ka’ba; textile; silk textile
materials: Silk embroidered with silk thread.

66718328-7241-56c8-a45c-d60aff5e7c2d.name: Cup with inscription.
66718328-7241-56c8-a45c-d60aff5e7c2d.description: Cup with inverted bevelled rim, circular mouth, body in the shape of a bi-truncated cone with low carination, a vertical handle oval in cross-section which joins the carination to the rim, and a flat base with a diagonal foot-ring. The decoration was made using the partial *cuerda seca* technique, with the calligraphic motif drawn with a line of manganese and filled in with green glaze. The text is incomplete although we can read in *kufic* characters *baraka kamila \[wani\]ma ^sa\[mila\]* – 'full blessing and total happiness'. The sentence is not accompanied by any secondary motifs. This is one of the oldest objects with partial *cuerda seca* decoration conserved at Mértola and its ornamental and calligraphic style are somewhat different from the other objects which we can date to the AH 6th / AD 12th century. The object has been restored.
66718328-7241-56c8-a45c-d60aff5e7c2d.short_description: Cup decorated in part using *cuerda seca* with a *kufic* inscription reading ‘*baraka kamila \[wani\]ma sa\[mila*\]’ (‘full blessing and total happiness’). It suggests the need to protect the content of this piece of tableware from Mértola Castle.
66718328-7241-56c8-a45c-d60aff5e7c2d.dates: Hegira second half of 5th or beginning of 6th century / AD second half 11th  or beginning 12th century.
66718328-7241-56c8-a45c-d60aff5e7c2d.dimensions: Height 10.2 cm, width 10.2 cm, diameter (of mouth) 9.1 cm, diameter (of base) 5.3 cm.
66718328-7241-56c8-a45c-d60aff5e7c2d.method_for_datation: It was dated to either the end of the Taifa period or the Almoravid era through stratigraphy.
66718328-7241-56c8-a45c-d60aff5e7c2d.method_for_provenance: Found in the archaeological excavations carried out by the Campo Arqueológico de Mértola in the Castle of Mértola.
66718328-7241-56c8-a45c-d60aff5e7c2d.obtention: This is a type of ceramic made in various regions of al-Andalus, but whose production has not yet been recorded in the west of the Iberian Peninsula.
66718328-7241-56c8-a45c-d60aff5e7c2d.bibliography:
Gómez Martínez, S., *A Cerâmica em Corda Seca de Mértola*, Mértola, 2002.  
Torres, C. and Macias, S. (eds.), *O Portugal Islâmico*, Lisbon, 1998, p.100.
66718328-7241-56c8-a45c-d60aff5e7c2d.author: Susana Gómez Martínez
keywords: ceramic; cuerda seca; calligraphy; inscription
materials: Ceramic made with coarse-grained straw and paste mix, modelled on a wheel, fired in an oxidising atmosphere and decorated with the partial *cuerda seca* technique.

667d3cdf-1c40-5a61-84fe-460d9be0bae9.name: Memorial stone.
667d3cdf-1c40-5a61-84fe-460d9be0bae9.description:
This half-cylinder memorial stone, or stele, made of blue marble, has a rectangular inscription framed with a border. Both the *kufic* characters and the plaited border are carved on a sunken base and decorated with chisel work. The inscription, which contains a number of prayers to God and identifies the deceased, reads: 'In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate, oh, you men! \[have faith\] that God's promises are true and do not allow yourselves to be seduced by earthly pleasures, and do not let temptation lead you away from God. This \[is\] the tomb of ibn Ahmad Muhammad ibn Mugit … He died, God have mercy on him, on the night … year seven and forty and four hundred'.  
This type of funerary monument, which seems to originate from Tunisia, in al-Andalus only appears in the region of Toledo and all such pieces share the same formal characteristics. They are cylindrical or semi-cylindrical, widening at the edges, and the inscription, which is always rectangular, is sunken and framed with a border. The funerary inscription tends to include the same information: the name of the deceased and the date of his death, sometimes with prayers to him and even the person reading the inscription. The remainder of the epitaph is religious in character.  
Hispano-Muslim tombs are generally very simple, but are very varied. This stone, placed at the head of the tomb, is one example of this variety.
667d3cdf-1c40-5a61-84fe-460d9be0bae9.short_description: This funerary stone, known as a *cipo*, is characteristic of Toledo. These cylindrical or semi-cylindrical stelae were placed at the head of the graves of important people.
667d3cdf-1c40-5a61-84fe-460d9be0bae9.dimensions: Height 127 cm, width 50.5 cm, inscribed area 107 x 46 cm.
667d3cdf-1c40-5a61-84fe-460d9be0bae9.method_for_provenance: Both the type of funerary monument and the features of the inscription on it (*kufic* characters embellished with chisel work) indicate that the piece was made in the Taifa kingdom of Toledo. It came from the convent of San Bartolomé de Toledo.
667d3cdf-1c40-5a61-84fe-460d9be0bae9.obtention: The piece was obtained by the National Archaeological Museum from the old Natural History Museum as part of the organisation of the state collection in 1867 (the month and day are unknown). It was undoubtedly part of the original collection of the Museum, which was founded the same year.

Revilla Vielva, R., *Catálogo de las Antigüedades que Se Conservan en el Patio árabe del Museo Arqueológico Nacional*, Madrid, 1932, p.102, no. 238.
667d3cdf-1c40-5a61-84fe-460d9be0bae9.dynasty: Taifa kingdom of Toledo, dynasty of Banu Dhi'l-Nun (Dhu'l-Nunids)
667d3cdf-1c40-5a61-84fe-460d9be0bae9.author: Margarita Sánchez Llorente
keywords: Gravestone; marble; carving; funerary inscription; Taifa kingdoms; Toledo; funerary stele; funerary object
materials: Chiselled and carved marble.

66dee6a2-095c-5e95-9ab7-3051179223bf.name: *Zubdat al-Tawarikh* (‘Cream of Histories’).
66dee6a2-095c-5e95-9ab7-3051179223bf.description:
The work is written in Turkish with large *naskhi* script in black ink on 90 leaves of delicate finished (*aharlı*) paper. Within are 55 miniatures depicting subjects in the text, some of them one to a page and some two. On pages 1b–2a two round medallions carry an inscription stating the work's subject and saying that it was prepared for the Treasury of Sultan Murad III (r. AH 982–1003 / AD 1574–95). The text is written 37 lines to a page; the titles and chapter headings are gilded. Their illumination features floral compositions with arabesques (*rumi*) and Chinese-inspired motifs (*hatayi*-style), while that of the first two pages' medallions includes large floral motifs (*halkar*\-style).  
  
The work's dark-green cover is lacquered using a technique known as *Edirnekari*. The outer covers are richly decorated with gold and silver in floral compositions, while the inner covers feature medallions, pendants and corner-pieces. The binding is not original.  
  
The work, which was written by the court panegyrist (*Şehnameci*) Sayyid Loqman Aşuri, consists of two main sections. The first begins with the universe and the signs of the zodiac and continues with stories taken from the Torah, the New Testament, and the Qur'an which tell of the lives of prophets and those who rendered service to the faith. These are illustrated with paintings. The first part ends with genealogical trees of the Prophet Muhammad, the Four Orthodox Caliphs, and the sultans and high officials of Muslim dynasties such as the Umayyads, the 'Abbasids, the early Islamic period, the Ghaznawids, the Ilkhanids, the Seljuqs and the Timurids. The second part opens with Sultan Osman, the founder of the Ottoman dynasty, and goes up to Sultan Murad III, with 12 portraits of Ottoman sultans. It ends with descriptions of the political events of these sultans' reigns.  
  
This work was made for the Treasury of Sultan Murad III, and the quality of its paintings, its binding and its calligraphy make it one of the greatest works of Ottoman art created for a sultan.
66dee6a2-095c-5e95-9ab7-3051179223bf.short_description: This manuscript includes stories of the prophets, the birth of Islam and histories of Muslim states. It was written on the order of Sultan Murad III by the historian Sayyid Lokman and illuminated by famous *naqqash* (painters) Molla Kasım and Ustad Osman. It is a unique work of Ottoman art.
66dee6a2-095c-5e95-9ab7-3051179223bf.type: Manuscript, miniature, paper, ink, leather binding, lacquered
66dee6a2-095c-5e95-9ab7-3051179223bf.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts.
66dee6a2-095c-5e95-9ab7-3051179223bf.method_for_datation: It is stated on the work that it was prepared for the Treasury of Sultan Murad III (r. 982–1003 / 1574–95) in 993 (1583).
66dee6a2-095c-5e95-9ab7-3051179223bf.method_for_provenance: The work was almost certainly written in Istanbul by order of the Sultan.
66dee6a2-095c-5e95-9ab7-3051179223bf.obtention: Transferred to the Museum in 1915 from the Library of the complex in Aksaray (Istanbul) founded by the wife of Sultan Mahmud II and mother of Sultan Abdülaziz ('Abd al-'Aziz) I, Pertevniyal Valide Sultan (d. 1300 / 1883; queen mother from 1277–92 / AD 1861–76).

66ef3821-0608-5a20-9446-662a31c4e610.name: *Divan-ı* Ali Şir Nevai (Social Gathering for Entertainment)
66ef3821-0608-5a20-9446-662a31c4e610.description:
This copy of Ali Şîr Nevâî's *Divan*, a collection of poems written under his pseudonym, Fânî, is dated Hegira 943 / AD 1536–1537, and is signed by Mir Ali al-Bukhârî. It is written in Chagatai Turkish in *Nastaliq* calligraphy in two columns on papers of various colours with different patterns and *zerefşan* (gold leaf).  
On page 1a is a text written in a circular medallion with superscript text. This states that the work was prepared for Abdülazîz Khan, b. Ubeydullah Khan, one of the rulers of the Shaybânî Dynasty, an Islamic dynasty that ruled in Mâverâünnehir, Khârezm and Khorasan. At the top of the same page is the seal of Sultan Mahmud I's foundation, and below it is the seal of Derviş Mustafa Efendi, inspector of Evkaf. On the following facing pages is a scene of entertainment in the countryside. The title page is decorated with floral and geometric motifs. There are a total of eight miniatures in the work.  
The binding comprises two covers, the outer of which is leather over cardboard. It is decorated with Chinese clouds and various floral motifs on a gilt ground. The inner cover is made of brown leather, and the backgrounds of borders, corners, and edges of panels are navy blue. These sections with navy blue grounds are decorated with floral motifs obtained by the *kat’ı* (paper cutting) technique.
66ef3821-0608-5a20-9446-662a31c4e610.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts
66ef3821-0608-5a20-9446-662a31c4e610.obtention: The item was brought to the Museum from the Mahmud I Library on 13 April 1914.
materials: Finished (*aharli*) paper, ink, gilding, leather binding

6727ef2a-3a08-5d1f-a254-abd5bdf97f5f.name:
Isfandiyar’s second exploit: he kills two lions  
Folio from a dispersed copy of Firdausi’s *Shahnameh* (Book of Kings)
6727ef2a-3a08-5d1f-a254-abd5bdf97f5f.short_description: Recounting the story of Iran from mythical times through to the arrival of the Muslim Arabs in the mid-7th century AD, the epic poem the *Shahnameh* (Book of Kings) was originally completed in 1010 by the poet Firdausi. These dramatic scenes centering on Isfandiyar, son of King Gushtasp, were included in a 1341 Shahnameh that is now dispersed. The story of Isfandiyar’s exploits recalls the seven trials that the great hero Rustam underwent in his quest to liberate King Kay Kavus from captivity in a much earlier Shahnameh story. Isfandiyar endured his labours en route to rescuing his two sisters, who were captured during the ongoing war between Iran and Turan. Isfandiyar decided to take the shortest but most dangerous route to the Brazen Hold, the Turanian fortress made of brass where his sisters were imprisoned.
6727ef2a-3a08-5d1f-a254-abd5bdf97f5f.obtention: Former Prince Saddrudin Aga Khan Collection
6727ef2a-3a08-5d1f-a254-abd5bdf97f5f.bibliography: Simpson, Marianna Shreve, “A Reconstruction and Preliminary Account of the 1341 Shahnama, With Some Further Thoughts on Early Shahnama Illustration,” in Robert Hillenbrand (ed), *Persian Painting from the Mongols to the Qajars*, London / New York: I.B. Tauris Publishers, 2000: 217­–47. ISBN: 9781850436591.
keywords: Folio; work-on-paper; works-on-paper; Shahnama; Shahnameh
materials: Ink, coloured pigments and gold on paper

672e5d81-e294-5bdc-9691-e88fb689a760.name: Page from a Qur’an.
672e5d81-e294-5bdc-9691-e88fb689a760.description:
The Fatiha *sura* ('the Opening', verses 1 and 2), taken from a Qur'an copied on parchment.  
The writing combines the *kufic, naskhi* and the *rayhani* styles. Its identity has still not been well established. The laying out of the cursive script is more rectangular than curved.  
Vowel-points are absent from this writing, but, in keeping with the system developed by al-Khalil ibn Ahmad, there is an abundance of orthographic signs. Vowels are marked in red, *sukun* and *shadda* in blue and *hamza* and *maddah* in brilliant green.  
Standing out on this page is a strip containing the title and number of verses in the following *sura*, written in gold.  
The title is inscribed in a series of superimposed frames in which geometric decoration alternates with floral decoration using the multi-lobed fleuron. Some strips are engraved in gold and all the surrounds are brown. A palm-leaf motif made up of floral arabesques projects towards the edge of the page.  
At the top of the page in the right-hand margin there is a geometrically decorated gold and brown lozenge; the corners each have a crown in the same colour and the sides have blue and brown circles on the outer edge.  
The central area contains gilded *kufic* script indicating the number of the verses.
672e5d81-e294-5bdc-9691-e88fb689a760.short_description: This page is from a Qur'an copied on vellum. Bands of geometric decoration with the name of the *sura* and the number of verses it contains, in gold, are particularly distinctive. The colophon of the Qur'an mentions the deed of gift by the governess of Prince Badis to the Great Mosque of Kairouan.
672e5d81-e294-5bdc-9691-e88fb689a760.initial_owner: Fatima al-Hadinah, governess to the Zirid prince, Badis.
672e5d81-e294-5bdc-9691-e88fb689a760.dimensions: Length 45.5 cm, width 31 cm; 5 lines, 1 folio.
672e5d81-e294-5bdc-9691-e88fb689a760.method_for_datation: The deed of gift clearly mentions that the legacy took place in 410 / 1020.
672e5d81-e294-5bdc-9691-e88fb689a760.method_for_provenance: This Qur'an was copied, illuminated and bound by Ali ibn Ahmad al-Warraq for Fatima al-Hadinah, the governess of the Zirid prince, Badis. The work was supervised and financed by Durah al-Katibah – 'Durah the lady-scribe', the governess's secretary. The colophon of the Qur'an mentions the deed of gift by Badis's governess to the Great Mosque of Kairouan. The deed is authorised by the *qadi* (judge) of Kairouan, Abdullah ibn Hashim.
672e5d81-e294-5bdc-9691-e88fb689a760.obtention: After the abolition of the *habus* foundation in Tunisia, this Qur'an was obtained by the Bardo Museum. In 1986 it was transferred to the Museum of Islamic Art at Raqqada where it is currently on display.
672e5d81-e294-5bdc-9691-e88fb689a760.bibliography:

*De Carthage a Kairouan* (exhibition catalogue), Paris, 1982, p.273, plate no. 357.

672e5d81-e294-5bdc-9691-e88fb689a760.author: Mourad Rammah
keywords: Calligraphy; floral decoration; geometric decoration; rihani; religious manuscript
materials: Parchment.

67588ccf-7bc8-58e5-9aa6-c4888f344477.name: Flask
67588ccf-7bc8-58e5-9aa6-c4888f344477.description: This large free-blown bottle of green glass is unique for having survived completely intact except for a silvery iridescence on the surface. Its three loop handles are too small to have supported the weight of the bottle with its unknown contents. Instead, they may have been used in conjunction with a stopper on the bottle’s thick, short neck. Slightly above the vessel’s centre, three stamped discs with three short lines of angular *kufic* script surrounded by a circle have been applied. The Arabic text reads "Abu Ja‘far al-Mu‘ammar" (the work of Abu Ja'far), perhaps referring to the maker of the glass vessel or the owner of the glass workshop where it was produced.
materials: Glass, green, applied discs with impressed inscription; free-blown, tooled, worked on the pontil

67922d20-5d70-50d8-8bad-67dac73d8269.name: Inscribed limestone panel.
67922d20-5d70-50d8-8bad-67dac73d8269.description:
An inscribed limestone panel documenting the rebuilding of the Castle of Ajlun in Shaban in AH 659 (July 1261), during the reign of the Mamluk Sultan al-Zahir Baybars (AH 658–76 / AD 1260–77).  
  
In AD 1927 an earthquake struck Jordan and Palestine which caused the collapse of the south-west corner of the Castle of Ajlun. In 1963 the Department of Antiquities of Jordan conducted a restoration programme of the south-west side of the castle and a clean up of the moat that surrounds it. While the operation was in progress this inscribed panel was found, which refers to the rebuilding of the third floor of the castle and which can, therefore, be securely dated to the Mamluk period.  
  
The inscription consists of three lines written in naskhi (cursive) script that reads:  
  
" عمل من ايام مولانا السلطان الملك الظاهر (ركن) الدنبا و الدين بيبرس الصالحي اعز الله انظاره بنظر العبد الفقير الراجي عفو الله و غفرانه (ملك) الامراء عز الدين ايبك العلائي بتاريخ العشرين من شعبان سنة تسعة و خمسين و ستماية".  
  
'Done, during the days of our master the Sultan, the king al-Zahir, the pillar of the world and religion, Baybars al-Salhi, may God bless his peers, under the supervision of Izz al-Din al-‘Alali, the poor servant and seeker of amnesty and forgiveness of God the king of princes in the year 659.'
67922d20-5d70-50d8-8bad-67dac73d8269.short_description: An inscribed limestone panel, written in naskhi (cursive) script, that documents the rebuilding of the third floor of the Castle of Ajlun on the 20th of Sha‘ban in AH 659 (July 1261), by Amir ‘Izz al-Din Aybak al-‘Ala’i, during the reign of the Mamluk Sultan al-Zahir Baybars (658–76 / 1260–77).
67922d20-5d70-50d8-8bad-67dac73d8269.method_for_datation: The inscription itself bears the dates of the reconstruction of the third floor of the castle.
67922d20-5d70-50d8-8bad-67dac73d8269.method_for_provenance: The panel was found in the immediate vicinity of the castle, in the moat.
67922d20-5d70-50d8-8bad-67dac73d8269.obtention: The panel was recovered in 1963 during restoration of the Castle of Ajlun and the cleaning of the surrounding moat.

67ae5352-aaad-57a1-9050-4df90cfc07e6.name: *Suz u gudaz* (‘Burning and Melting’)
67ae5352-aaad-57a1-9050-4df90cfc07e6.short_description: *Suz u gudaz* (‘Burning and Melting’) is a romance, an allegorical poem that tells of the soul’s yearning for God through the story of a Hindu woman who, following the custom known as *sati*, ended her life on her husband’s funeral pyre. The poet Muhammad Riza, known as Naw‘i (d.1619), was born in Khabushan in north-eastern Iran, but later travelled to India where he composed the poem for Prince Daniyal, son of the Mughal emperor Akbar (r. 1556–1605). The three paintings shown here depict the worship of fire, the young man telling his father of his beloved, and the two lovers seated in a garden with an attendant standing nearby.
67ae5352-aaad-57a1-9050-4df90cfc07e6.dates: Hegira mid 11th century / AD mid 17th century
keywords: illustration; miniature painting; calligraphy; script; illumination
materials: Coloured pigments and gold on paper

681543eb-7d4b-5d8f-91c4-bdb708f84dc9.name: Qazwini, Zakariya Ibn-Muhammad al-, Tuhfatu i-Gharaʾib (ʿAjaʾibu i-Mahluqat wa Gharaʾibu i-Mawjudat) (The Gift of Oddities)
681543eb-7d4b-5d8f-91c4-bdb708f84dc9.short_description: This manuscript is a Persian copy of Zakariya Ibn-Muhammad al-Qazwini’s (1203-1283) Arabic original “Tuhfatu i-Gharaʾib” (“The Gift of Oddities”) calligraphed by the scribe Pir Husain al-Katib. This copy can be localised in Shiraz and was inspired by the Herati style however it also reflects Turkmen and Safavid styles as well. The date 1492 is mentioned in the colophon and soon after its production, it is likely that it came into the collection of Shah Tahmasp (1514-1576), whose seal can be found within. The manuscript has richly embellished double opening pages situated within a decorative blue and gold colour scheme interspersed with floral scrolls and colourful buds and flowers. There are 204 illustrations scattered across various pages of the manuscript showing constellations, zodiacal signs, celestial symbols, animals, and fantastical creatures, among other depictions. These paintings mostly occupy a small section of the text area, and often protrude into the empty margins that surround the written text. There are occasional colour abrasions in the illustrations, as well as some miniatures having been painted over in the early Safavid period, but they are mostly well-preserved.
681543eb-7d4b-5d8f-91c4-bdb708f84dc9.dimensions: 240 x 170mm (text area 145 x 95mm). ff. I, I*, 310.
681543eb-7d4b-5d8f-91c4-bdb708f84dc9.method_for_provenance: Seal of Tahmasp I. (1514–1576). This object is presumably from the collection of Jakob von Wallenburg (d. 1806). It was also part of the collection of Graf Wenceslaus von Rzewuski (d. 1831), after which it entered the collection of Joseph Freiherr von Hammer-Purgstall (d. 1856; his seal is on f. 310b).
681543eb-7d4b-5d8f-91c4-bdb708f84dc9.obtention: Entered the Austrian National Library in 1842.

681543eb-7d4b-5d8f-91c4-bdb708f84dc9.binding_desc: The dark brown leather binding with a renewed green flap was likely produced in early 16th-century Tabriz, and restored in 1921 in Vienna. The front and back cover include a cut-out medallion with corner pieces created as recessed leather inlays with gold relief stamping. From a central rosette, a flower tendril extends upwards and downwards in an S-shape. Within, four symmetrically arranged cranes or herons are depicted in mid-flight. The extensions directly above and below attached to the central medallion include a seated hare. The spine, which has been renewed, has three cartouches with gold-stamped leather inlay, showing floral tendrils ending in animal heads. The leather doublures also show a cut-out medallion design containing delicate arabesque leather filigree on a blue ground, with golden contour lines.

68ecd47c-38f6-579b-9162-d8283100397d.name: *Siyer-i Nebi* (‘Biography of the Prophet’).
68ecd47c-38f6-579b-9162-d8283100397d.description:
The work is written in Turkish on delicate finished (*aharlı*) paper using 13 lines per page of large *naskhi* script. The text is written within gilded margins in black ink; proper names are written in red ink. The areas between the lines of text are filled with gilding whose edges are traced in black. The six-volume *Siyer-i Nebi* or 'Biography of the Prophet' tells of the life of the Prophet Muhammad and of the history of Islam up until his death. The volume in the Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts is a copy of the fourth volume and has 545 folios. A total of 193 miniatures depict the subjects within. The first page, an illuminated title page, is decorated with gilding. On those pages with miniatures, the painting is situated between the top and bottom two lines of text. The volume's brown leather binding is adorned with an oval medallion with palmette pendants and corner-pieces.  
  
The fourth volume begins with the birth of the Prophet's daughter, Fatima, and goes on to describe her marriage to 'Ali; the miracles of Muhammad; the love of Talha and Gamza; tales of heroic Muslim women; the preparation for the battle of Badr and the battle itself; Muhammad's wounding at the battle of Uhud; the death of the Prophet's uncle Hamza; the distribution of the spoils of war; the story of Ka'b and his daughter; and the killing of the Muslims' enemy, Sufyan ibn Khalid.  
  
*Siyer-i Nebi* was prepared in six volumes by the palace atelier at the behest of Sultan Murad III in the AH 10th / AD 16th century. Today one volume is lost, while the others are dispersed in libraries around the world. The manuscript in the Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts is a copy (made in the AH 11th- / AD 17th-century) of a manuscript of the fourth volume of *Siyer-i Nebi* in the Chester Beatty Library in Dublin, (T. 419). The miniatures are stylistically typical of the period.
68ecd47c-38f6-579b-9162-d8283100397d.short_description: This AH 11th- / AD 17th-century copy of *Siyer-i Nebi*, literally 'Life of the Prophet', has an important place in Ottoman art not only because of subject but also because of its binding, the figurative style of its miniatures, and its architectural compositions.
68ecd47c-38f6-579b-9162-d8283100397d.type: Manuscript, miniature, paper, ink, leather binding

68ecd47c-38f6-579b-9162-d8283100397d.initial_owner: The original owner is unknown, but a seal belonging to the wife of Sultan Mahmud II, Pertevniyal Valide Sultan (d. AH 1300 /AD 1883; queen mother from AH 1277–92 / AD 1861–76), bearing the date AH 1279 / AD 1862–63, is found on pages 1a and 545a.
68ecd47c-38f6-579b-9162-d8283100397d.method_for_datation: The style of the miniatures is characteristic of the 11th / 17th century.
68ecd47c-38f6-579b-9162-d8283100397d.method_for_provenance: Manuscripts of this quality and cost can only have been made in the palace atelier.
68ecd47c-38f6-579b-9162-d8283100397d.obtention: The manuscript was transferred to the Museum in 1334 / 1916 from the library of the complex in Aksaray (Istanbul) founded by the wife of Sultan Mahmud II and mother of Sultan Abdülaziz I ('Abd al-'Aziz), Pertevniyal Valide Sultan (d. AH 1300 /AD 1883; queen mother from AH 1277–92 / AD 1861–76).

690ddb14-8419-58b9-8cc0-666d98a20849.name: Abu Mansur Muwaffaq ibn 'Ali al-Harawi, *Kitab al-Abniya 'an haqa'iq ad-adwiya* ('The Book of Fundamentals on the True Nature of Remedies')
690ddb14-8419-58b9-8cc0-666d98a20849.short_description: This is the oldest known surviving Islamic manuscript in the Persian language. It is a copy of the 10th-century writer Abu Mansur Muwaffaq ibn 'Ali al-Harawi’s so-called *Kitab al-Abniya 'an haqa'iq ad-adwiya* (‘The Book of Fundamentals on the True Nature of Remedies’), the content of which he attributes to the Samanid writer Mansur b. Nuh around 350-365 AH / 961-976 AD. According to the colophon, this manuscript was written in monumental calligraphic angular (*kufic*) script by 'Ali b. Ahmad al-Asadi at-Tusi Ash-Shatr in 447 AH / 1055-56 AD, possibly in Nakhchivan, Azerbaijan. This writer was also a poet who wrote the heroic epic entitled *Garshaspnama*, which was based on the famous ‘Book of Kings’ (*Shahnama*). The copy is dedicated to an *ar-ra'is al-jalil al-amjad* Abu'l-Qasim. In the margins, Turkish glosses from a later time reveal the manuscript’s stay in Turkey after which it can be traced to the inventory of the Austrian National Library in 1811.
690ddb14-8419-58b9-8cc0-666d98a20849.method_for_provenance: On fol. 1a, a dedication to a certain *ar-ra'is al-jalil al-amjad* Abu'l-Qasim was added, while the work itself is attributed to the Samanid writer Mansur b. Nuh (350-365 AH / 961-976 AD). Later Turkish marginal glosses prove the manuscript's stay in Turkey.
690ddb14-8419-58b9-8cc0-666d98a20849.obtention: Unknown but part of the Austrian National Library before 1811.
690ddb14-8419-58b9-8cc0-666d98a20849.bibliography: Duda, Dorothea, *Islamische Handschriften I. Persische Handschriften, Die illuminierten Handschriften und Inkunabeln der Österreichischen Nationalbibliothek*, vol. 4, Vienna: Verlag der Österreichischen Akademie der Wissenschaften, 1983: 51-52.
690ddb14-8419-58b9-8cc0-666d98a20849.binding_desc: The brown neo-classical leather binding with gold printing was created in 19th-century Vienna.

6945b03a-e793-5c51-8b45-3e3ebf550370.name: Ceramic bowl.
6945b03a-e793-5c51-8b45-3e3ebf550370.description:
The shallow shape of the bowl and the attempt to imitate the whiteness of porcelain are evidence of the admiration the Muslim potters had for Chinese ceramics. Early Abbasid potters created a tin-glaze or under-fired alkaline glaze in order to conceal the earthy colour of their wares with an opaque whiteness imitating Chinese porcelain. The decoration on this bowl includes four spontaneously flowing streams of green running from the border towards the centre. In the middle of the dish are three lines of angular Arabic *kufic* script that are decorative and not clearly legible.  
It is possible to read the first line as: “was made by which …" This is unusual as the proper phrasing should be "which was made by…". The second line is not entirely legible, but can be read as: “Muhammad”, possibly indicating the name of the craftsman. There are similar ceramic bowls exhibiting the same name. The third line reads: "enjoy your meal". Such wares were regularly decorated with aphorisms and good wishes to the owner.
6945b03a-e793-5c51-8b45-3e3ebf550370.short_description: The fashion for Chinese ceramics among early Muslim potters is evidenced by the opaque whiteness and crackled effect of the glaze as applied on this Abbasid dish. Its designer, possibly named Muhammad, is trying to imitate Chinese porcelain.
6945b03a-e793-5c51-8b45-3e3ebf550370.method_for_datation: The dating is approximated to the AH 3rd– 4th/ AD 9th–10th century or Abbasid period, based on stylistic and comparative evidence. Most bowls in this Eastern style are attributed to the period of the Buyid Dynasty, also known as the Buwayhids, an Islamic Dynasty of Persian origin and Shi'ite faith, who ruled in Iraq between 338–447/ 943–1055 while maintaining loyalty to the Abbasid caliphate in Baghdad.
6945b03a-e793-5c51-8b45-3e3ebf550370.method_for_provenance: This type of ware was made in Mesopotamia and al-Jazira and shows Eastern influences. There were various centres of production.
6945b03a-e793-5c51-8b45-3e3ebf550370.provenance: Al-Jazira (the region located between the Euphrates and Tigris rivers, hence known as “the island”; currently consisting of northeast modern Syria and northwest Iraq), or Mesopotamia.

694dde47-bada-58b2-bcc0-6d5bd86a4ac0.name: Great lantern of al-Mu‘izz.
694dde47-bada-58b2-bcc0-6d5bd86a4ac0.description: The lantern is made up of a bronze hook supporting a shallow-domed hemispherical basin with an outwardly inclined upper rim. Attached to the six-faceted outer sides of the basin are three perforated chains with geometric and stylised floral decoration in the form of tracery and tri-lobed leaves. This is a common type of decoration in Middle-Age Kairouan. The chains support the large hammered-brass basin, which is shaped like a circular vase and allows light to shine through the myriad perforations. At the lowest point of the basin a six-point star has been punched out. This is surrounded by three inscriptions, one around the collar; another between the ring supports and a third circling the star. On the first strip, *kufic* calligraphy proclaims: 'Praise be to God … May he bestow blessings, good fortune, happiness, success, prosperity, health and glory on all who embrace Him.' On the circumference of the base is inscribed: 'The work of Muhammad son of Ali al-Qaysi al-Saffar \[the metalworker\] for al-Mu'izz.' This lantern closely resembles a mosque lamp kept at the Chicago Art Institute and a lantern of Persian origin belonging to the David collection in Copenhagen (Denmark). Both date from the AH 4th or 5th centuries (AD 11th century). All the evidence suggests that the lantern of al-Mu'izz, which lit up the Great Mosque of Kairouan, is an example of Byzantine–inspired craftsmanship, which was in vogue throughout the Arabic-Islamic world during the AH 4th and 5th centuries (AD 10th and 11th).
694dde47-bada-58b2-bcc0-6d5bd86a4ac0.short_description: Used to light the Great Mosque of Kairouan, this lantern is an example of Byzantine-inspired craftsmanship fashionable in Arab-Islamic society in the AH 4th–5th / AD 10th–11th centuries. A bronze hook supports a shallow basin from which three chains suspend a large circular brass basin perforated with holes for light.
694dde47-bada-58b2-bcc0-6d5bd86a4ac0.method_for_datation: The last inscription states that the lantern was a gift from the Zirid prince, al-Mu'izz ibn Badis (r. 406–54 / 1016–62) to the Great Mosque of Kairouan. This donation could be contemporaneous with the legacy of the *Mudawwana* volumes, the work of the great Sunni legal expert Sahnun ibn Said (160–240 / 777–855), from the same prince to the Great Mosque of Kairouan in 424 / 1032. It was certainly before the Hilalian invasions of 443 / 1051.
694dde47-bada-58b2-bcc0-6d5bd86a4ac0.method_for_provenance: This lantern was part of the furniture of the Great Mosque of Kairouan. It was specially made by a lamp-maker for the reigning Zirid prince, so it was probably fabricated in a Kairouanese workshop.
694dde47-bada-58b2-bcc0-6d5bd86a4ac0.obtention: After the founding of the Museum of Islamic Art at Raqqada in 1986 it was decided to return this lantern, which was on display at the Bardo Museum, to its original location.

69654e77-fcb8-5e56-8ab2-fb9b8b39f35b.name: Bronze coin (*fils*).
69654e77-fcb8-5e56-8ab2-fb9b8b39f35b.description:
An Umayyad bronze coin (*fils*) from the period that followed Abd al-Malik's coinage reform of AH 77 / AD 696, distinguished by the formula of the faith, the Shahada, and a purely epigraphic style that incorporated Qur'anic verses. This fils was minted in Jarash, which was part of Jund al-Urdun (one of the five military and administrative provinces in the early Islamic period).  
  
On the obverse, within concentric circles is an Arabic legend from the Qur'an written in *kufic* script that reads from right to left: 'La 'ilaha illa-Allah' ('There is one God; Muhammad is the messenger of God'), which is the second part of the Shahada.  
  
On the reverse, within a circle of dots there is an Arabic legend in *kufic* script that reads: 'Muhammad Rasul Allah' ('Mohammad is the messenger of God').  
  
The marginal legend between two circles reads: 'bism Allah duriba hadha al-Fils bi Jarash' ('In the name of God. This Fils is minted in Jarash').
69654e77-fcb8-5e56-8ab2-fb9b8b39f35b.short_description: This bronze fils has a *kufic* legend on the obverse La 'ilaha illa Allah (there is no God but Allah), and on the reverse Muhammad Rasul Allah (Muhammad is the messenger of God) with bism Allah duriba hadha al-fils bi Jarash (in the name of God, this fils was minted in Jarash).
69654e77-fcb8-5e56-8ab2-fb9b8b39f35b.method_for_datation: The name of the mint 'Jarash' appears only on bronze coins minted during the Islamic period of the Umayyads and stops with the fall of the dynasty. Also, since representational images are replaced by epigraphic inscriptions on this coin, it was minted after ‘Abd al-Malik's administrative reforms of 77 / 696–7.
69654e77-fcb8-5e56-8ab2-fb9b8b39f35b.method_for_provenance: Provenance for this coin is established by the inclusion of the mint name 'Jarash' in the inscription.
69654e77-fcb8-5e56-8ab2-fb9b8b39f35b.obtention: The object was purchased from an antiquities dealer in 1998.

69bdb01a-4161-5c8b-8079-4bbee1cbfb1d.name: *Noah’s Ark*
69bdb01a-4161-5c8b-8079-4bbee1cbfb1d.short_description:
Timur’s son Shah Rukh (r. AH 808-851 / AD 1405-1447) ordered the historian Hafiz-i Abru to write a continuation of Rashid al-Din’s famous history of the world, Jami al-tawarikh. Like the Il-Khanids, the Timurids were concerned with legitimizing their right to rule, and Hafiz-i Abru’s “A Collection of Histories” covers a period that included the time of Shah Rukh himself.  
  
The style of the manuscript’s miniatures is slightly old-fashioned compared with the otherwise refined Timurid painting, but the scene on the stormy sea is quite dramatic, with the fluttering sail, the ark breaking out of the picture frame and the swollen bodies. The animals that are to populate the earth are rendered both humorously and fairly realistically.
69bdb01a-4161-5c8b-8079-4bbee1cbfb1d.type: Miniature from Hafiz-i Abru’s *Majma' al-tawarikh*, manuscript

69f100f8-b478-59cb-921a-5cdfd266ab6e.name: Vase.
69f100f8-b478-59cb-921a-5cdfd266ab6e.description:
This vase is composed of a raised base, a pear-shaped body and a long neck ending on top with the mouth of the vase. The mouth is characterised by a flat edge and four pierced holes. The neck in turn contains three decorative bands. The first band is ornamented with vegetal and geometric motifs interspersed by three medallions, each of which is filled with vegetal decoration made up of six petals of silver, edged in gold. The second band is adorned with vegetal decorative motifs, interrupted by three circular cartouches. Each cartouche is filled with vegetal motifs and depictions of flying ducks. The areas between the cartouches bear inscriptions in Mamluk *naskhi* script that read: 'One of the things made for the sublime Excellency, al-Sayfi Toghostomor al-Malaki al-Nasiri.' The third band is adorned with decorations that are identical to those on the first band. The neck of the vase is attached to the body by a prominent circular band decorated with vegetal ornamentation.  
The body of the vase is composed of five bands edged in gold and decorated in silver. The first band is decorated with vegetal motifs, interrupted by three-lobed roundels, each of which is adorned by a lotus blossom. The second band is decorated by three large segmented roundels, each of which contains a blazon mounted on top with a band. Each blazon has in its centre a one-headed eagle with a depiction of a cup underneath it. The band contains an inscription in *naskhi* script, inlaid in gold against a background of vegetal decoration in silver, the text of which reads: 'One of the things commissioned for the honourable Excellency/ the sublime master, the great *amir*, al-Sayfi /Toghostomor al-Malaki al-Nasiri'. The text alludes to Toghostomor, who was one of the *amir*s of Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun who ruled three times: AH 693–4 / AD 1294–5; AH 698–708 / AD 1299–1309; AH 709–41 / AD 1309–40. Amir Toghostomor held a number of offices in the sultan's palace amongst which was the position of cup-bearer, i.e. the person responsible for the sultan's drinks. The third decorative band is also interrupted by three lobed medallions, inside each of which is a depiction of a lotus blossom. As for the forth and fifth bands, they are characterised by vegetal decorative motifs, lotus blossoms and flying ducks.  
The base of the vase is decorated by a band interrupted by three cartouches. Inside each cartouche there is an undulating or spiral decorative pattern set against a background of vegetal decorative motifs. The band also bears an epigraphic inscription indicating that the owner of the vase is Amir Toghostomor.
69f100f8-b478-59cb-921a-5cdfd266ab6e.short_description: This brass vase, decorated with vegetal and geometrical motifs, birds, and epigraphic inscriptions, bears the name of its owner, Amir Toghostomor, the Sultan's cupbearer, and his blazon composed of an eagle with a cup underneath. Such masterpieces were widespread in the Mamluk period.
69f100f8-b478-59cb-921a-5cdfd266ab6e.method_for_datation: The vase is dated based on the inscriptions mentioned above, which allude to Toghostomor al-Malaki al-Nasiri as the owner of the object.
69f100f8-b478-59cb-921a-5cdfd266ab6e.method_for_provenance: The provenance of this object was narrowed down to Cairo in Egypt in view of the fact that Amir Toghostomor was responsible for serving drinks to Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad. This is in addition to the spread of the type of decorative style present on the vase to other pieces which have been attributed to Cairo. Furthermore the city was famous for its inlay work, to the point that the historian al-Maqrizi mentions in his *Khitat* (1999) that at that time there was not a house in the city that was entirely devoid of inlayed works.
69f100f8-b478-59cb-921a-5cdfd266ab6e.obtention: This vase was bought from the antiquities dealer, Ralph Harari in 1945.

6a2319dc-c001-58b4-a048-bd55561d140e.name: Yataghan
6a2319dc-c001-58b4-a048-bd55561d140e.short_description: This is the earliest known Imperial Ottoman *yataghan* believed to be commissioned by Sultan Bayezid II (r. AH 885-917 / AD 1481-1512). It is a Turkish weapon used by elite troops of the Ottoman army (janissaries) from the AH mid-9th to 13th century / AD mid-15th to 19th century. An inscription executed in *thuluth* script in gold overlay on both sides of the blade and along its spine, bearing the names of the Sultan, its owner, maker and benedictory inscriptions enumerating the Sultan’s attributes.

6a2ad1b6-4e61-5b64-aa4c-e23e31a8188c.name: *Sübhatü'l Ebrar* by Molla Camii
6a2ad1b6-4e61-5b64-aa4c-e23e31a8188c.description:
Molla Camii was a poet and scientist of the Naqshbandi order who was born and raised in Samarkand during the Timuri period (1414–1492). He was a highly renowned figure during his lifetime, and was frequently invited by the Ottoman sultans.  
In this miniature Prophet Abraham and a fire-worshipping priest are depicted. Prophet Abraham informs the pagan priest that he can invite him to his table only if the priest accepts Islam. The elderly priest, declaring that he would not alter his beliefs for a mere morsel of bread, rises from the table and departs. At this point, a voice from the heavens is heard saying it is unjust to compel an elderly man to leave the table hungry, regardless of his beliefs. Prophet Abraham then realises his error and invites the priest back to the table. The priest, after being invited a subsequent time, becomes a believer upon being told what had happened.  
In the miniature, Prophet Abraham's head is haloed and his face is veiled. He points to the food, indicating that the priest should join him.
materials: finished *(aharlı)* paper, ink, leather binding

6a7f88ad-e38f-5e65-b83b-d07699dcfcd7.name: *Zubdat al-Tawarikh* (‘Cream of Histories’)
6a7f88ad-e38f-5e65-b83b-d07699dcfcd7.short_description: Muslims consider the Qur’an the third and final portion of God’s revelation to mankind: it completes, but does not supplant, God’s earlier revelations to the Jews and Christians. The prophets of the Old and New Testaments are therefore also prophets in Islam. This manuscript is a history of the world beginning with Adam and ending with the Ottoman sultans of the sixteenth century. It includes depictions of various prophets common to all three religions (such as Abraham and Ishmael), as well as specifically Islamic prophets (such as Alexander and Khizr). The manuscript ends with a depiction of Sultan Murad III (r. AH 982–1003 / AD 1574–95), during whose reign the manuscript was produced. Each prophet or sultan is identified by an inscription.
keywords: illustration; miniature painting; calligraphy; script; illumination; lacquer; Edirnekari technique; gilding; ink; paper; painting; watercolour; zodiac
materials: Coloured pigments and gold on paper

6a9c4079-15d5-59d8-8184-2fa80fcb8787.name: Teardrop-shaped gold ring bezel
6a9c4079-15d5-59d8-8184-2fa80fcb8787.short_description: This engraved gold ornament probably formed the bezel of a ring, to judge by its flattened, open back. Its inscription is hard to read, apart from an apparent repetition of the names `Ali and Muhammad. Generally, rings like this either carry the owner’s name or religious blessings. The form and decorative layout on this bezel is of Safavid style.
keywords: Bezel; Ring; Gold; inscription; calligraphy

6ad7e7f5-5b8d-5bfc-afb9-c3c90a19d9a8.name: Vase.
6ad7e7f5-5b8d-5bfc-afb9-c3c90a19d9a8.description: Vase with vertical bevelled rim, circular mouth, cylindrical neck, globular body, with two grooved strap handles with a pinnacle-shaped protuberance at the top which join the neck and belly of the vessel, and a convex base with diagonal foot-ring. It shows remnants of the base of a filter between the neck and body. The exterior is decorated using the partial *cuerda seca* technique, in which only some parts of the design are filled with green or greenish honey-coloured glaze and others with dotted lines. The decoration is divided into six successive horizontal bands of plant, wavy and calligraphic motifs. On the rim is a narrow border of schematic palmettes. Most of the neck is occupied by a wide band with large lotus flowers, and below this is a frieze of tooth-shaped motifs. On the shoulder is a calligraphic ornamental border in which the word '*baraka*' is repeated several times in florid *kufic* script and, on the belly, a band of phytomorphic medallions. Next to the base is a frieze of palmette leaves. The object has been restored.
6ad7e7f5-5b8d-5bfc-afb9-c3c90a19d9a8.short_description: Almoravid or Almohad pot decorated in part using *cuerda seca*. The decoration is arranged into six successive horizontal bands with plant, undulating and calligraphic motifs. The lotus-flower motifs and the band inscribed with the word ‘*baraka*’ in flowery *kufic* script are particularly noteworthy.
6ad7e7f5-5b8d-5bfc-afb9-c3c90a19d9a8.dimensions: Height 34.8 cm, width 32 cm, diameter (of mouth) 17.8 cm, diameter (of base) 13.4 cm.
6ad7e7f5-5b8d-5bfc-afb9-c3c90a19d9a8.method_for_datation: The stratigraphic context in which the object was found was very disordered, which led to its being dated by comparison with objects of similar form, decorative technique and theme, in particular from Almería and Málaga.
6ad7e7f5-5b8d-5bfc-afb9-c3c90a19d9a8.method_for_provenance: The abundance of this type of ceramic in Málaga and Almería (Spain), where kilns in which they were made have been found, has led researchers to attribute its production to these localities.
6ad7e7f5-5b8d-5bfc-afb9-c3c90a19d9a8.obtention: Found in the archaeological excavations carried out by the Campo Arqueológico de Mértola in the citadel of the Castle of Mértola.

6b03ecfa-3333-5fb8-b1a6-fd52388b653a.name: Textile fragment.
6b03ecfa-3333-5fb8-b1a6-fd52388b653a.description:
This is a fragment from a shawl or turban made from fine linen and decorated with a wide band of delicately woven vegetal decoration in green, blue and yellow silk. In the lower portion of this band, is a line of inscription in *kufic* script woven in brown silk that reads: 'In the name of God, the Blessings of God on Abd Allah al-Amin Muhammad, Commander of the Faithful, may God grant him a long life, who has commissioned the production of this in the *tiraz al-'amma* \[…\] Egypt at the hands of al-Fadl bin al-Rabi', a supporter of the Commander of the Faithful'.This is considered to be the oldest woven silk inscription on linen. In the Islamic-period a shawl or turban, such as the one from which this fragment comes, was usually decorated at both ends by a decorative band next to which was a band of inscription, and then a thin strip; the shawl or turban would have been finished with a fringe.  
This piece was made in *tiraz al-'amma* (the public workshop). Beside the public *tiraz*, there were textile establishments which were set up by the caliphs to produce garments and textiles for the caliph and his entourage; these were called *tiraz al-khasa* (exclusive workshops). Some of the fine *tiraz al-'amma* textiles, indicate that these were commissioned when needed by the caliphs alongside *tiraz al-khasa*. The storehouses of the Abbasid Caliph, Muhammad al-Amin (r. AH 193–8 / AD 809–13) were filled with clothes, hangings and carpets, to the point where it took al-Fadl ibn Rabi' four months to complete the inventory of the contents of these treasuries, demonstrating the great interest that this caliph took in a variety of apparel, turbans and coverings.
6b03ecfa-3333-5fb8-b1a6-fd52388b653a.short_description: This fragment bears the name of the Abbasid Caliph al-Amin Muhammad and is considered to be the oldest woven silk inscription on linen. The Fatimids established many government textile factories called *Tiraz*. Some specialised in making textiles for the caliph and his court; others were allocated for the general public.
6b03ecfa-3333-5fb8-b1a6-fd52388b653a.method_for_datation: The textile is dated based on the mention of the Abbasid caliph, Muhammad al-Amin and his follower al-Fadl ibn al-Rabi' in the inscription band which embellishes this textile fragment.
6b03ecfa-3333-5fb8-b1a6-fd52388b653a.method_for_provenance: It is thought that Fustat is the most likely place of production in view of the fact that Egypt is mentioned as the place of manufacture in the inscription band.
6b03ecfa-3333-5fb8-b1a6-fd52388b653a.obtention: This piece was bought in 1903, from an antiquities dealer, Paul Philip.

6b0ea1b6-8a90-55b4-aeb3-3d454a64eeec.name: Casket.
6b0ea1b6-8a90-55b4-aeb3-3d454a64eeec.description: An ivory casket with a truncated pyramidal lid, fitted with mounts of nielloed silver. The carved decoration, which includes intertwining leafy stems and an Arabic inscription stating that the casket was made for the daughter of the Caliph ‘Abd al-Rahman III, is nearly identical to that on another casket in the Victoria and Albert Museum, with the exception of a few spelling mistakes in the inscription. For many years it was thought that this casket was a copy of the other casket held at the V&A and made by the 19th-century Spanish forger Don Francisco Pallás y Puig (1859–1926), but recent radiocarbon analysis confirms that this object is quite likely to be original, and it, along with its ‘twin’, may have been made as a pair for the Caliph’s daughter.
6b0ea1b6-8a90-55b4-aeb3-3d454a64eeec.short_description: A finely carved ivory casket decorated with gracefully intertwining tendrils and an Arabic inscription stating that it was made for the daughter of the Spanish Umayyad Caliph ‘Abd al-Rahman III. She may have used it as a jewel-box.
6b0ea1b6-8a90-55b4-aeb3-3d454a64eeec.initial_owner: Daughter (name unknown) of the Spanish Umayyad Caliph ‘Abd al-Rahman III.
6b0ea1b6-8a90-55b4-aeb3-3d454a64eeec.dimensions: Height 8.5 cm, length 13 cm, width 8.5 cm.
6b0ea1b6-8a90-55b4-aeb3-3d454a64eeec.method_for_datation: Recent radiocarbon analysis showed the ivory used to make this casket dates to the 3rd / 9th century; the inscription, as with that on the other V&A casket (UK2 06, 301–1866) names the Spanish Umayyad Caliph ‘Abd al-Rahman III and implies that he is dead, making the likely date of production sometime shortly after AH 350 / AD 961.
6b0ea1b6-8a90-55b4-aeb3-3d454a64eeec.method_for_provenance: The Spanish Umayyads were centred at Córdoba, while the carved marble decoration on the walls of the reception hall of Madinat al-Zahra features a similar floral pattern.

6b90a9c0-f193-55c4-9a03-d29b7b481484.name: *Kiswah* Belt
6b90a9c0-f193-55c4-9a03-d29b7b481484.short_description:
Religious leaders in the Muslim world would commission the crafting of the *Kiswah* - the cover of the Kaaba - including key components such this belt embellished in gold and silver thread. Craftsmen embroider Qur’anic verses and words of protective value to provide a generous offering to the house of God. This belt was manufactured in Egypt.  
  
Once a new veil is bestowed upon the cubic building, the previous cover is broken up beneath the new *Kiswah* and donated to individuals and institutions such as museums to honor the yearly tradition.

6b90a9c0-f193-55c4-9a03-d29b7b481484.method_for_datation: The date and origin were established in a comparison of colour and calligraphy of other Kiswas.
6b90a9c0-f193-55c4-9a03-d29b7b481484.method_for_provenance: The Kiswa covers the Kaaba in Mecca, Saudi Arabia.

6bb34fe7-eaef-56c1-b556-3d1d89dfb069.name: Marriage tent
6bb34fe7-eaef-56c1-b556-3d1d89dfb069.short_description: A complete early 20th century Egyptian tent adorned with colourful textile panels in interior part. *Khayamiyya* or Egyptian art of tent-making is created using a hand-applique technique in which fabric pieces are cut, folded and skillfully hand-sewn to canvas, producing impressive tents and wall hangings. These vibrant textiles are widely used in ceremonial contexts such as weddings, funerals, street parties and religious events. This tent was used for the wedding of a daughter of the last Khedive of Egypt in 1903. It can be erected with the decoration reversed should it be thought more appropriate.

6bbafa48-66dc-52f4-bf7a-3cc4fe5e25c9.name: Funerary panel
6bbafa48-66dc-52f4-bf7a-3cc4fe5e25c9.short_description: This small panel, rectangular in shape, bears a decoration carved in bas-relief on one of the two faces, which suggests that it was designed to be embedded in the wall of a religious monument. The panel is almost complete and in a good condition. The lower corners and the upper right corner are missing. There are gaps on top. A niche design occupies the central section of the panel, framed on three sides by an epigraphic band. The niche is composed by a pointed horseshoe arch resting on two lateral columns with pyramidal bases and vase-shaped capitals. A short inscription, divided on two lines, is engraved inside the arch. The two inscriptions are engraved with a thin, shallow stroke, and executed in a late *kufic* style with slightly bilobed apexes, provided with diacritical marks. The text of the frame, on one line, contains an epitaph and reads on the right side: *\[hadha\] qabr al-Hakim al-Faqih Ahmad b.*, on the upper side: *Sulayman al-Shuruti*, and on the left side: *rahmatu llah ʿalayhi wa-salla llahu ʿa*\[…\]. These are translated as: '\[This is\] the tomb of al-Ḥākim al-Faqīh Aḥmad b. // Sulaymān al-\[…\] // May God’s mercy be upon him and may blessings of God be upon \[…\]'. The text inside the arch reads: *Allahu akbar*. The text enclosed in the outer frame is preserved in its entirety, except for the first and last words, which have been lost. The epitaph is undated and dedicated to a law scholar (*faqīh*) whose nisba has not yet been deciphered. Note that the invocation at the end of the text contains an expression (*salla Allah ʿala…*) that is usually intended for the Prophet.
6bbafa48-66dc-52f4-bf7a-3cc4fe5e25c9.holder: University Museum of Islamic Art | The Bumiller Collection
6bbafa48-66dc-52f4-bf7a-3cc4fe5e25c9.method_for_datation: The shape and size of the panel, as well as the palaeographic features of the two texts suggest a date no earlier than the late 16th century. A close comparison with the other similar panels with niche designs found in Ghazni is missing. The other specimens are ascribed to a more ancient period, between the 11th and 13th centuries, and differ both in the shape of the niche and in the writing styles and (and above all) in the content of the texts. In no case, in fact, is there an epitaph.

6c5debca-9932-5c4a-89ab-f8f3d13de354.name: Dinar
6c5debca-9932-5c4a-89ab-f8f3d13de354.description: Gold Dinar of Hijaz, King Hussein bin 'Ali, AH 1334. On November, 1916 the notables, ulama of Hijaz and a majority of the sheiks of Bedouins and sedentary tribes, assembled at the great Mosque of Mecca to pay allegiance to al-Hussein and proclaim him “King“ of Arab Countries. On this occasion a coin bearing his name at Mecca, as King of the Arabs was struck. But Britain, France and Italy recognized him only as “King of the Hijaz” on 3 January 1917. On obverse: "*bi-l-bilad al-'arabiyya al-husayn bin 'ali / 'abduhu / hashimi / wa ibn 'abdihi / al-nahidh*" ("Hussein bin Ali / God’s Servant / Hashimi /and son of God’s Servant / leader of Arab renaissance"). On reverse: "*duriba bi-makka al-mukarrama / sana 1334 / dinar / sana 8 / 'asima al-hukuma al-'arabiyya*" ("Dinar minted at Makka al-Mukarrama in 1334 \[AH\] in the reign year 8 capital of Arab Government"). All regular coins of Hijaz bear the accessional date of ١٣٣٤ (AH 1334) of al-Hussein bin 'Ali, plus the regional year, many bronze coins had a light silver wash.
6c5debca-9932-5c4a-89ab-f8f3d13de354.author: Aida Naghawi
keywords: Hussein bin Ali; dinar; Arab Hashemite Government; Mecca al Mukarrama; coin; currency; coinage; numismatics
materials: Gold

6c834b03-f120-537f-ad07-f35c0f191253.name: Hanging (*sitara*) for the Mosque of the Prophet, Medina al-Munawwarah
6c834b03-f120-537f-ad07-f35c0f191253.short_description: The interior walls of the Shrine of the Prophet in the Madina were traditionally honoured with elaborate hangings. During the Ottoman period, it was customary for the Sultan to send hangings for the shrine  on the occasion of his ascension to the throne or when wear and tear demanded them to be replaced. The old  hangings were returned to Istanbul.Judging by their inscriptions, it has been suggested that  black-grounded Ottoman textiles like this one may have been commissioned specifically to cover the tomb of the Prophet (pbuh). In addition to qur'anic inscriptions, the calligraphic panels include a large green medallion with a hadith of the Prophet: ‘ (For) whosoever may visit my grave, my intercession will become an obligation’. Below, elaborate arabesque scrolling surrounds the emblem or tughra of the sultan Abd al-Hamid II (1293 H/1876 AD – 1327 H/1909 AD), who commissioned this hanging.
6c834b03-f120-537f-ad07-f35c0f191253.holder: Sharjah Museum of Islamic Civilisation /Sharjah Museums Authority
6c834b03-f120-537f-ad07-f35c0f191253.dates: Hegira mid 13th century / AD mid 19th century
6c834b03-f120-537f-ad07-f35c0f191253.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
keywords: tughra; tugra; sitara
materials: Silk, cotton, silver and gilt silver metal thread

6cac4f71-4c6d-5af5-91b7-33d7f396babe.name: *Iyar-i Danish* (‘Touchstone of Wisdom’)
6cac4f71-4c6d-5af5-91b7-33d7f396babe.short_description: The text of *Iyar-i danish* (‘Touchstone of Wisdom’) derives from the collection of Sanskrit animal fables known as Panchatantra and thought to have been compiled sometime before AD 500. Since then, several versions of the fables have appeared, in ancient Pahlavi, Persian and Arabic. The version known as *Iyar-i danish* was compiled at the Mughal court for the emperor Akbar (r. 1556–1605). The fables are part of the genre of literature known as ‘mirrors for princes’, consisting of stories intended to instruct rulers in the art of statecraft. Each chapter of the text consists of a frame story dealing with a specific moral. The characters of the frame story then each tell their own stories of behaviour exemplifying the moral in question.
keywords: fables; stories; literature; manuscript; animal; Kalila wa dimna; lion; fox; miniature painting; illustration; education
materials: Coloured pigments and gold on paper

6cd1576c-84dc-565e-8f5b-d3d3ed636ea8.name: Al-Hariri, *Maqamat* ('Assemblies')
6cd1576c-84dc-565e-8f5b-d3d3ed636ea8.short_description: The Arab poet Al-Hariri of Basra, or Abu Muhammad al-Qasim ibn Ali ibn Muhammad ibn Uthman al-Hariri (d. 516 AH / 1122 AD), wrote the *Maqamat al-Hariri* (‘Assemblies of Hariri), which is a collection of fifty stories written in the *Maqama* style of rhymed prose with intervals of poetry. Al-Hariri also extensively utilises Arabic idioms and proverbs. While this style of writing was developed a century earlier, Al-Hariri elevated this genre into a major literary form through this work. In his *Maqamat*, the anecdotes are told by the roguish wanderer and eloquent trickster Abu Zayd to the narrator, al-Harith b. Hammam al-Basri. This copy was written in calligraphic large Mamluk *naskh* script by Abu'l-Fada'il b. Abi Ishaq in 734 AH / 1334 AD. The quality of the manuscript, its courtly title page, and large format suggest that it was created in Cairo, then capital of the Mamluk Sultanate and Caliphate. The sultan who possibly commissioned the manuscript and who may be the one depicted on the dedicatory title page is An-Nasir Muhammad b. Qala'un, who was in power for the third time from 709 AH / 1309-10 AD to 741 AH / 1340-41 AD. The manuscript includes seventy paintings, which must have been completed by a group of artists or a workshop. It is likely that multiple pages are no longer extant. The images that are preserved reflect a Mamluk style of painting, including bright colours on a golden background, more monumentalised scenes, and a reduction to essential elements in expression and composition, especially when compared to the Persian-Seljuk style of Baghdad and Mosul book-painting. The figures’ facial features follow the Turkish-Mongolian ideal of beauty that emerged under the Seljuks in Persia. The essential principle of composition throughout the manuscript is the juxtaposition of individual figures with figural groups, whereby means of deliberate contrast or symmetry are employed. These compositions underline the textual structure of the stories. The manuscript probably entered the Austrian National Library between 1820 and 1840.
6cd1576c-84dc-565e-8f5b-d3d3ed636ea8.dimensions: 373 x 260 mm (c. 260 x 160mm), ff. II, II*, 195 folios.
6cd1576c-84dc-565e-8f5b-d3d3ed636ea8.method_for_provenance: On fol. 1a, a note in the margin with incomplete names.
6cd1576c-84dc-565e-8f5b-d3d3ed636ea8.obtention: Unknown but came into the Austrian National Library between 1820 and 1840.
6cd1576c-84dc-565e-8f5b-d3d3ed636ea8.bibliography:

6d275aae-efca-5e92-b1e9-cd4d92480102.name: Vertical-sided bowl.
6d275aae-efca-5e92-b1e9-cd4d92480102.description:
The decoration of the bowl, which is limited to the outside, consists of a large inscription in *kufic* characters with strokes finished with an apex and certain letters finished with volutes, all contained between two solid lustre bands. The main inscription is superimposed by four letters in cobalt-blue. Although very contemporary, the meaning of the inscription is related to the *baraka lisahibihi* type, ‘blessed be the holder’.  
It is relevant to note that decoration consisting of purely epigraphic motifs is quite rare in Mesopotamian lustre-ware, and thus it can reasonably be assumed that this piece was influenced by ceramics from the Samanid period in Khurasan and Transoxania (AH 4th–5th / 9th–10th centuries), to which significant production of non-lustre-ware china, decorated only with epigraphic motifs, is attributable.
6d275aae-efca-5e92-b1e9-cd4d92480102.short_description: This bowl is practically unique in its shape and decoration, with pieces decorated exclusively with calligraphy being rare in the early years of the Abbasid era.
6d275aae-efca-5e92-b1e9-cd4d92480102.holder: Museum of Civilisations | Museum of Oriental Art “Giuseppe Tucci”
6d275aae-efca-5e92-b1e9-cd4d92480102.method_for_datation: From stylistic analysis. The decoration is clearly influenced by ceramics from the Samanid period in Khurasan and Transoxania (4th–5th / 9th–10th centuries).
6d275aae-efca-5e92-b1e9-cd4d92480102.method_for_provenance: The simplicity of the piece is characteristic of objects from Samarra.

6d56bfde-b2d7-5b3d-b418-0b9d3e98d0e8.name: Qur’an Cabinet
6d56bfde-b2d7-5b3d-b418-0b9d3e98d0e8.short_description:
This Qur’an cabinet from Istanbul would embellish rooms in private homes, mosques, *madrasas* (Islamic education centres), and mausoleums. Crafted in the Ottoman style, the box stands on four legs, mother-of-pearl inlaying, geometric patterns and calligraphy.  
  
This rare type of Qur’an cabinet (called *sunduq* or *kursi*) attracts with an unusual form several compartments for religious items and scripts, and the dome-shaped cover. The calligraphy in *Diwani* style reads *Al Fatiha* (the opening chapter of the Qur’an) and *Al Zalzalah* (the 99th chapter).  
  
In the 19th century, the mother-of-pearl style called Damascene became increasingly popular in Ottoman Turkey. Artisans arranged precious materials including mother-of-pearl, tortoiseshell, metals and ivory into interlocking asterisks, octagons and hexagons.
6d56bfde-b2d7-5b3d-b418-0b9d3e98d0e8.owner: Sheikh Faisal Bin Qassim Al Thani
