9be9d769-5c24-5c6d-9cf1-7cfea3f480c3.name: Bottle
9be9d769-5c24-5c6d-9cf1-7cfea3f480c3.description:
Lavishly enamelled, purple blown glass piece, with figurative, geometric, botanical and pseudepigraphic motifs. It features a round, flattened, piriform body; oval foot and two vertical handles extending from a bulbous neck.  
  
At the centre of the piece is a tondo-style portrait of a man on one side and a woman on the other. Both figures are dressed in courtier fashion. From the bottle's neck to its shoulder appears an inscription in white, pseudo-*kufic* script, between gilded lines.  
  
This is a highly valuable piece, given its age and rarity. To this day, its origin remains unclear. Experts have suggested Venetian provenance; however, it may also have been blown in the Crown of Aragon (Mallorca, Barcelona or Valencia), where high-quality glass was produced “a la façon de Venise”. Since the piece was found at a Majorcan antique market and had come from a palace in the city, Mallorca appears to be the most plausible place of production.  
  
The use of the vessel also remains uncertain. Commonly known as the Catalan term pixter, these bottles have traditionally been displayed as ornamental or flower vases. Authors such as Justina Fernández García take the view that these are luxurious containers–either for holding scented water or simply for decoration. They are quite similar in form to the so-called ampullas or pilgrim flasks, made from a great variety of materials by cultures widely separated by both space and time.  
  
Pilgrim flasks were traditionally made in pairs as wedding gifts, which may have been the case with this example, given its figurative decoration.
9be9d769-5c24-5c6d-9cf1-7cfea3f480c3.method_for_provenance: Analysis of style and technique and location of piece

9beb3626-1910-5e59-a90a-ae27e1cb3c8d.name: Door wings and a knocker.
9beb3626-1910-5e59-a90a-ae27e1cb3c8d.description:
Both of the wooden wings belonging to the door of the Ulu Cami (Great Mosque) in Cizre were clad in sheets of bronze and then decorated with brass strips and plates attached with iron nails. The border band has a decoration of quatrefoils fitted using round-headed nails. Each wing has three medallions, each with a 12-pointed star in the centre. The areas in between are filled with half-medallions that make up two half- and two full-medallions along the join when the wings are shut. The spaces in between the medallions and the geometric motifs are filled with metal plates decorated with arabesque-palmette motifs in openwork. Traces of pigment suggest that the background of these motifs was originally painted in red and blue to make them stand out more boldly. The half- and quarter-medallions along the outer edges of the door wings imply that the composition extends to infinity. Near the centre of the door wings are two loops for mounting the knockers, one of which is now on display in Copenhagen. The cast bronze knocker still on the door is formed of two symmetrical dragons that are engraved and which join at the centre with a lion's head. The dragons, have pointed ears, almond eyes and wings; their scaly bodies loop around in a spiral to form knots, and their tails join and end in eagle's heads.  
  
On the upper portion of the door wings is an inscription frieze with cast bronze letters. As some letters are missing, the inscription cannot be read in full. The legible part reads: 'May Allah give power to Abul Kasım Mahmud Sanjar Shah, our lord'. The person mentioned is the atabeg of Cizre, Mahmud Sanjar Shah, who ruled from AH 605–39 / AD 1208–41.
9beb3626-1910-5e59-a90a-ae27e1cb3c8d.short_description: Magnificent portals of monumental mosques symbolise the gates of Paradise. The naming of the sultan, geometric decoration symbolising infinity on the door-wings and the dragon and lion motifs on the doorknockers are an expression not only of the divine power of God but also of the power of the sultan.
9beb3626-1910-5e59-a90a-ae27e1cb3c8d.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts.
9beb3626-1910-5e59-a90a-ae27e1cb3c8d.initial_owner: Mahmud Sanjar Shah (AH 605–639 / AD 1208-1241), atabeg of Cizre, from the Artuqid dynasty.
9beb3626-1910-5e59-a90a-ae27e1cb3c8d.dimensions: Door wings: each, height 300 cm, width 112 cm (224 cm in total); knocker: height 27.5 cm; width 24 cm, depth 3 cm.
9beb3626-1910-5e59-a90a-ae27e1cb3c8d.method_for_datation: The patron was the atabeg of Cizre, Mahmud Sanjar Shah, who ruled from 605–639 / 1208–41. It is likely that the knockers were produced together with the wings for the door of the Ulu Cami (Great Mosque) in Cizre, itself built in 550 / 1155.
9beb3626-1910-5e59-a90a-ae27e1cb3c8d.method_for_provenance: The door wings and knockers were specially prepared for the door of the Ulu Cami (Great Mosque) in Cizre. Thus, it is highly likely that they were produced in Cizre or in southeastern Anatolia.
9beb3626-1910-5e59-a90a-ae27e1cb3c8d.obtention: The door wings and knocker were transferred to the Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts from the Mardin Museum in 1976.

9cc9092e-917f-5963-aa95-2f593ab99290.name: Wooden beam.
9cc9092e-917f-5963-aa95-2f593ab99290.description:
A wooden beam taken from the Dome of the Rock during restoration works of the 1960s. The beam is made from cedarwood, likely to have been imported from Lebanon. It contains an epigraphic inscription written in Fatimid foliated *kufic* script. The inscription is placed inside a rectangular frame that begins and ends with a tapered niche, and which is adorned with decoration carved in relief. It includes the name of the craftsman who made it and participated in the restoration works in the Dome of the Rock during the Fatimid period in the reign of Caliph al-Zahir bi-Amrillah (r. AH 411–27 / AD 1021–36). It is likely that this craftsman undertook the decoration of other artefacts inside the Dome of the Rock. The inscription beginning with the *Basmala*, reads: “In the Name of God, the Most Beneficent, the Most Merciful. The Work of 'Abd al-Baqi bin al-Hasan bin Ismai'l al-Dimashqi. May God support him”. Despite our lack of knowledge about this craftsman, the fact that his name contains the title “al-Dimashqi” indicates that there was a continual flow of craftsmen from Damascus into Jerusalem during the Fatimid period. Damascus was (and is still) famous for its wood-carving, and Jerusalem was supplied with a steady stream of skilled Damascene craftsmen to work on the construction of the Dome of the Rock at the end of the AH 1st /AD 7th century.  
The beam does not contain any other decoration. It has fortuitously preserved its splendour without damage, which confirms the skill of its workmanship in the treatment of the wood before it was mounted at the Dome of the Rock.
9cc9092e-917f-5963-aa95-2f593ab99290.short_description: This beam from the Dome of the Rock was made from cedarwood that was probably imported from Lebanon. The beam bears an inscription in Fatimid foliated *kufic* script within a rectangular frame that begins and ends with a tapered recess. It is decorated and the text is carved in relief. The piece records the carver who made it in the time of Caliph al-Zahir.
9cc9092e-917f-5963-aa95-2f593ab99290.holder: Islamic Museum, al-Aqsa Mosque / al-Haram al-Sharif.
9cc9092e-917f-5963-aa95-2f593ab99290.dimensions: Length 183 cm, width 18.5 cm, depth 20 cm.
9cc9092e-917f-5963-aa95-2f593ab99290.method_for_datation: The beam was dated by way of reliable knowledge concerning the areas that underwent restoration in the Dome of the Rock during the Fatimid period. In addition, the Fatimid script used in the epigraphic inscription is a reliable distinguishing mark.
9cc9092e-917f-5963-aa95-2f593ab99290.method_for_provenance: It is not known whether this beam was crafted in Jerusalem or at another site. Usually, however, the piece would be carved and constructed on site. It is likely, therefore, that it was carved in Jerusalem, while the cedarwood was imported from Lebanon. The craftsman was probably from Damascus, as is evident from the inscription.
9cc9092e-917f-5963-aa95-2f593ab99290.obtention: According to the registers of the Islamic Museum, the piece was transferred from the Dome of the Rock to the Museum in 1960.
9cc9092e-917f-5963-aa95-2f593ab99290.bibliography: Hamilton, R. W., *The Structural History of al-Aqsa Mosque: A Record of Archaeological Cleaning from the Repairs of 1938–42,* London, 1949.
9cc9092e-917f-5963-aa95-2f593ab99290.author: Nazmi Al-Ju'beh
keywords: Wood; carving; cedar; kufic script; wooden beam
materials: Carved and finished wood.

9ce61178-e421-548d-99f8-805b537a5ef8.name: Column capital.
9ce61178-e421-548d-99f8-805b537a5ef8.description:
A marble column capital, which is typical of the capitals associated with the Mamluk period, especially the second half of it. This style of column capital endured for a long time during the Ottoman epoch in Palestine. The capital is elongated in form and consists of rows of *muqarnas* that diminish to the point of almost disappearing. In this way the capital makes the transition from one level to the next, and one extension to the other, in a flowing manner rather than in a sudden leap as in many other forms of capital. The capital exhibited here is characterised by its simplicity, elegance and the intricacy of its design, not to mention the technical difficulties its execution must have posed.  
The capital begins as a cylinder and is of the same diameter as the pillar on which it would rest. The cylindrical form narrows by degrees, facilitating the transition to a multi-sided column, and within which is an inscription in *naskhi* script. The inscription is difficult to read because it is damaged, as well as having a proliferation of gilding and colours, but perhaps it is a quote from the Qur'an. Each side forms the beginning of a *muqarnas*, diminished, simple and progressive. Each elevation of the *muqarnas* increases its size to end at the apex of the capital. The capital widens without any transitional decoration except with facets of marble that reach a square ledge above the capital. Traces of gilding remain on the capital, which may indicate to us that it was affixed to one of the *mihrab*s of the mosque, as many of the *mihrab*s were gilded.
9ce61178-e421-548d-99f8-805b537a5ef8.short_description: This elongated marble capital alludes to the prevailing style of capitals during the Mamluk period. It is decorated by a rows of muqarnas that diminish to the point of almost disappearing. This gives a beautiful fluency in the transition between levels and from one extent to the next without forcing a sudden leap. The capital contains inscriptions that are difficult to read.
9ce61178-e421-548d-99f8-805b537a5ef8.holder: Islamic Museum, al-Aqsa Mosque / al-Haram al-Sharif.
9ce61178-e421-548d-99f8-805b537a5ef8.dimensions: Height 36 cm, base 33 cm x 33 cm.
9ce61178-e421-548d-99f8-805b537a5ef8.method_for_datation: Dating of the capital was possible by comparing it with similar ones; the manufacturing technique and form of *muqarnas* used bears a resemblance to capitals that are still *in situ* in a number of Mamluk buildings in Jerusalem.
9ce61178-e421-548d-99f8-805b537a5ef8.obtention: It is not known exactly how the Museum acquired this column capital, but it is likely that it was brought from a Mamluk building within the environs of the Haram al-Sharif.

Hamilton, R. W., *The Structural History of al-Aqsa Mosque: A Record of Archaeological Cleaning from the Repairs of 1938–42,* London, 1949.  
Wilkinson, J., *Column Capitals in al-Haram al-Sharif*, Jerusalem, 1987.

keywords: Marble capital; column capital; muqarnas; Mamluk capital; marble.
materials: Hewn marble.

9e1f46e4-2853-5545-a194-7e72c163548f.name: Concerning the punishment of an *Idolator* (one of the weak Muslims)
9e1f46e4-2853-5545-a194-7e72c163548f.short_description: This folio, along with two others in the Aga Khan Museum Collection (AKM89 and AKM40), comes from a manuscript assembled at the court of Shahrukh (d. 1447) and disassembled by the art dealer Émile Tabbagh in the 1920s and 30s. The manuscript’s content draws primarily from a world history prepared by Rashid al-Din (d. 1318) for the Mongol Ilkhan Oljeitu in 1307. It is not a simple copy of Rashid al-Din’s work, but rather a hybrid manuscript with a tangled history made even more complex by its dispersal. This folio reveals one of the abiding mysteries of the manuscript: here, similar to a group of other dispersed folios, an illustration appears in place of a block of missing text.
9e1f46e4-2853-5545-a194-7e72c163548f.obtention: Former Prince Saddrudin Aga Khan Collection
keywords: Folio; work-on-paper; works-on-paper; Manuscript
materials: Ink, watercolour, and gold pigment on paper

9ee175ff-6be6-5799-bfa1-a85506cb4cbd.name: Door
9ee175ff-6be6-5799-bfa1-a85506cb4cbd.short_description: This Mamluk wooden door with its ivory-inlaid panels presents an outstanding example of Mamluk wood carvings of the first half of the 14th century. The door consists of a pair of folded panels, displaying geometric strap-work composition forming a twelve-pointed star with twelve lobes. The lobes are carved and inlaid with ivory. The door displays two calligraphic panels; one containing Qur’anic verses and the second is an aphorism. It is mounted to a 19th century frame representing an elegant Oriental mount. The frame is decorated with interwoven geometric composition and displays one epigraphic panel of knotted calligraphic composition within cartouche.

9f13783f-37c2-5e26-9fc8-82aec3de2188.name: Marble plaque.
9f13783f-37c2-5e26-9fc8-82aec3de2188.description:
A marble plaque, approximately rectangular in shape, the apex of which is an ornamented crown. In the centre of the plaque is a mosque lamp, carved in high relief and suspended from the crown by thick ropes. Flanking either side of the lamp, at the bottom of the composition, there are engraved carvings of two candlesticks with tapering wicks. The neck and base of the lamp are embellished with vegetal motifs and braided bands; in the centre of the body is an inscription that states: 'God is the Light of the Heavens and the Earth'. Vegetal decorations appear above and below the carved inscription, which is contained within a rectangle and delineated by two beaded borders.  
Although, this form of decoration does not appear in any known Mamluk glass mosque lamps, nevertheless the general form and the carved inscription are distinguishing characteristics of Mamluk mosque lamps. The candlesticks, in relief, that appear on the plaque, are decorated with vegetal scrolls and diamond-shaped motifs. The background of the plaque is decorated with vegetal scrolls composed of grape clusters, heart-shaped buds and split leaves, in addition to a pair of stylised lotus blossoms below the lamp. Traces of brown paint also appear in the background.  
A number of Mamluk carved plaques, embellished in engraved decoration in marble, stone and plaster bear testimony to the widespread popularity of the sculptural arts (in wood and stone) during the Mamluk period. They also bear witness to the creativity and originality of the craftsmen in the design of vegetal and geometric compositions.
9f13783f-37c2-5e26-9fc8-82aec3de2188.short_description: This example of Mamluk-period marble engraving depicts a mosque lantern (*mishkah*), two candlesticks and an inscription saying 'God is the Light of the Heavens and the Earth'. Such marblework bears witness to the skill of the craftsmen in that era.
9f13783f-37c2-5e26-9fc8-82aec3de2188.method_for_datation: The object is known to date to the 8th / 14th century because it was made for the Madrasa Bedeiriyya in Cairo, built during this time period.
9f13783f-37c2-5e26-9fc8-82aec3de2188.method_for_provenance: This plaque was found in the Madrasa Bedeiriyya, which lies in the neighbourhood of the Madrasa Salihiyya al-Najmiyya in the Fatimid Street Al-Muizz Li-Din Allah in Cairo. The Madrasa Bedeiriyya was founded in 758 / 1357 by Nasir al-Din Muhammad ibn Bedeir al-'Abbas who worked as a lecturer of *fiqh* (jurisprudence) of the Shaf'i school. It is likely that the plaque was produced in Cairo for the *madrasa*.
9f13783f-37c2-5e26-9fc8-82aec3de2188.obtention: The plaque was found on site at the Madrasa Bedeiriyya. The Council for the Preservation of Arab Monuments undertook the preservation of the plaque in the eastern court of the mosque of al-Hakim bi Amrillah in 1880, where the first acquisitions of the Museum of Islamic Art were housed before they were transferred to the present Museum building in 1903.

9f32f495-7efd-5361-b956-96c4eb2d3e09.name: Variation of the Basmala
9f32f495-7efd-5361-b956-96c4eb2d3e09.description: This work is made of patterned dark red silk with mounted calligraphy on paper. The Arabic calligraphy in black ink forms a central abstract pattern in the shape of a leaf. The title of the work appears in black ink on the left, above two red seals. A third red seal appears on the top right.
materials: Ink and red seal colour on rice paper, mounted on silk

9f6f6d17-a330-58b4-8043-735c770a690a.name: Dagger (*Kard*)
9f6f6d17-a330-58b4-8043-735c770a690a.short_description: This outstanding dagger with its lapis-lazuli hilt has a deeply engraved calligraphic inscription on its blade that is compartmentalised within a continous arabesque scroll. The calligraphy reads “Ya Muhammad, Ya ‘Ali” alternatively. The quality of the blade indicates a royal commission and an experienced metal smith. The dagger is signed on its spine with the attribute name of Ghulam Shah ‘Abbasi, in gold damascened foliage. The attribution ‘Ghulam Shah ‘Abbasi or ‘Slave of Shah ‘Abbasi’ indicates a period in Iranian history when Nadir Shah rose to power and deposed the last members of the Safavid dynasty.
9f6f6d17-a330-58b4-8043-735c770a690a.bibliography: Islamic Arts Museum Malaysia, *Symbols Of Power And Beauty: The collection of the Islamic Arts Museum Malaysia*, Kuala Lumpur: IAMM Publications, 2015: 52-53.
materials: Iron, gold, lapis-lazuli; inlay, damascene, rivet

9f8c366b-751a-5e96-aa3d-860859207596.name: Carpet
9f8c366b-751a-5e96-aa3d-860859207596.short_description: This prayer rug with a silk pile on the ground brocaded with metal threads forms part of a prestigious set of Safavid Persian Niche rugs. Most of the preserved rugs of this group were intended as diplomatic gifts from the Safavid court to the Ottomans. The poetic inscription on the border is executed in *nasta\`liq* script, in Persian verse and includes the name of Sultan Murad. Most probably it refers to the Ottoman Sultan Murad III (r. AH 982-1003/ AD 1574-1595).
9f8c366b-751a-5e96-aa3d-860859207596.obtention: Rudolf Martin (1864–1925), Zurich and Munich, reportedly bought from a Russian prince in the early 20th century; thence by family descent; Sotheby’s London, 7 October 2009, lot 276; sold to Qatar Museums

9f93aaa3-18ce-5348-92f9-9826ae78f586.name: Textile.
9f93aaa3-18ce-5348-92f9-9826ae78f586.description: This large textile is embroidered on ivory-coloured organzine with lightweight pale-green silk satin (*atlas*) used as a base. The piece is particularly intricate and extremely refined, and most of it was needle-embroidered using silver-plated copper thread. The principal decorative motif is an ornate centre that resembles a prayer niche (*mihrab*), which is formed by a poly-lobed arch standing on two small columns, within which hangs a mosque lamp. A double rectangular cornice rounds off the decoration of the fabric. Its entire surface has been finely worked with a rich variety of motifs, including naturalistic vegetal motifs (flowers, leaves and small cypress trees) and epigraphic motifs. The repeated appearance of the *tughra*, the official monogram of the sultan as stamped on state documents, is of particular interest. Other inscriptions reproduce religious words and expressions relating to the Qur'an, both to ward off evil (‘*ana gelse red*’’ – ‘if difficulties arise, drive them away’) and for good omens (‘*el'an ba ' d-din*’ – ‘always with faith’). This fabric results from the manufacture of prayer mats (*seccade*) during the Ottoman era at the end of the AH 13th / AD 19th century. This piece may have been produced in Turkey or Egypt, although it was probably made in Ottoman Palestine.
9f93aaa3-18ce-5348-92f9-9826ae78f586.short_description: This sumptuously decorated fabric is a *seccade*, or prayer mat, finely decorated with naturalistic, plant and epigraphic motifs. It also includes the *tughra* (monogram) of Sultan Mustafa IV.
9f93aaa3-18ce-5348-92f9-9826ae78f586.holder: Museum of Civilisations | Museum of Oriental Art “Giuseppe Tucci”
9f93aaa3-18ce-5348-92f9-9826ae78f586.method_for_datation: From stylistic analysis, confirmed by the *tughra*, which is a late reproduction of the *tughra* of the Ottoman Sultan Mustafa IV (1222–3 / 1807–8).
9f93aaa3-18ce-5348-92f9-9826ae78f586.method_for_provenance: Through comparison with textile in the Museo del Tesoro di S. Pietro in the Vatican (see Orlando in Bibliography).

9fb409e3-528f-533c-9017-82d63273b965.name: Bowl
9fb409e3-528f-533c-9017-82d63273b965.short_description: The Seljuq era was distinguished by its extensive use of lustre techniques – painting with metal oxides then fired in a reduction kiln – to produce fine ceramics. The high quality achieved by the ceramic painters is borne out by countless bowls, bottles and vases decorated with thin brushstrokes that outline geometric shapes, floral patterns and human figures.
keywords: Ceramic; pottery; lustre
materials: Frit body, lustre decoration

9fd48483-773e-56ef-a4ac-80ac9b4f89d0.name: *Ataifor* (bowl).
9fd48483-773e-56ef-a4ac-80ac9b4f89d0.description: This *ataifor* is a dish with a convex base, curved sides and a smooth rim. The piece is made from reddish clay; the outside is covered with a honey-coloured greenish glaze and the inside with a white glaze. The inside of the receptacle is decorated with elements in green and manganese on a white base. The large circular border that runs round the edge of the plate, with fan-shaped palmettes joined by undulating stems, gives the piece a tri-lobed appearance. The central strip completes the decoration with an inscription in archaic *kufic*, where the phrase ‘al-Mulk’ (power) is repeated. The letters outlined using dark manganese lines are filled with copper green, creating a contrast with the white base that was common in the ceramics of the era.
9fd48483-773e-56ef-a4ac-80ac9b4f89d0.short_description: This bowl or *ataifor*, produced in the palace workshops of Madinat al-Zahra, is thought to have symbolic significance: the word ‘al-Mulk’, ‘the power’, represents sovereignty, while the white, green and black represent the Umayyad dynasty, Muhammad, and the austerity of the Qur’an respectively as well as the sovereignty of the caliph.
9fd48483-773e-56ef-a4ac-80ac9b4f89d0.method_for_datation: The writing style could date it to the second third of the 4th / 10th century. The simple *kufic* inscription belongs to an initial stage of production at Madinat al-Zahra, before the reign of al-Hakam II (350–66 / 961–76).
9fd48483-773e-56ef-a4ac-80ac9b4f89d0.method_for_provenance: The *ataifor* came from archaeological excavations at Madinat al-Zahra. Both its shape and decoration are characteristic of palatine production at Madinat al-Zahra.
9fd48483-773e-56ef-a4ac-80ac9b4f89d0.obtention: The *ataifor* was given to the National Archaeological Museum by the State on 5 February 1943.

9febac67-8cd1-54f6-9ba1-89627a2c4d62.name: Candlestick socket.
9febac67-8cd1-54f6-9ba1-89627a2c4d62.description:
A candlestick socket whose inscription is marked for its singularity as well as for its animated style. Most of the inscription, which runs around the lower end of the candlestick neck, assumes the forms of human figures, specifically those of warriors wielding swords, dressed in armour, and holding lances; some of the lettering is in the form of bird's heads. The inscription reads: 'To the Amir Katbugha, Glory, Long Life and Triumph over Enemies'. It is apparent from the inscription that the craftsman was offering glory to Katbugha, and wishing him a long life and victory over his enemies, specifically those who had in fact participated in the murder of the Sultan al-Ashraf Khalil ibn Qalawun. It appears that the craftsman deliberately employed ambiguous phraseology in his bid to avoid what might befall him at the hands of Katbugha's enemies if circumstances changed. In the upper zone of the candlestick neck, another inscription in Mamluk *thuluth* script unwinds, it reads: 'That which was intended for the treasury of his sublime Excellency, the lord al-Zayni Zayn al-Din Katbugha al-Mansuri al-Ashrafi'. Three decorative roundels filled with geometric designs and inlaid with gold, interrupt the inscription.  
The epigraphic decoration present on this candlestick reflects some of the social and economic aspects of life in the Mamluk period, animating a period usually only found in historical narrative accounts. In the latter half of AH 692 / AD 1293 a cadre of Mamluk princes under the leadership of Amir Baydara, an officer of the sultanate, killed Sultan al-Ashraf Khalil ibn Qalawun, attacking him as he returned from a hunting expedition, and thereby paving the way for Baydara to assume power. Some Mamluk officers refused to take part in the plot and, under the leadership of the Amir Katbugha they staged a revolt against those who had killed the sultan. The rebels in turn killed Amir Baydara and his cohorts, displaying their bodies in the streets of Cairo. This series of events is according to the narrative account written by the historian, Al-Maqrizi in his *Khiţaţ* of 1853.The Mamluk officers agreed that the brother of Sultan al-Ashraf Khalil, Muhammad ibn Qalawun, should ascend the throne. He was, however, only nine years of age, so Amir Katbugha occupied the position of proxy to the sultanate, dispatching affairs of state on behalf of Muhammad ibn Qalawun for two years (694–6/1294–6). All these events are reflected in the inscriptions and ornamentation of this candlestick, which was made for Amir Katbugha al-Mansuri. The Museum was able to acquire only the neck of the candlestick; the body is currently housed in Walters Art Gallery, Baltimore; bought by the gallery in 1925.
9febac67-8cd1-54f6-9ba1-89627a2c4d62.short_description: This is one of the most precious Islamic masterpieces due to its superb decoration, such as the inscription in the form of human figures, animals and birds. This style appeared in the late Ayyubid period and continued in the Mamluk. The candlestick was made for Amir Katbugha. The body of the candlestick is in the Walters Art Gallery, Baltimore, USA.
9febac67-8cd1-54f6-9ba1-89627a2c4d62.dimensions: Height 14 cm, diameter (of the lip) 8.5 cm.
9febac67-8cd1-54f6-9ba1-89627a2c4d62.method_for_datation:
In accordance with the above, the owner of this piece was Amir Katbugha al-Mansuri. Sultan al-Ashraf Khalil ibn Qalawun had drawn Katbugha into his closest circle of trusted companions and associates, conferring upon him the title *nisba* (attribution of close affinity or kinship), whereupon his name became Katbugha al-Mansuri al-Ashrafi. Following the murder of Sultan al-Ashraf Khalil ibn Qalawun, Katbugha ruled as proxy to Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun for two years until he relinquished the reins of power to Sultan Lajin. Katbugha died at the age of 63 in 702 / 1302, during the second reign of Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun.  
By analysis of the inscriptions and the titles mentioned in it, it is apparent that the candlestick was made for Katbugha after the death of Sultan al-Ashraf Khalil ibn Qalawun in hegira Muharram 693 (AD December 1293) and that, in view of the fact that the text is devoid of any title indicating Sultan Lajin or al-Nasir Muhammad, it could be deduced that it was inscribed before Katbugha ruled as proxy for the short period of two years before Sultan Lajin in hegira Muharram 694 (December 1294). In the light of these conclusions, the date of this piece could tentatively be pinpointed to 694 / 1294, and to be even more precise, it would have been commissioned when Katbugha was handling state affairs as a representative of the young Sultan Muhammad ibn Qalawun during his first period of rule.
9febac67-8cd1-54f6-9ba1-89627a2c4d62.method_for_provenance: The provenance for this object can be located with some certainty to Cairo in light of the evidence as mentioned above.
9febac67-8cd1-54f6-9ba1-89627a2c4d62.obtention: The candlestick socket was bought by the Museum in 1917.

a0292759-10a9-5092-8afb-5b3e2db3b197.name: *Presentation of the Child in the Temple*
a0292759-10a9-5092-8afb-5b3e2db3b197.description:
The production of knotted carpets in Portugal has been documented since the 14th century, mostly in association with the Moorish community. With the expulsion of the Muslims and Jews in 1496 by King Manuel I (1469‒1521; r.1495‒1521), the Portuguese carpet workshops were inevitably abandoned and the manufacturing tradition was lost. Aside from local production, Portuguese consumers imported high-quality items as well. This ensured the supply of luxury goods to the wealthier clientele. Despite that Spanish carpets were esteemed throughout the 15th century, according to representations in paintings, by the second quarter of the 16th century, they were replaced by Ottoman carpets produced in the regions of Anatolia and Uşak.  
Although, surprisingly, there are no surviving examples of this type of carpet in Portugal, its presence in paintings, as well as in other documentary sources such as in inventories, confirms their presence in Portuguese interiors, thus enabling us to identify the patterns and original colours of the imported carpets. This is the case with this painting, where a Turkish carpet, placed on the floor near the altar, displays most probably a “small-pattern Holbein” design: it comprises a repeated pattern of alternating quatrefoils and octagonal medallions, with *kufic* script motifs represented in detail on the red border.
a0292759-10a9-5092-8afb-5b3e2db3b197.method_for_datation: Technical information provided by José Alberto Seabra de Carvalho
a0292759-10a9-5092-8afb-5b3e2db3b197.obtention: Transferred from the Convent of Santa Joana, Lisbon, Portugal, at an unknown date

a082fcd1-6ab8-5065-913f-e8b18e48249c.name: Acte habous
a082fcd1-6ab8-5065-913f-e8b18e48249c.description:
This historical and religious document, dated 1952, records the donation of a tour d’eau (water turn) as a waqf—an Islamic charitable endowment. Issued in Marrakech, it reflects a long-standing tradition in Islamic societies where essential resources like land, property, or water rights are donated for the benefit of the community or religious institutions.In this case, the water right was endowed to ensure ongoing access to irrigation or domestic water use, often for a mosque, madrasa, or a public fountain (*sabil*).  
  
Such donations were considered acts of piety and social responsibility, intended to bring spiritual merit to the donor while serving the collective good. The document is not only a legal record but also a cultural artefact that illustrates how water was governed as both a sacred trust and a communal asset in Moroccan society.It highlights the intricate connection between Islamic law, environmental ethics, and local governance, where water—an essential and scarce resource—was managed through deeply rooted moral and religious frameworks. This *waqf stands as a testament to how water endowments helped structure equitable access, social cohesion, and religious devotion in everyday life.*

a0a31a62-7361-5268-8ad7-1a7b0126f09d.name: Alhambra vase.
a0a31a62-7361-5268-8ad7-1a7b0126f09d.description:
This piece is one of the so-called 'Alhambra vases'. Formally, all of these are similar: a large egg-shaped body and a narrow, unglazed base from which two large, flat handles emerge, and an octagonal neck reinforced with vertical mouldings.  
The decoration of pale gold on a white base is arranged horizontally in broad bands of different widths that are separated from one another by other smooth, narrower bands. The central, and widest, band contains vegetal motifs and an inscription in *kufic* characters in white on a golden background, in which the word 'forgiveness' is repeated several times. Both above and below the central band there are other similar bands decorated with plant arabesques and gold circles, all joined by a thread. The decoration of the main body is completed by another two bands, one on the lower part with small arches and another nearer the neck with a *kufic* inscription, now almost completely disappeared.  
The neck, which has eight sides separated by mouldings, is decorated with stylised vegetal motifs. The handles, attached close to the body, are decorated with the hand of Fatima (*hamsa*) on each side.  
The Alhambra vases constitute the most important examples of Nasrid ceramic production. These pieces became extremely well known for their delicate decoration and large size, and were exported to other places. The best-preserved examples are to be found in Palermo (Regional Museum of Sicily), St Petersburg (Hermitage), Stockholm (National Museum of Fine Arts) and Madrid (Institute of Valencia de D. Juan and the National Archaeological Museum). Some are decorated exclusively in gold and others in gold and cobalt-blue, always on a tin-glaze background.  
Although its form derives from large storage vessels, its cumbersome size and the absence of any strengthening elements in the handles suggest a purely ornamental function.
a0a31a62-7361-5268-8ad7-1a7b0126f09d.short_description: The so-called ‘Alhambra vases’ were luxury items because of the technical complexity of their manufacture and the beauty of their decoration and lustrework. The intended use is not known, but their renown led them to be exported to Sicily and Mamluk Egypt.
a0a31a62-7361-5268-8ad7-1a7b0126f09d.method_for_datation: It is difficult to determine the date of manufacture of these vases. Nonetheless, all writers agree that, on the basis of the inscription, the oldest examples are those decorated solely with gold on white, which were produced from the last third of the 7th / 13th century and, in particular, during the 8th / 14th century.
a0a31a62-7361-5268-8ad7-1a7b0126f09d.method_for_provenance: Although all of these pieces are known generically as the Alhambra vases, they were produced in Malaga and exported. From the 7th / 13th century, Arab writers begin to mention Malaga as a large centre for the production and export of ceramics with gold or metallic highlights.
a0a31a62-7361-5268-8ad7-1a7b0126f09d.obtention: The piece was found by chance at the beginning of the 20th century during work to shore up vaults in the monastery of Santa María de la Defensión in Jerez de la Frontera (Cadiz). It was donated to the National Archaeological Museum on 29 July 1930.

a0dd981d-e256-57f4-ba5c-7f37591cb8b5.name: Coin (*dirham*)
a0dd981d-e256-57f4-ba5c-7f37591cb8b5.description:
This Umayyad coin, minted during the reign of al-Walid I (AH 86–96 / AD 705–15), bears an inscription in its centre that reads ‘*â ila illâ Allâh wahda-hu lâ sharîk la-hu*’ (‘There is no God but Allah, the One, there is none like unto him’) and the edge reads ‘*bismi-llâh duriba hadâ-l-dirhâm bi fî sanat ihda wa tis in*’ (‘In God’s name this *dirham* was minted in Sijistan in the year one and ninety \[91\]’).  
The front face bears two inscriptions, one in the centre and one on the edge. The central inscription reads ‘*Allâh ahad Allâh al-samad lam yalid wa lam yûlad wa lam yakun la-hu kufû’ an ahad*’ (‘God is one, God is eternal. He does not beget, nor is he begotten and there is none like unto him’) and the edge inscription reads ‘*Muhammad rasûl Allâh arsala-hu bi-l-hudâ wa al-haqq li-yuzhira-hu alâ al-dîn kulli-hi wa la-hu kariha al-mushrikûn*’ (‘Muhammad is the messenger of God. He has sent His messenger with the guidance and the true religion, and will make it dominate all religions, in spite of the idol worshipers’).
a0dd981d-e256-57f4-ba5c-7f37591cb8b5.short_description: *Dirham* minted during the reign of al-Walid I. The basic coin in the Arab world until the arrival of the Mongols, the *dirham* takes its name from the Greek *drachma*. Coins usually weighed 2.97 grams.
a0dd981d-e256-57f4-ba5c-7f37591cb8b5.holder: Museum of Civilisations | Museum of Oriental Art “Giuseppe Tucci”
a0dd981d-e256-57f4-ba5c-7f37591cb8b5.method_for_datation: From the inscription on the edge of the obverse.

a0e649a0-0f53-5503-9c38-d0a4035fdc34.name: Page of manuscript with Moses, Muhammad and the Archangel Gabriel.
a0e649a0-0f53-5503-9c38-d0a4035fdc34.description:
This single sheet from a manuscript features, between bands of script, the prophets Moses and Muhammad and the Archangel Gabriel conversing in heaven. Angels, perched on five clouds behind these three principal characters, appear to be listening. The scene portrayed is one from Muhammad’s visionary ascension to heaven. Muhammad stands on the right-hand side in a long green robe and turban, and Moses, wearing a long dark red robe, is on the left, in front of his heavenly throne, which is denoted by an inscription in Arabic lettering. Moses is gesturing his hands in speech. Muhammad, with whom he is conversing, stands on the opposite side. A white veil conceals his face, while his hands are hidden in the long sleeves of his gown. The heads of both prophets are crowned with halos, within which their names, written in a black script, can be deciphered. The Archangel Gabriel stands between Muhammad and Moses, turning towards Muhammad. He is characterised by a twin pair of multicoloured wings and a crown. Gabriel already featured in the Old Testament as the gate-keeper of Paradise. As one of two angels standing in the presence of God (Luke 1: 19), it was Gabriel who explained the story of the Messiah (Daniel 8: 16ff.). He was supposed to have announced the wording of the Qur’an to Muhammad. In Sura 2 verse 97 it is written that: Gabriel ‘has by God’s grace revealed it \[the Qur’an\] to you \[Muhammad\] to your heart’.  
The text above the three personages, which describes the story, is written in Ottoman Turkish. It includes the account of Muhammad discussing with God the number of daily prayers. Both eventually agreed on five daily prayers. Moses is Muhammad’s heavenly adviser and Gabriel is his companion. The direct speech of all those involved is written in Arabic. The text is taken from a biography of the prophet which had appeared from the AH 1st century / AD 7th century on. The generic term for this type of biography is *sira*, which translates as ‘life facts’ or ‘way of life’. This single sheet probably came from a handwritten work completed for the Ottoman Sultan Murad III (r. AH 982–1003 / AD 1574–95).
a0e649a0-0f53-5503-9c38-d0a4035fdc34.short_description: This painted page from a book shows the Archangel Gabriel with the Prophets Moses (left) and Muhammad (right). Surrounded by angels they discuss the question of daily prayers. This happened during Muhammad’s ascent to heaven. Because it was forbidden to show Muhammad, his face is veiled.
a0e649a0-0f53-5503-9c38-d0a4035fdc34.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum
a0e649a0-0f53-5503-9c38-d0a4035fdc34.initial_owner: Possibly Sultan Murad III (r. AH 982-1003 / AD 1574–95).

a0e649a0-0f53-5503-9c38-d0a4035fdc34.method_for_datation: The date has been established through the handwriting on the single manuscript page, which was transcribed for the Ottoman Sultan Murad III (982–1003 / 1574–95).
a0e649a0-0f53-5503-9c38-d0a4035fdc34.method_for_provenance: Both the text and the style of this page suggest that this consists of a single leaf written by a single writer in the same handwriting, which was made for the Ottoman Sultan Murad III.

a0fd9b25-3128-5a5c-90c1-29e46c8df6bd.name: Jami, Nur ad-Din ‘Abd ar-Rahman Ibn-Ahmad, Resaʾil-i Hazret-i Molla Jami
a0fd9b25-3128-5a5c-90c1-29e46c8df6bd.short_description: This manuscript is a copy of Nur ad-Din ‘Abd ar-Rahman Ibn-Ahmad Jami’s “Resaʾil-i Hazret-i Molla Jami” dated to the second half of the 16th century, and was likely produced in Istanbul. The decoration includes nine initial decorative panels that are not uniformly designed, but reflect the Ottoman style of the late 16th century. The binding, however, is of the late 17th and early 18th centuries.
a0fd9b25-3128-5a5c-90c1-29e46c8df6bd.dimensions: 355 x 238mm (233 x 140mm). ff. II, II*, 97 folios.
a0fd9b25-3128-5a5c-90c1-29e46c8df6bd.method_for_datation: Two colophons: AH 989 / AD 1581 (fol. 22b); AH 983 / AD 1575.
a0fd9b25-3128-5a5c-90c1-29e46c8df6bd.method_for_provenance: There is a seal of Joseph Freiherr von Hammer-Purgstall (d. 1856) on f. 96b, dated AH 1223 / AD 1808-9.
a0fd9b25-3128-5a5c-90c1-29e46c8df6bd.obtention: Obtained in 1842 by the Austrian National Library.

a0fd9b25-3128-5a5c-90c1-29e46c8df6bd.binding_desc: This 17th- or 18th-century Ottoman binding is composed of dark brown leather over pressboard and includes a typical leather flap. The textured centrepiece is cut out, inlaid, and decorated with stencilled floral vines and cloud ribbon loops in two shades of gold. The flap shows a similar but smaller pointed medallion with the same decorative motifs. The medallions are surrounded by small golden rosette punches, gold outline and short golden rays. Additionally, there are gold lines and a gold-stamped lace band around the edges of the binding. The doublures are made of dark brown leather, except for golden double lines along the edges, which appear to have been redecorated.

keywords: Illumination; nasta’liq
materials: Ink, opaque watercolour and gold on paper. Calligraphic *nasta‘liq* in 27 and 25 lines per page (Persian and Turkish).

a1287c84-f5da-5d02-b42f-6900fa4dc40c.name: Bowl
a1287c84-f5da-5d02-b42f-6900fa4dc40c.short_description: This cup or small bowl offers a gleaming example of the level of mastery that lapidary art reached in Iran. It bears the name of its maker, Ahmad ibn Shukrallah al-Farsi and a series of cartouches with poetic verses in Persian. This cup is a rare example of the use of agate. In Iranian context, the cup (*jam*) retains an important symbolic meaning in the performance of kingship and is connected to the *jam-e Jam*, the magical cup of Jamshid.

a12eaf5f-47ff-5d15-9ffe-37f288c5e2fd.name: The Ruzbihan Qur'an
a12eaf5f-47ff-5d15-9ffe-37f288c5e2fd.short_description: This is one of the most magnificent Qur’ans ever produced. The text was copied by Ruzbihan Muhammad al-Tab‘i al-Shirazi. It opens with facing *shamsa*s inscribed with verse 17:88 of the Qur’an, followed by a superb double-page frontispiece containing *al-Fatiha* (the Opening), the first *sura* (chapter) of the Qur’an. The beginning of the next *sura*, *al-Baqara* (the Cow), is indicated by an elaborately illuminated heading. Surrounding the final *sura*s of the text is another double-page illuminated opening, from the border of which emerge long, sun-like rays. Text pages consist of blocks of lines of black *naskhi* script set between longer lines of large *thuluth* or *muhaqqaq* script in blue or gold ink.
a12eaf5f-47ff-5d15-9ffe-37f288c5e2fd.dates: Hegira mid 10th century / AD mid 16th century
keywords: koran; calligraphy; script; illumination; floral decoration; arabesque; border decoration; religious manuscript
materials: Coloured pigments and gold on paper

a1c3a6cb-5c96-54dc-bcd3-570ffc9d4e35.name: Coin
a1c3a6cb-5c96-54dc-bcd3-570ffc9d4e35.short_description: Gold one-hundred *muhur* presentation coin in the name of the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan (r. AH 1037-69 / AD 1627-58), struck at Lahore, dated AH 1048 / AD 1638-39, 12th regnal year. Such coins were presented to officals and nobles as an expression of appreciation and of the grandeur and generosity of the ruler. This one is inscribed in Arabic and Persian in *nasta\`liq* script: on the obverse, "There is no god but God the One, \[and\] Muhammed is His prophet, struck in 1048, at the abode of the Sultanate, Lahore"; and on the reverse; "Shihab al-din Muhammad, Second Lord of the Auspicious Planetary Conjunction, Shah Jahan Padshah Ghazi, twelfth regnal year".
keywords: Coin; coinage; India; gold; numismatics

a21ffaa4-2f94-5760-8200-a9816e236687.name: Eight-pointed star-shaped tile
a21ffaa4-2f94-5760-8200-a9816e236687.short_description: Tile in the shape of an eight-pointed star with a blue border. It is decorated with an eight-pointed star featuring a design in low relief: a running deer in a field of vegetation reserved in white against the lustre-painted ground. The text of the first Sura, *Fatiha* (*The Opener*), in Arabic, is inscribed between the parallel sides of the concentric polygons. The inscription, in *naskhi* characters, is painted in lustre on a white ground.

a283f125-e8c1-5168-96bd-8168ea1e6199.name: Copper door panel.
a283f125-e8c1-5168-96bd-8168ea1e6199.description:
An inscribed copper panel that once adorned the door of the Madrasa al-Ashrafiyya, founded by Sultan al-Ashraf Qaytbay, situated near the western wall of the Haram al-Sharif, next to Bab al-Silsila (Gate of Chains). The Madrasa al-Ashrafiyya is considered to be one of the most important schools of Mamluk Jerusalem, and the third most significant Islamic building in Jerusalem in terms of beauty, splendour and skilled architectural style, after the Dome of the Rock and al-Aqsa Mosque. The panel shown here was taken from the door of the *madrasa* during restoration work carried out in 1928, after it was badly damaged as a result of the earthquake in Jerusalem in 1927. It would seem that the door of the *madrasa* was destroyed and all that remained of it was its copper decorative panels.  
The composition comprises inscriptions that fill two medallions placed either side of a round-cornered rectangle. The two medallions contain *thuluth* script that reads: “Glory to our lord, Sultan Abu al-Nasr Qaytbay. May he have strength in his triumph”. The principle inscription, inside the soft-cornered rectangle, is in rounded *thuluth* script, it reads: “Glory to our lord, the Sultan, the Sovereign, the Just, al-Malik al-Ashraf Abu al-Nasr Qaytbay”. Another inscription inside the rectangle reads: “Sultan of Islam and Muslims, Destroyer of Polytheists and Unbelievers, al-Malik al-Ashraf Abu al-Nasr Qaytbay, Glory to his triumph”. In the middle of the rectangle a Qur'anic verse “al-Tawba” (“the Repentance” 9: 18) is inscribed in kufic script: “The mosques of Allah shall be visited and maintained by such as believe in Allah and the last day, establish regular prayers, and practice regular charity, and fear none (at all) except Allah. It is they who are expected to be on true guidance”. The background outside the medallions and the rectangle contains interwoven vegetal motifs.
a283f125-e8c1-5168-96bd-8168ea1e6199.short_description: This copper panel adorned Madrasa al-Ashrafiyya in Jerusalem, which was built by Mamluk Sultan al-Ashraf Qaytbay at the Western Wall of al-Haram al-Sharif. The panel is worked with epigraphic decoration, which bears the name of the sultan. Vegetal decorative motifs cover the entire panel and fill all the spaces between and around the inscription.
a283f125-e8c1-5168-96bd-8168ea1e6199.holder: Islamic Museum, al-Aqsa Mosque / al-Haram al-Sharif.
a283f125-e8c1-5168-96bd-8168ea1e6199.initial_owner: Al-Malik al-Ashraf Abu al-Nasr Qaytbay (r. AH 872–901 / AD 1468–96).
a283f125-e8c1-5168-96bd-8168ea1e6199.method_for_datation: Dating of the panel was made possible by the inscription, which mentions the name of Sultan al-Ashraf Abu al-Nasr Qaytbay. It is known that this panel is associated with Madrasa al-Ashrafiyya built in around 886 / 1482, and this assertion is further supported by historical sources.
a283f125-e8c1-5168-96bd-8168ea1e6199.method_for_provenance: The copper engraving could have been done anywhere in Egypt, Palestine or Syria. For this reason it is difficult to ascertain the place of production but its presence on the door of the Madrasa al-Ashrafiyya in Jerusalem makes it likely that it was made in a workshop on site.
a283f125-e8c1-5168-96bd-8168ea1e6199.provenance: Probably Jerusalem, but possibly Egypt or Syria.
a283f125-e8c1-5168-96bd-8168ea1e6199.obtention: The piece was transferred in 1928 from the Madrasa al-Ashrafiyya in Jerusalem to the Islamic Museum.

a2a367cc-4a36-54aa-889e-518896791ecf.name: Dish
a2a367cc-4a36-54aa-889e-518896791ecf.short_description: This massive, cast bowl rests on a flat 2mm wide footring with 103mm diameter and has a flat 2cm wide rim. The rim is bulged at its edge. The engraved decoration is confined to its interior. The centre is decorated with a roundel demarcated by five concentric circles. The central motif is a harpy in profile with its head facing towards the viewer. The harpy has a pointed head. The wing and parts of the tail as well as eyes, nose and mouth are indicated by sketchy lines. The drawing is surrounded by an inscription band repeating the same word four times, maybe a stylized abstraction of the word *baraka* or *salama*. The words are separated by four circles. The plain wall contrasts and emphasizes the densely engraved medallion and similarly decorated rim. Here, an illegible word is repeated and interrupted by four medallions this time filled with a stepping bird in profile. The background of the harpy and the inscriptions are filled with foliage.
a2a367cc-4a36-54aa-889e-518896791ecf.holder: University Museum of Islamic Art | The Bumiller Collection
a2a367cc-4a36-54aa-889e-518896791ecf.method_for_datation: Harpys occasionally occur on 12th/13th century metal bowls and trays but are by far not as frequent as human headed winged lions. The most similar design can be found on a square tray in the V&A (inv. no. 181-1951).
a2a367cc-4a36-54aa-889e-518896791ecf.obtention: Gift by Mrs Renate Kirchhof, Bonn 2019

a2a367cc-4a36-54aa-889e-518896791ecf.author: Verena Daiber
keywords: Metalwork; dish; harpy; inscription
materials: Copper alloy

a319402b-f899-522c-a00d-0966b699e425.name: Cloth
a319402b-f899-522c-a00d-0966b699e425.short_description:
This devotional textile would hang from the ceiling or walls inside the Kaaba, the Muslim house of God in Mecca. Qur’anic verses in different calligraphy styles appear printed on red silk. Sultans would drape the Kaaba’s interior walls in silk from China or India as a religious offering since the Mamluk sultan al-Nassir Hassan in 1359.  
  
In medallions, *Tughra* calligraphy illustrates prayers and God’s names “the Merciful” and “the Generous”. The opening chapter of the Qur’an *al-Fatiha* and the *shahada* or declaration of faith rest between serrated lines in *thuluth* calligraphy.  
  
Protected from environmental factors inside the Kaaba, Muslim rulers would not change the interior silks annually but wash them twice a year. As a form of worship, the bestowal of this cloth would simultaneously achieve closeness to the shrine for blessings, reinforce the sanctity of the Kaaba and remind of the sultan’s power and prestige.

a34c1a9f-ced6-5d46-9b24-f76e88d32863.name: Sword.
a34c1a9f-ced6-5d46-9b24-f76e88d32863.description:
This sword, produced in the Mongol style, consists of four parts: the blade, hilt, cross-guard and scabbard. This style of weaponry, which filtered through to Persia, was known by the name of *al-Shamshir.*  
The blade is narrow and tapers at the head. It is attached at the top by a wooden hilt in the middle of which is a notch 1.5 cm wide. Inserted in the blade is a copper band decorated with gold lines. A cross-guard separates the blade from the hilt assuming a cruciform shape, and the long side of which is perpendicular to the hilt and the sword blade, its two sides ending in two ornamental globules. There is an inscription on each side of the cross-guard.  
The blade also bears decorative engraved inscriptions such as Qur'anic verses, popular sayings and poetry stanzas. One of the two edges of the sword bears illuminated inscriptions with an illuminated frame. One of them reads: “There is no hero like 'Ali and no sword like Zulfikar”. And another reads: “Oh Judge of Necessities”. Written on the blade at the hilt is the following text: “Victory is from God and Conquest is near, year AH 785 \[AD 1383\]”. There are two non-illuminated inscriptions engraved on the blade within a cartouche. The first reads: “The work of As'ad Allah”. And the second: “‘Abbas bi Nadir Shah”. In the middle of the blade is an inscription that extends approximately 43 cm. It consists of what is probably popular poetry and begins with the verse: “Unsheath the sword of destruction from its scabbard of support and cleave with it, the preponderance of envy and aggression”.  
The scabbard is made of wood, copper-plated at the top to about 18.5 cm. There are three engraved inscriptions written in *thuluth* script on the copper section. The inscriptions are contained within a linear frame that is surrounded by depictions of flowers and vegetal stems. The copper section is adjacent to two bands each of which is 7 cm wide. A 27.5 cm-long copper section at the end of the scabbard holds five inscriptions; its decoration is similar to that on the copper hilt. In the area between the two copper sections, the scabbard is covered with a piece of carpet-like fabric 47 cm long, woven in red, brown and gold. The inscriptions on the scabbard include popular sayings and poetry in praise of the sword and supplications to God for victory.
a34c1a9f-ced6-5d46-9b24-f76e88d32863.short_description: This sword consists of the scabbard, blade, hilt and cross-guard. It is in the Mongol style, which was taken to Persia. It has a narrow blade and the cross guard has a cruciform shape.  The sword is filled with inscriptions and vegetal decoration. The date engraved on it does not concur with the lifespan of its maker, As'ad Allah.
a34c1a9f-ced6-5d46-9b24-f76e88d32863.holder: Islamic Museum, al-Aqsa Mosque / al-Haram al-Sharif.
a34c1a9f-ced6-5d46-9b24-f76e88d32863.dimensions: Entire length 107 cm, length (of blade) 90 cm, width (of blade) 3.3 cm, length (of Scabbard) 93 cm.
a34c1a9f-ced6-5d46-9b24-f76e88d32863.method_for_datation: This sword has an inscribed date on it, but like tens of other swords it poses a historical puzzle. The date of production engraved on it does not agree with the life-span of the original owner, Shah ‘Abbas I. In addition, it does not concur with the life-span of its craftsman, As'ad Allah, who was a renowned sword-maker and a contemporary of Shah ‘Abbas. It is worth noting that there are about 300 swords distributed in museums worldwide that are associated with As'ad Allah and bear his name. The oldest of them is the sword exhibited here, which dates to 785 / 1383; the most recent dates to 1223/ 1808. Thus, the association of the swords to this skilled craftsman continued for more than four centuries.
a34c1a9f-ced6-5d46-9b24-f76e88d32863.method_for_provenance: Iran has been narrowed down as the place of manufacture of this sword because the craftsman associated with it and original owner have links with Iran.

a3a8aae6-65cc-5236-8f7a-c26a5394e549.name: Incense Burner
a3a8aae6-65cc-5236-8f7a-c26a5394e549.short_description:
This is a hollow cast incense burner in the shape of a bird. It is perforated in the chest, wings and around the neck. Openings are on the crest, neck, chest and underside. Those on the underside are very small and positioned at both ends of the surface.  
The eyes are slightly elevated, engraved feathers reach till the shoulders. A *kufic*\-inscription runs across the shoulders and is interrupted by the wings. A perforated spiralling tendril ornament is on the chest, with an opening in the middle. The wings are ribbed and have engraved twirls, tendril-medallions and an elevated centre. A tendril ornament with a central axis of symmetry runs across the back. Schematic feathers cover the remaining body.  
Incense was inserted into the chest opening and could escape through the heavily perforated surface.

a45839e2-37d8-5fb0-8ec9-90569c5bc248.name: Floor mat
a45839e2-37d8-5fb0-8ec9-90569c5bc248.description: An almost complete mat has perimetrical bands with lozenge designs and triangular motifs. It combines brocaded decoration with self-patterned elements such as the beaded medallions in the centre. Two parallel lines of inscriptions are included in the composition and repeat the same word *baraka* (blessing) in a poorly executed *kufic* script. Geniza records describe how such reed mats were used to cover the floor surface and how detailed descriptions might be given to weavers in order to fill every available space. Based on this information, this small mat could be part of a larger commission, used to fill specific recesses or the entrance of a room.
a45839e2-37d8-5fb0-8ec9-90569c5bc248.method_for_datation: The form of the repetitive word in the *kufic* script places it to this period

a49a47fe-f470-5805-9a91-aceb1f2dd325.name: Bowl painted in blue and black
a49a47fe-f470-5805-9a91-aceb1f2dd325.short_description: The type of thin-walled bowls of an elegant bi-conic shape/decorated with refined blue and black painting belongs to the best achievements of Iranian ceramics of the AD 12th–13th centuries. The inner surface of the museum bowl is decorated with a cross-shaped composition with radial inscriptions in Persian, scratched on black ribbons in the "dry kalam" technique. The inscriptions make up a love poem: "Since you cannot love me for a moment / Do not break further my wounded heart. / Be less cruel, less tyrannical to me, / Until my heart slowly leaves you". Masterly drawn flowers, long-tailed birds and "willow branches" betray the hand of a subtle artist.
a49a47fe-f470-5805-9a91-aceb1f2dd325.method_for_datation: Arthur Sambon's auction catalogue (1914, origin, inscription reading). Stylistic analysis by  V. Krachkovskaya (1926, date); T. Starodub (1976, specified origin).

a507b49f-de2b-5383-b587-8eef58a18a27.name: "Amr has the Infidels Thrown into the Sea"
a507b49f-de2b-5383-b587-8eef58a18a27.alternate_name: Folio from a Khavarannama (The Book of the East) of ibn Husam al-Din
a507b49f-de2b-5383-b587-8eef58a18a27.description: This painting, with its vibrant color palette and lively action, is taken from a manuscript of the Khavarannama (Book of the East), a gathering of tales relating the adventures of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, son-in-law of the Prophet Muhammad. These mostly imaginary accounts of the exploits of 'Ali and his companions against demons, dragons, and kings were composed in emulation of the great Persian poet Firdausi’s Shahnama, but have the important religious figure of 'Ali as their main protagonist.

a5415d97-5be6-5b62-af8d-da90cb25b7f5.name: Sufi assembly
a5415d97-5be6-5b62-af8d-da90cb25b7f5.short_description: The miniature features a nocturnal landscape with a dervish surrounded by six male characters wearing costumes typical of the age of Shah Abbas I (1588-1629). The exquisite finesse of the drawing is enhanced by the subdued colour range, the gold highlights and the beautiful *nasta'liq* calligraphy of the Persian verses: ‘Don’t drink the wine-cup, for every drop is a king’s blood,/Don’t listen to the music, for every tune is just a tale of sorrow./The night has fallen; the drunken feast has neither lamp nor candle; /Join us, for the gathering of maids most fair is pleasant.’ (Translated into English from the Romanian version by Viorel Bageacu, 1987). The verses, as well as the image, are replete with Sufi symbolism.

a607d090-ec21-5282-9640-2e98c5e970b6.name: Door knocker.
a607d090-ec21-5282-9640-2e98c5e970b6.description:
A door knocker that belonged to the Madrasa al-Shadhbakhtiyya in Aleppo, commissioned by the Ayyubid ruler al-Malik al-Zahir Ghazi (r. AH 582–613 / AD 1186–1216). The school was named after Shadhbakht, an '*atiq*, or freed slave, of al-Malik al-‘Adil Nur al-Din Mahmud bin Zangi (r. AH 541–69 / AD 1146–74).  
The door knocker is a bronze flower-shaped ring that takes the form of six semi-circles with intermitting small protrusions. At the top of the knocker is a bolt that would have been used to attach it to the door. Along the body of the knocker is an easily legible Arabic inscription in *thuluth* script that reads: “In the days of al-Malik al-Zahir, who begs for the mercy of God, Shadhbakht the freed slave of al-Malik al-‘Adil Nur al-Din, may God have mercy upon them.” Some simple decorative vegetal motifs are located between the words of the inscription.  
Education in the early Islamic period took place in the mosques, and much of religious education continues to do so. Nevertheless, the Seljuq, Atabeg and Ayyubid periods witnessed a flourishing of specialised education centres dedicated to the study of theology and legal issues. These were known as *madrasas*.
a607d090-ec21-5282-9640-2e98c5e970b6.short_description: A flower-shaped door knocker that was once attached to the gate of the Madrasa Shadhbakhtiyya in Aleppo is inscribed with the patron's name in an easily legible and finely decorated script.
a607d090-ec21-5282-9640-2e98c5e970b6.initial_owner: Al-Malik al-Zahir Ghiyath al-Din Ghazi (r. AH 582–613 / AD 1186–1216).
a607d090-ec21-5282-9640-2e98c5e970b6.method_for_datation: A text recorded on the door of the *madrasa* mentions that it was constructed during the reign of al-Malik al-Zahir Ghazi in 589 (1193).
a607d090-ec21-5282-9640-2e98c5e970b6.method_for_provenance: Since the piece belongs to the door of the Madrasa al-Shadhbakhtiyya in Aleppo, it is assumed that the door knocker was manufactured in Aleppo.

a610d51e-269b-57af-bb7c-ff15d5cae8f8.name: Pen box
a610d51e-269b-57af-bb7c-ff15d5cae8f8.short_description: Pen boxes with separate compartments for the *qalam* and all the other accessories were used all over the Islamic world. They were fashioned in numerous shapes, most of which are rectangular with either square or rounded ends. A different type is the East Iranian wedge shape, made in two parts, with an inner, compartmented box that could be entirely removed. These pen boxes were probably pushed through the belt, a fashion which was retained up until Ottoman times.

a65b9f90-12e9-50e4-9065-9d1274ef0a10.name: Incense Burner.
a65b9f90-12e9-50e4-9065-9d1274ef0a10.description:
An incense burner of great beauty and fine workmanship that is also in very good condition. The engraved inscriptions on it indicate that the Mamluk sultan, al-Zahir Sayf al-Din Abu Said Muhammad Jaqmaq endowed it to al-Haram al-Ibrahimi (the Ibrahimi Mosque) in Hebron (al-Khalil), where it remained for a number of centuries until it was transferred in 1928 to the Islamic Museum in Jerusalem. The burner is elongated in form and has ribbed and curved surfaces. It is composed of three sections: the bottom section, the top section and the attachment and chains. The bottom section of the burner is a spherical container in the shape of an inverted dome in concordance with the top section of the burner, which takes the form of an elongated dome. The upper part of the bottom section is spherical, transforming into a ribbed surface with 12 faces and terminating in a ribbed edge that also has 12 faces. The spherical surface contains gilded epigraphic decorations that read: “There is no God but God, Muhammad is the prophet of God and Ibrahim \[Abraham\] is the friend of God. This blessed burner was endowed by our lord, the Sultan, the Sovereign, the Ruler, al-Zahir Abu Said Muhammad, May God strengthen his triumph, to al-Haram al-Ibrahimi”. The burner rests on a slightly elevated base, which widens towards the bottom; it is ribbed with 12 sides and is decorated with gold lines.  
The upper section is the cover or lid. It is in the shape of a dome faced by two spherical forms: the upper, smaller one and the lower. This section of the burner contains two inscriptions. The bottom of the cover has a ribbed surface of 12 faces, each containing vegetal decoration in the form of a lotus blossom. The cover terminates in a ribbed edge.  
There are three suspension loops on the top of the lower section attached to which are chains; the chains are attached to the three suspension loops on the bottom of the burner. The attachment and chains is in the form of a small dome, the apex of which is connected to the hook for hanging. The dome of the attachment is ornamented with vegetal decoration in addition to 12 small spheres, which adhere to the ribbed neck. There is a gilded inscription on the attachment that reads: “The burner is thus the burner of the humble servant, Abd al-Qadir bin Muhammad Qabzi”.
a65b9f90-12e9-50e4-9065-9d1274ef0a10.short_description: This burner was donated, as indicated by its gilded inscriptions, by Sultan al-Zahir Jaqmaq.  It is an elongated burner with ribbed surfaces with twelve divisions.  It is composed of three sections: the bottom, the upper section with the lid, and the attachment and chains. It is decorated with vegetal motifs.
a65b9f90-12e9-50e4-9065-9d1274ef0a10.holder: Islamic Museum, al-Aqsa Mosque / al-Haram al-Sharif.
a65b9f90-12e9-50e4-9065-9d1274ef0a10.initial_owner: Sultan al-Zahir Sayf al-Din Abu Said Muhammad Jaqmaq (r. AH 842–57 / AD 1438–53).

a65b9f90-12e9-50e4-9065-9d1274ef0a10.method_for_datation: This piece was dated by the inscriptions that indicate this incenser belonged to Sultan al-Zahir Jaqmaq.
a65b9f90-12e9-50e4-9065-9d1274ef0a10.method_for_provenance: It is probable that the incenser was made in Cairo for its construction resembles other objects from the ateliers in Cairo during this period. The incenser was endowed to the Haram al-Ibrahimi in Hebron by the Mamluk sultan, al-Zahir Sayf al-Din Abu Said Muhammad Jaqmaq, an assertion based on the inscription.
a65b9f90-12e9-50e4-9065-9d1274ef0a10.provenance: Probably custom-made in Cairo specifically for al-Haram al-Ibrahimi (the Ibrahimi Mosque) in Hebron (al-Khalil).
a65b9f90-12e9-50e4-9065-9d1274ef0a10.obtention: The piece was transferred from the Haram al-Ibrahimi (the Ibrahimi Mosque) in Hebron to the Islamic Museum in Jerusalem in 1928.

a6c524e9-ce3d-5461-9dd8-c2fb3bba06a7.name: Pair of wooden doors
a6c524e9-ce3d-5461-9dd8-c2fb3bba06a7.short_description: The pair of doors bears a symmetrical geometric design with small star-shaped or polygonal plaques, each decorated with an arabesque. Two panels which carry Arabic inscriptions determine a Christian provenance from a church of Cairo as they are excerpts from the Bible (Luke 2:14 and Psalm 44:10). An analogous example is the doors of the *minbar* in the mosque al-Salih Tala’i‘ dated 1299 (AH 699).

materials: Wood, ivory

a6d99b72-8bf4-59da-85c1-3680ed3adc6d.name: Jug
a6d99b72-8bf4-59da-85c1-3680ed3adc6d.short_description: Jug with rounded carination and flaring neck. The handle connects Jug with rounded carination and flaring neck. The handle connects the rim with the largest diameter of the body and is topped with a thumb rest. The object is entirely covered with an off-white slip. The rim is accentuated with a black slip painted band. The vessel is decorated with a purplish-black inscription band around the largest diameter of the body – reading *al-hamdu lillah* – the neck and along the handle. The inscription on the handle reads *Allah al-ʿalim bi-l-umur* (God is omniscient on all things). Also on the inner side of the neck we find a short illegible epigraphic decor. The combination of the widespread form with floriated *kufic* inscriptions is unusual. The small jug could be a drinking vessel.
a6d99b72-8bf4-59da-85c1-3680ed3adc6d.holder: University Museum of Islamic Art | The Bumiller Collection
a6d99b72-8bf4-59da-85c1-3680ed3adc6d.method_for_datation: Comparable script design is found on large conical bowls in the Nishapur excavations and in the Khalili Collection. Many examples of similar script but with inverted colours (white script on black slip) are found in Iranian museums. This type is common in Central and Northern Iran, but not found in Central Asia.

a80ae3b6-0e85-5e1b-93e6-f4552c3eac51.name: *Ataifor* (bowl).
a80ae3b6-0e85-5e1b-93e6-f4552c3eac51.description:
This *ataifor*, with a ring in the base and curved sides, is made of yellowish material and coated with a white glaze. The inside is decorated in green and manganese. The decorative theme is made up of a large circular border running round the edge of the plate in which it is possible to see the remains of a *kufic* inscription with the phrase ‘al-Mulk’ (power). The decoration is finished with two narrower strips that cross in the centre, with markings that appear to be a simplification of *kufic* writing but that are in fact meaningless. The decorative technique used, epigraphic motifs in copper green and manganese black visible through the white glaze, produces an impressive chromatic effect.  
Madinat al-Zahra was the most important centre for the production and distribution of ceramics glazed and decorated in green and manganese during the Caliphate. Ornamentally, the clarity of the design and the austerity of the compositions, with extensive areas of the base undecorated, differentiates them from other works produced at the same time in al-Andalus.  
The function of this type of ceramic is still unclear, but what is clear is that production at Madinat al-Zahra constituted a fundamental technological advance. The use of copper and manganese oxides in the decoration and the glazing, which made the containers waterproof and stopped liquids soaking the earthenware, created a type of special crockery which was considered a luxury.
a80ae3b6-0e85-5e1b-93e6-f4552c3eac51.short_description: Found in an archaeological dig at the palatine city of Madinat al-Zahra, this bowl or *ataifor* would have been part of the domestic crockery at the caliph’s home. This can be inferred from the inscription ‘al-Mulk’, ‘the power’, presumably referring to the power of the caliph.
a80ae3b6-0e85-5e1b-93e6-f4552c3eac51.method_for_datation: The *kufic* script belongs to an initial stage of production at Madinat al-Zahra, before the reign of al-Hakam II (350–66 / 961–76).
a80ae3b6-0e85-5e1b-93e6-f4552c3eac51.method_for_provenance: The piece came from archaeological excavations at Madinat al-Zahra. Most of the ceramics are characterised by an open not a closed shape, and the majority of them are *ataifors*. The phrase ‘al-Mulk’, related to Umayyad power and legitimacy, is the inscription most frequently found in this type of ceramic.

a87439ea-aee1-50f5-a0b5-501d95e7044f.name: *Divan-i Shahi* (Collection of Poems by Shahi)
a87439ea-aee1-50f5-a0b5-501d95e7044f.short_description:
This manuscript is a *divan*, a collection of poems, by Amir Shahi Sabzavari. Amir Shahi Sabzavari, also called Shahi, was a poet and calligrapher at the court of Prince Baysunghur in Herat. Shahi died in 857 AH / 1453 AD.  
The manuscript contains 60 folios in total, of which five are illustrated. According to the colophon the scribe of this manuscript was Abd al-Wahid. Some of the folios are signed by their painter Abd al-Gani, who is also responsible for the astonishing lacquer binding.  
Judging by a portrait on the frontispiece that looks like Sultan Suleiman I. , the manuscript must have been finished during his reign between 926-936 AH /1520-30 AD. The manuscript was part of the collection of Polish orientalist Waclaw Rzewuski until his death in 1831 AD, when the manuscript was bought for the Imperial Court Library in Vienna.
a87439ea-aee1-50f5-a0b5-501d95e7044f.method_for_datation: Dorothea Duda recognizes portraits of Sultan Selim I. on the binding of the manuscript. She suggests that the manuscript might have been started during the reign of Sultan Selim I. but finished during the reign of Sultan Suleiman I., who succeeded his father in 1520. This is supported by the presence of an additional portrait of a man on the frontispice that looks like Sultan Suleiman I. The inclusion of both rulers therefore indicates a probable date of production somewhere between 926-936 AH /1520-30 AD.
a87439ea-aee1-50f5-a0b5-501d95e7044f.method_for_provenance: The provenance was established through documentation in the inventory book of the Imperial Court Library by Joseph Freiherr von Hammer-Purgstall.
a87439ea-aee1-50f5-a0b5-501d95e7044f.obtention: Following the death of  the explorer and orientalist Waclaw Seweryn Rzewuski in 1831 AD, the manuscript was bought directly from his collection for the Imperial Court Library in the same year.
a87439ea-aee1-50f5-a0b5-501d95e7044f.bibliography:
Duda, Dorothea, *Islamische Handschriften I. Persische Handschriften, Die illuminierten Handschriften und Inkunabeln der Österreichischen Nationalbibliothek*, vol. 4, Vienna: Verlag der Österreichischen Akademie der Wissenschaften, 1983: 185-187.  
Duda, Dorothea, "Islamische Lackeinbände - ihre künstlerische Entwicklung und ihr Verhältnis zum Buch als Gesamtkunstwerk", *Journal of Turkish Studies* , 26 : I (2002), 163-203.
a87439ea-aee1-50f5-a0b5-501d95e7044f.artist: 'Abd al-Gani painted the binding as well as folios 1b-2a and fol. 18a.
a87439ea-aee1-50f5-a0b5-501d95e7044f.binding_desc:
The richly decorated lacquer binding on this manuscript is an artwork in itself. Executed in the Shirazi style, this binding has courtly scenes painted on its front and back cover. The doublures of the manuscript are decorated with a medallion surrounded by floral ornaments, painted in two kinds of gold on a black background.  
The front cover depicts a group of men set in an outdoor scene. The men in the upper half of the painting are wearing Ottoman turbans, while some men on the lower half are wearing head gear that look like a mixture of the hats the *Janissaries* wore and those the *silahdars* wore. As the *Janissaries* were part of the elite infantry of the Ottoman army and *silahdars* were close aides of the Ottoman sultans it can be assumed that the binding was in fact manufactured within the realms of the Ottoman Empire.  
Additionally, Duda notes that the man in the middle of the front cover and the man sitting on a throne on the back cover have similarities with formal portraits of Sultan Selim I. She consequently advocates that at least the binding must have been commissioned during the reign of Selim I.

keywords: Divan; Shahi
materials: Blue, green and gold ink on thin, white paper. Calligraphic *Nasta'liq* script of 11 lines per page. 2 decorative pages, 5 miniature paintings.

a878caed-2598-567c-80a3-7ec37561865b.name: Seljuq Rug
a878caed-2598-567c-80a3-7ec37561865b.description: Carpets from the 13th century Aladdin Mosque in Konya are known as the “Konya Group”. They were identified in 1906 as the first finds from this period. These carpets are of key importance in the history of World Carpet Art. This example was specially woven to be used in a mosque. It is decorated with religious motifs and*kufic*writing. A light blue eight‒pointed star design on a dark blue background covers the entire central field. The main border is divided into square sections with stylised*kufic* characters arranged back‒to‒back in light red on a dark red ground. On the small borders, bird motifs are stylized to form leaves on branches.

a89685ed-d6b6-5d4f-ba6b-53f166d90f5d.name: Fragment of lintel (*izar*).
a89685ed-d6b6-5d4f-ba6b-53f166d90f5d.description:
This lintel, which has been slightly damaged on the lower right-hand side, is sculpted with an inscription interrupted by a section in an architectural style filled with vegetal motifs.  
The inscription reproduces a Qur'anic text, the beginning of verse 47 of Sura 11 'the Messenger', which suggests that this lintel was originally used in a religious building. The upstrokes of the angular *kufic* characters end in concave bevels. Only the upstrokes of *nun* and *ha* finish with a simple movement, mimicking the elegant appearance of a swan's neck. The low letters, such as *dal* and *waw*, are crowned with decorative motifs formed of joined concave and bevelled upstrokes. All of the letters sculpted in the round are surrounded by a raised line that amplifies their edges.  
The vegetal background behind the script seems to play a secondary role to the letters themselves. The movement of the stem, the number of floral motifs and their silhouettes are all made to fit the height, spacing and shape of the up strokes. This large and sober decoration, sculpted in champlevé, uses the thick stem and single palm in all of their forms: curved at the base into a ring, with triangular calyxes, and fanned. Smooth symmetrical palms with lower lobes with pointed edges, similar to fleurons, are also used. The outer edges of all of the lobes of these different types of flowers are decorated with small festoons that appear to be a simplification of the digits of acanthus leaves.  
The sobriety and elegance of the *kufic* characters and the rigour and simplification of the vegetal forms used in the decoration of this lintel are characteristic of Almohad aesthetics, to which this piece appears to be linked.
a89685ed-d6b6-5d4f-ba6b-53f166d90f5d.short_description: The sobriety and elegance of the *kufic* characters used in the Qur'anic inscription, and the rigour and stylisation of the plant forms that decorate this lintel, originally from a religious building, are characteristic of Almohad aesthetics.
a89685ed-d6b6-5d4f-ba6b-53f166d90f5d.dates: Hegira second half of the 6th century / AD second half of the 12th century.
a89685ed-d6b6-5d4f-ba6b-53f166d90f5d.dimensions: Height 16 cm, length 106.5 cm, depth 7.5 cm.
a89685ed-d6b6-5d4f-ba6b-53f166d90f5d.method_for_datation: The elegance of the calligraphy characters and the understated plant decoration belong to an artistic style identifiable on dated Almohad monuments.

a8b1900c-9427-5c3f-8152-c6361cbe0b53.name: Calligrapher’s license
a8b1900c-9427-5c3f-8152-c6361cbe0b53.short_description: This licence, written in black *naskhi*, follows at the end of a manuscript that also contains two chapters of the Holy Qur’an, *Al-Buruj* ("The Big Stars") and *Al-Tariq* ("The Night-Comer"). It is contained within a triangular cartouche with gilt borders, flanked by flower sprays. The licence is issued to Hafiz Abdallah Hilmi by Salih Nahif.
