e722241c-4515-59f7-bedf-15c25aea04a3.name: Qur’an.
e722241c-4515-59f7-bedf-15c25aea04a3.description:
Written in *naskhi* script in black ink on delicate finished (*aharlı)* paper, the pages have thick gilded marginal lines and 13 lines of text per page. There are 346 pages in all. The first *sura* (*al-Fatiha*) and the first four verses of the second (*al-Baqara*) are illuminated with gilding between the lines of text. The chapter headings on the two facing pages on which these verses are written, as well as the areas outside the marginal lines, are covered with leaves of gilding and very colourful illumination in the Turkish Baroque-Rococo style. All the chapter headings are written in white *tawqi'* script on top of gilded illumination. Individual verses are separated by individuated gold rosettes, and rose motifs of various forms in the page margins mark the end of every five and 10 verses. The leather binding is brown on the outside and green on the inside. The exterior of the binding has floral designs rendered freely and naturalistically in green and yellow gilding.  
  
The calligrapher of this Qur'an, Mustafa Izzet Efendi (AH 1215–92 / AD 1801–76), was born in Tosya and came to Istanbul for his education. He learned calligraphy from Mustafa Vasıf and Yesarizade Mustafa Izzet Efendi. His most famous works are *hilya*s (prose descriptions of the Prophet Muhammad) and sheets with calligraphic exercises called *istif.* The inscriptions on the drum of the dome of Ayasofya, among the Islamic world's most famous, are by him.  
  
Two different artists worked on this Qur'an's decoration. They are Mehmet Salih, who was chief bookbinder at the Ottoman court in the time of Sultan Abdülmecid \['Abd al-Majid\], and his apprentice Rashid Effendi.  
  
Beginning in the 12th / 18th century, Turkish art experienced change under the influence of European art. This style, known as Turkish Baroque-Rococo, is reflected in the arts of the book. This Qur'an is the most beautiful example of its application to book decoration.
e722241c-4515-59f7-bedf-15c25aea04a3.short_description: Illumination is a natural part of Qur'ans. Illuminators used naturalistic floral motifs influenced by Europe alongside classical elements to illuminate the Qur'ans during the AH 12th–13th / AD 18th–19th centuries.
e722241c-4515-59f7-bedf-15c25aea04a3.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts.
e722241c-4515-59f7-bedf-15c25aea04a3.initial_owner: Pertevniyal Valide Sultan (d. 1300 / 1883; wife of Sultan Mahmud II and mother of Sultan Abdülaziz (‘Abd al-‘Aziz) I; queen mother from 1277–92 / AD 1861–76).
e722241c-4515-59f7-bedf-15c25aea04a3.method_for_datation: According to the date found on the manuscript it was written in Safar 1259 (AD March 1843).
e722241c-4515-59f7-bedf-15c25aea04a3.method_for_provenance: The manuscript was found at the tomb of Pertevniyal Valide Sultan, who donated it to be read at the complex bearing her name in AH 1284 / AD 1868. The work's calligrapher and illuminators were court artists. For this reason it is almost certain to have been made in Istanbul.
e722241c-4515-59f7-bedf-15c25aea04a3.obtention: Transferred to the Museum from the tomb of Pertevniyal Valide Sultan in 1926.

e76ff42a-8d69-50d8-ac1f-2bbd53a08547.name:
Bijan takes the reins of Gushtaham’s horse  
Folio detached from a *Shahnameh* (Book of Kings) by Abu’l-Qasim Firdausi (d. 1010)
e76ff42a-8d69-50d8-ac1f-2bbd53a08547.short_description: Recounting the legendary history of Iran’s shahs (kings) up to the Arab conquest in 642 AD and the country’s adoption of Islam, Firdausi’s epic poem the *Shahnameh* (Book of Kings), completed in 1010, inspired many illustrated copies. The present folio was detached from a copy that is known as the “Big Head” *Shahnameh*. This name refers to the characteristic feature of the majority of its paintings: the large heads of its human figures.
e76ff42a-8d69-50d8-ac1f-2bbd53a08547.obtention: Former Prince Saddrudin Aga Khan Collection
e76ff42a-8d69-50d8-ac1f-2bbd53a08547.artist: Dated 1494, copied by Salik b. Sa‘id, and dedicated to Sultan 'Ali Mirza
keywords: Folio; work-on-paper; works-on-paper; Shahnama; Shahnameh; Big-Head; Painting; human; human-figure
materials: Opaque watercolour, gold and ink on paper

e78c6ccf-a931-5f61-a53f-9a33b0ed0065.name: Sepulchral stele.
e78c6ccf-a931-5f61-a53f-9a33b0ed0065.description: The stele has a shaped base decorated with an elegant frieze with plant volutes in a style exemplified by the funerary stelae of Palermo. Both edges have been damaged. The Arabic script is in elongated *kufic* characters in the Fatimid style. According to M. Amari (see Bibliography), it reads: ‘ In the name of God the compassionate … give peace. Each soul must savour its own ability, because the day of resurrection (now) whoever misses hell, barely, and makes it to Paradise, has attained a great triumph. The life of this world … illusion. The power … Prophet. This is the tomb of Ayyub (son of …) Mukhallaf, the fuller, who died on Saturday in the first ten days of Rajab of the year five hundred and seventeen \[25 August to 3 September 1123\]. God have mercy on him’. The textile industry was very widespread in Sicily, as attested by another inscription from AH 462 / AD 1072 still kept at the Regional Gallery of Sicily (San Giovanni list no. 61), which mentions Ibrahim, a *dibag* (silk cloth) weaver.
e78c6ccf-a931-5f61-a53f-9a33b0ed0065.short_description: Tomb with *kufic* inscriptions. Tombs and stelae often bore formulas taken from the Qur’an, sometimes with expressions of the virtues of the deceased. In this case, the dead man’s trade is mentioned (weaver), evidence of the vitality of textile production by Muslim craftsmen in Sicily at that time.
e78c6ccf-a931-5f61-a53f-9a33b0ed0065.holder: Regional Gallery of Sicily, Abatellis Palace
e78c6ccf-a931-5f61-a53f-9a33b0ed0065.dimensions: Width 171 cm, height 19 cm, depth 27 cm.
e78c6ccf-a931-5f61-a53f-9a33b0ed0065.obtention: Deposited with the Royal Museum of Palermo.

e7be577c-7197-59de-94eb-bd3d5d7cdba0.name: Portrait of emperor Shah Jahan, his three sons, and Asaf Khan
e7be577c-7197-59de-94eb-bd3d5d7cdba0.short_description: In this royal family portrait, Emperor Shah Jahan (r. 1628–58), sitting in haloed profile upon a gold-footed throne under a high white canopy, accepts a jewelled gift from his father-in-law, Asaf Khan. At his right are his three eldest sons—Dara Shikoh (1615–59), Shah Shija (1616–59), and the ill-fated Awrangzeb (r. 1618–1707), whose death effectively marked the end of the great Mughal Empire. All figures are resplendent in turbans decorated with jewels, pearl necklaces, different types of daggers (*khilanum*, *katar*, and *kard*), lavishly embroidered sashes, and gilded swords. An illuminated carpet lies underfoot.
e7be577c-7197-59de-94eb-bd3d5d7cdba0.obtention: Former Prince Saddrudin Aga Khan Collection

e80bcaa9-4d37-5613-9f67-15e7d790f6a9.name: Wall inscription.
e80bcaa9-4d37-5613-9f67-15e7d790f6a9.description:
A wall inscription that is *in situ* at Aqaba Castle. The inscription border, in *naskhi* script, runs along one wall inside the main entrance and continues on both sides in one of the rooms immediately inside the entrance.  
  
The inscription states that the castle was built by Amir Khayr Bay al-Ala\`i during the reign of the Sultan Qansuh al-Ghuri (AH 906–22 / AD 1500–1516) the penultimate Burji Mamluk Sultan of Egypt, who was preoccupied with maintaining the security of the lands and waterways in Egypt and Syria. The date, which is not clear in the inscription, would have read hegira 910 (AD 1504) or hegira 920 (AD 1514). The inscription states that the castle's builder was Amir Khayr Bay al-Ala\`i, whom the contemporary Egyptian historian Ibn Iyas mentions was known as al-Mi\`mar (the builder). The stress on the letter 'n' in the word **بنّا** 'Banna' (Builder), and the word **بنِِا** 'Bena', meaning building, both written in the same script, but the latter with thestress on the letter (n), confirms that Amir Khayr Bay al-Ala\`i was the builder of Aqaba Castle.
e80bcaa9-4d37-5613-9f67-15e7d790f6a9.short_description: A wall inscription that runs along the walls of a room immediately inside the entrance to the Aqaba Castle, and states that the castle was built by Amir Khayir Bay al-Ala’i during the reign of Sultan Qansuh al-Ghuri. The date is not clear but would have read 910 (AD 1504) or 920 (AD 1514).
e80bcaa9-4d37-5613-9f67-15e7d790f6a9.dimensions: Height (above the ground) 140 cm, length: 14 m, width: 66 cm.
e80bcaa9-4d37-5613-9f67-15e7d790f6a9.method_for_datation: The panel is dated by the inscription that mentions the name of the Mamluk Sultan Qansuh al-Ghuri (r. 906–22 / AD 1500–1516).
e80bcaa9-4d37-5613-9f67-15e7d790f6a9.method_for_provenance: The provenance is well known as the stone inscription is *in situ* on the wall inside the main entrance and in one of the rooms near the entrance at Aqaba Castle.
e80bcaa9-4d37-5613-9f67-15e7d790f6a9.obtention: The inscription panel is *in situ* at Aqaba Castle.

e88ac084-acaa-583b-abc2-fa8a32e7027e.name: Qur’anic manuscript of Sultan Bayazid.
e88ac084-acaa-583b-abc2-fa8a32e7027e.description:
A Qur'anic manuscript with an embossed and gilded binding made up of two covers (front and back) and a library marker. In the centre of each cover is a long medallion with palmette shaped extensions. Surrounding the medallion, in all four corners of the cover, are four cornerpieces. The bands create a broad frame that encompasses within it decorative cartouches. The library marker has part of the same decoration of the covers. The decorative motifs on the bands of the cover, as well as the medallion, are composed of gilded vegetal stems and blossoms. The inside cover is framed by an illuminated spiral decoration and, inside the frame, by decorative forms in the shape of cartouches surrounding a medallion.  
Folio 1b is the *waqf* charter of the Qur'anic manuscript. Folio 3b–4a forms the frontispiece composed of two identically decorated pages that form the axial junction of the volume. The margins of the spread are decorated with depictions of vegetal stems and blossoms as well as geometric lines, all of which are gilded. Following the margins on the inside, are decorative bands that surround each page on three sides, and which are decorated with confronting pyramidal shapes in gold and blue. These bands are separated from the written text by frames in successive colours. Following them on the inside, are bands decorated with ornamentation similar to the previous bands, but these are smaller in size. The text on these two pages is written in illuminated *thuluth* script, with six lines on each page. The lines are separated by motifs of violet-coloured clouds.  
Each of the remaining folios is divided into five rectangular sections, each with a single line from the Qur'an, written in illuminated *rihani* script figuring in the first, third and fifth rectangular area. Four lines in *naskhi* script are written in the second and the forth rectangular section. Two sides of each of these rectangles are appropriated as two long sections embellished with illuminated spiralling vegetal decoration. The markers for every fifth and tenth part are symbolised by decorative forms in the margin; formed of a circular disk with an illuminated circumference, the centre of which is a circle with a blue background. The name of the chapter, the verse number and the place where they appear are accentuated in gold within an illuminated frame that has a blue background.
e88ac084-acaa-583b-abc2-fa8a32e7027e.short_description: This Qur’an was donated by Amir Bayazid, son of Sultan Suleyman the Magnificent, to the Dome of the Rock. It is bound with decorated and embossed leather. The beginning of the manuscript is decorated with vegetal and geometric forms. The pages are divided into five rectangles, three of which are written in illuminated rihani  script and the rest in naskhi script.
e88ac084-acaa-583b-abc2-fa8a32e7027e.holder: Islamic Museum, al-Aqsa Mosque / al-Haram al-Sharif.
e88ac084-acaa-583b-abc2-fa8a32e7027e.initial_owner: Amir Bayazid, son of Sultan Sulayman the Magnificent.
e88ac084-acaa-583b-abc2-fa8a32e7027e.dimensions: Length 37.5 cm, width 26.5 cm, depth 7 cm.
e88ac084-acaa-583b-abc2-fa8a32e7027e.method_for_provenance: It is likely that this Qur'an was copied in Istanbul, where the endower resided, or in Kütahya the hometown of the scribe who endowed the manuscript, and who was also the *Qadi* (Judge) of Kütahya. His name is on the first page of the Qur'an.
e88ac084-acaa-583b-abc2-fa8a32e7027e.obtention: The Qur'an manuscript was transferred from the Dome of the Rock to the Islamic Museum at an unknown date.

e9100be3-069e-5d04-b867-dbfe67ede897.name: Bowl with calligraphic and splashed decoration
e9100be3-069e-5d04-b867-dbfe67ede897.short_description: This earthenware dish was covered with an opaque white slip before receiving its ornamentation. Three sets of five or – once – four short brush strokes executed in green glaze highlight the edge of the dish. The centre shows an as yet unread manganese inscription and a green glaze dot. The dish was influenced by both Abbasid and Chinese luxury wares.
keywords: Bowl; glazed; Earthenware; calligraphy; inscription; Chinese influence

e9cd5ed9-9868-52d2-b520-c5f830442609.name: The last of the Abbasid Caliphs, Mustaʿsim (r. 1242–58)
e9cd5ed9-9868-52d2-b520-c5f830442609.short_description: This folio, along with two others in the Aga Khan Museum Collection (AKM40 and AKM41), comes from a manuscript assembled at the court of Shahrukh (d. 1447) and disassembled by the art dealer Émile Tabbagh in the 1920s and 30s. The manuscript’s content draws primarily from a world history prepared by Rashid al-Din (d. 1318) for the Mongol Ilkhan Oljeitu in 1307. It is not a simple copy of Rashid al-Din’s work, but rather a hybrid manuscript with a tangled history made even more complex by its dispersal. This folio is one of a group of folios that were originally prepared under Rashid al-Din’s own supervision and later incorporated into the Timurid manuscript.
e9cd5ed9-9868-52d2-b520-c5f830442609.obtention: Former Prince Saddrudin Aga Khan Collection
keywords: Folio; work-on-paper; works-on-paper
materials: Ink, watercolour, and gold pigment on paper

e9d20fa0-c214-51e8-a022-980c7d31384c.name: Tekke panel
e9d20fa0-c214-51e8-a022-980c7d31384c.short_description: *Hüsn-i Hat* is a type of calligraphy. Turks probably started to get interested in calligraphy after their arrival to Anatolia. The brightest period was during the Ottoman era. Calligraphy developed well beyond its functional role; it almost played a similar role to the paintings in Western art in terms of the level of its aesthetics. The script *"Ya Hazreti Şeyh Sultan Yusuf Sümbül Sinan Kaddes Allahu sırrahu"* (religious text, untranslatable) is written on a black background with *Zerendud* (gilded) calligraphy and designed as the *sikke* (tall felt hat) of the Sünbüli order. It stands over a small table in Rococo style and there are hyacinth flowers on either corner of the upper part. The sides of the plate are surrounded by two borders that are Rococo in design.
e9d20fa0-c214-51e8-a022-980c7d31384c.holder: Vehbi Koç Foundation Sadberk Hanim Museum
keywords: Caligraphy; Hüsn-i Hat; plate
materials: Black ink on paper

ea8bbe97-c193-5f18-8fc1-bff27b21d5c0.name: Qur’an binding.
ea8bbe97-c193-5f18-8fc1-bff27b21d5c0.description:
The decoration on both the exterior and interior of the deep-red leather binding is achieved by moulding. On the outer and inner covers, a wide border frames a sunken oval medallion with palmette pendants and corner-pieces. The edges of the medallion, pendants and corner-pieces are tooled and gilded. There are two differences between the outer covers and the doublures: On the doublures all the decoration is executed in gold on a black background, with the exception of the main ground of the medallion, which is gilded. The border of the doublures has an inscription of Qur'anic verses, while the borders on the outer binding hold a floral composition. The floral compositions both inside and outside are in the so called *saz* style, distinguished by its fantastical serrated leaves, and painted with gilding. On the doublures, in between oval medallions filled with floral compositions, the 'Throne Verse' (2: 255) is written in *thuluth* script with gilding. The flap of the binding is inscribed with *sura* 56, verses 77–9. The balance maintained between decorated and undecorated areas of the binding, as well as the surface differences in the decorated areas, lend the surface a sense of depth.  
  
This binding is a fine example of how the style of the famous AH 10th / AD 16th-century bookbinder Mehmed çelebi and his school continued to exert influence in the Ottoman court workshops of the AH mid-11th / AD 17th century, seen in details such as the *saz* style floral decoration and the sunken medallions and corner-pieces.
ea8bbe97-c193-5f18-8fc1-bff27b21d5c0.short_description: This Qur'an binding was made in the Ottoman palace ateliers. It is an important example of the AH 11th / AD 17th century, displaying all the characteristics of Turkish bookbinding art with great proficiency.
ea8bbe97-c193-5f18-8fc1-bff27b21d5c0.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts.
ea8bbe97-c193-5f18-8fc1-bff27b21d5c0.method_for_datation: According to the colophon it was written in AH 1054 / AD 1644. Although the name of the bookbinder is not known, the style of the floral composition on the binding suggests that it is from the same period as the calligraphy.
ea8bbe97-c193-5f18-8fc1-bff27b21d5c0.method_for_provenance: The quality of the calligraphy, binding and illumination suggest that the work may have been produced in the palace atelier in Istanbul.
ea8bbe97-c193-5f18-8fc1-bff27b21d5c0.obtention: Transferred to the Museum in 1911 from the tomb of Sultan Ahmed I.
ea8bbe97-c193-5f18-8fc1-bff27b21d5c0.bibliography: Ölçer, N. *et al, Museum of Turkish and Islamic Art*, Istanbul, 2002, p.296.
ea8bbe97-c193-5f18-8fc1-bff27b21d5c0.artist: Calligrapher: Mehmed bin Abdurrahman (Muhammad bin ‘Abd al-Rahman).
ea8bbe97-c193-5f18-8fc1-bff27b21d5c0.author: Sevgi Kutluay

materials: Finished (*aharli*) paper, ink, watercolour; the leather binding tooled and gilded.

eaae312b-a7ee-550a-b89f-f4dc899d92ed.name: Kohl jar.
eaae312b-a7ee-550a-b89f-f4dc899d92ed.description:
Small, lenticular rock-crystal bottle, broken at the top and the bottom. Its high-relief decoration is divided into different sections. At the top there is a strip inscribed in florid *kufic* script that reads 'Baraka min Allah / wa lahu al-afiya' (The blessing of God) on both sides. The next section depicts two birds of prey, presumably falcons, facing one another around a vegetal composition in the form of volutes.  
As is common in this type of piece, this jar has a 'bore' (central cylindrical hole) that would almost certainly have been used to keep kohl or antimony chloride, which was used as a cosmetic. This jar would have been mounted on some sort of support and would also have had a glass rod used to dip into the substances and apply it.  
The production of colourless quartz rock-crystal provided a level of transparency that medieval craftsmen had not yet achieved using glass. This, combined with the difficulty of the technique, meant that this craftwork was always sought after. Objects made of this material were sometimes offered as diplomatic gifts.  
There is no evidence of the production of such objects in al-Andalus, and their presence on the Iberian Peninsula in the AH 4th and 5th / AD 10th and 11th centuries was undoubtedly due to trade with Fatimid Egypt. Many of the Islamic rock-crystal pieces that came to the Caliphate of Córdoba from the East were dispersed subsequently around the Iberian Peninsula and reused during the Christian age, embellished with new and sumptuous precious-metal elements.
eaae312b-a7ee-550a-b89f-f4dc899d92ed.short_description: Objects carved from rock-crystal from Fatimid Egypt were much sought after for their beauty and quality, and consequently they were imported, exchanged as diplomatic gifts and considered to be valuable booty. The small size of the inside of this pot suggests that it was used to hold essence.
eaae312b-a7ee-550a-b89f-f4dc899d92ed.method_for_datation: The rock-crystal industry in Fatimid Egypt grew up a short time before 254 / 868 and survived until 452–4 / 1060–2. Most researchers agree on the Egyptian origin of the approximately 180 objects from this era that are held around the world, as well as on Kurt Erdman's method of classifying them purely on the basis of stylistic analysis.
eaae312b-a7ee-550a-b89f-f4dc899d92ed.method_for_provenance: According to its file, this jar came from Alcalá de Henares. There are currently 40 rock-crystal pieces in Spain, including various different bottles and chess pieces (there is another Fatimid piece in this material in the general inventory of the National Archaeological  Museum). Most of them, having been acquired during the Reconquest in the form of taxes or war booty, were deposited in churches or monasteries in various different regions of Christian Spain as offerings.
eaae312b-a7ee-550a-b89f-f4dc899d92ed.obtention: The piece was deposited with the National Archaeological Museum by the Artistic Recuperation Service on 21 November 1910.

ebe4dfb5-2c91-5b48-9947-a44e4359f085.name: Daghestan Prayer Rug
ebe4dfb5-2c91-5b48-9947-a44e4359f085.description:
A 19th century Caucasian prayer rug with a knotted pile. Its directional design consists of a single-plane lattice design crowned by an angled arch with a pointed summit, laid out on an ivory-coloured background and framed by a wide red and blue border.  
  
The lattice design of the centre field contains diamond-shaped compartments, each of which holds a single multi-coloured flower. The horizontally arranged rows of multi-coloured flowers contain repeats of three flowers, symmetrically distributed. The flower repeat arrangement is staggered across the succeeding rows, creating a diagonal uniformity of colour and shape distribution. Below the right edge of the prayer niche arch, and to the right side of the centre-field, near the edge of the border, is a figure of a quadruped, possibly a dog, rendered in pink and yellow with black outlines. This little animal, with its long curled up tale and long stretched back ears, has been inserted in place of a flower.  
  
The border of the carpet consists of a dark green/blue background overlaid with a red scroll of Arabesque design – a version of the Caucasian border scrolls inspired by Arabic *kufic* script.  
  
Such carpets are made for use in performing the daily prayers in Islamic culture. The arch end of the carpet indicates the side upon which the worshiper lays his forehead in prostration.
ebe4dfb5-2c91-5b48-9947-a44e4359f085.obtention: Gifted by Sir William and Lady Burrell to the City of Glasgow, 1944

keywords: prayer niche; prayer rug; vegetal lattice; floral motif; animal; geometric decoration
materials: Wool warp and weft; wool pile

ec6884a5-10bb-5f2d-a512-2a4dc076e53b.name: Basin of Badr al-Din Lu’lu’
ec6884a5-10bb-5f2d-a512-2a4dc076e53b.short_description:
The tradition of richly engraved and inlaid brassware with décor combining floral and geometric ornament, calligraphy, and figurative imagery developed in Khorassan in the 12th–early 13th century. Starting from the 1220s the technology and style moved westwards, particularly to Mosul, located in Jazeera (northern Iraq).  
An outstanding work by a Mosul artisan is this large basin made for Badr al-Din Lu’lu’, who ruled in Mosul between 1223–59. The inside surface of the piece is densely covered with engraving and silver inlay (now mostly lost) featuring courtly scenes together with symbols of planets and other celestial bodies, as well as signs of the Zodiac. A geometric ornament characteristic of Mosul metal ware makes up the background.  
The Arabic inscription running along the edge of the basin is of a special historical significance. The inscription given in the form of rhythmic prose lists titles and merits of Badr al-Din Lu’lu’ as a ruler and a pious Muslim. Among a few other famous inscriptions dedicated to Lu’lu’ this one is the longest and the most informative. Certain titles within the inscription allowed researchers to date the basin more precisely, to the last decade of Lu’lu’s reign, 1249–59.
ec6884a5-10bb-5f2d-a512-2a4dc076e53b.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis and inscription reading by V. Krachkovskaya (publication, 1947, date, origin).
ec6884a5-10bb-5f2d-a512-2a4dc076e53b.method_for_provenance: Publication of Vera Krachkovskaya (1927): the Khanenkos' collection. Proven by the entry in the old Museum Inventory Register (1925-1946).

ecbfd555-c941-5154-8936-9832dbbd13cf.name: Bowl
ecbfd555-c941-5154-8936-9832dbbd13cf.description:
The brass apodal bowl features an exterior decoration with a dense vegetal weave and large inscriptions in thuluth on a foliate background, interrupted by circular medallions with peonies.  
The inner base of the cup is decorated with a school of engraved fish following a circular pattern and a potentiated cross, the latter likely added when the object arrived in Europe.  
The inscription reads: "The high, lordly, sovereign, wise, active, just, ordering, zealous, Treasure, Help, Support, Assisted, \[official\] of Al-Malik an Nasir, may his victory be glorious."  
The epigraph follows the typical formula of Mamluk protocol for high-ranking figures. Although neither his name nor his specific function are indicated, the inscription suggests that the owner was an official of Sultan al-Malik al-Nasir al-Din Muhammad ibn Qulawun. This is the sultan who owned the large Borgia Collection Basin, also in the museum's collections. From this, it can be deduced that the bowl was made by 1341, that is, during the sultan's lifetime, according to the customary formula used in the inscription, which ends with the phrase "may his victory be glorious."  
The bowl, as also underscored by the decorative motif of engraved fish within, was used to hold drinking water or for ritual purposes.  
The bowl entered the museum collections thanks to Mario De Ciccio's donation to the Italian state in 1958, consisting of 1,300 pieces. These primarily consist of applied art objects from various periods and typologies, collected by the collector over a period of over 50 years, first in Palermo, his hometown, then in Naples, his adopted home since 1906, and also on the most highly regarded international art markets.

ecda8323-4cc5-5e96-a034-122e8ca1bb6c.name: Textile from the Prince Felipe of Castile burial
ecda8323-4cc5-5e96-a034-122e8ca1bb6c.description: This fragment came from the set of garments wore by the Castilian Prince Phillip in his burial at Villalcázar de Sirga (Palencia). The fragment is a very good example of the richness of the textile from al-Andalus. The textile has an inscription in Arabic that could be translated as “Glory to our Lord the Sultan”. This an early example of the interest in collecting important textiles, even before the important research made by Gómez-Moreno in the Royal Convent of the Huelgas (Burgos).

ece5f0c8-d2d1-5924-bc14-94c826dc2171.name: Bowl fragment.
ece5f0c8-d2d1-5924-bc14-94c826dc2171.description: A fragment from a stone-paste (fritware) bowl decorated in cobalt-blue and black under a transparent colourless glaze. This fragment, from the centre of the dish, is decorated with a roundel within which is Arabic calligraphy intertwined with organic stems and leaves. A band of black and white decoration surrounds the roundel. The design and technique of this bowl was common in both Syria and Egypt, making identification of the place of production very difficult. The difficulty lies in the fact that the potters of both Mamluk Egypt and Syria migrated in search of work between the cities of the two regions. The fashion for painting in black and blue under a transparent glaze started in Iran during the late AH 7th / AD 13th century, and spread quickly to Syria and Egypt. The main distinguishing features between wares made in Iran, Syria or Egypt are the different shapes and sizes of the pieces.
ece5f0c8-d2d1-5924-bc14-94c826dc2171.short_description: Arabic calligraphy was employed to decorate a wide variety of surfaces. Although not enough of the text survives to be deciphered, proverbs, poetic verses and prayers were frequently used. The strong vertical lines of the *naskhi*\-style script dominate the centre of the cobalt-blue and black bowl.
ece5f0c8-d2d1-5924-bc14-94c826dc2171.holder: Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum, Glasgow Museums.
ece5f0c8-d2d1-5924-bc14-94c826dc2171.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis: the material composition, glaze and decoration of this fragment are typical of ceramics made in the potteries of Syria. Several similar examples have been found in Fustat indicating that ceramics from the Middle East were brought to trade in Egypt.
ece5f0c8-d2d1-5924-bc14-94c826dc2171.provenance: Produced in Damascus, Syria; found at Fustat, Egypt.
ece5f0c8-d2d1-5924-bc14-94c826dc2171.bibliography:
Grube, E. J., *Cobalt and Lustre: The First Centuries of Islamic Pottery*, The Nasser D. Khalili Collection of Islamic Art, Vol.9, London, 1994.  
  
Lane, A., *Later Islamic Pottery: Persia, Syria, Egypt, Turkey*, London, 1971.
ece5f0c8-d2d1-5924-bc14-94c826dc2171.author: Noorah Al-Gailani
keywords: Commerce; calligraphy
materials: Stone-paste (fritware) with black and cobalt-blue decoration under a transparent, colourless glaze.

ed486397-6f2e-5e7e-898e-db4869717ed6.name: Ferdowsi, *Shahnama* ('The Book of Kings')
ed486397-6f2e-5e7e-898e-db4869717ed6.short_description: Abu'l-Qasim Mansur, called Ferdowsi (died 411 AH / 1020-1 AD) wrote the renowned, extensive epic poem called *Shahnama* (‘The Book of Kings’) around 1000 AD. This copy was written in *nasta’liq* script by the scribe Ibn Abu'l-Barakat Asadallah in 1025-1026 AH / 1616-17 AD, possibly near Isfahan, Iran. According to the two colophons (fol. 251a, 447a), the scribe completed the second part of the epic before the first. Stamps of three owners reveal that the manuscript was in the collection of a Muhammad b. Muhammad Hashim in 1029 AH / 1619 AD, of a Muhammad Nasir in 1051 AH / 1641 AD, and of Joseph von Hammer-Purgstall in 1223 AH / 1808-9 AD. The manuscript then became part of the Austrian National Library in 1842. Its 44 paintings of various sizes, artistic styles, and qualities reveal that it was likely made in a provincial capital that drew inspirations from the artistic centre of Isfahan, Iran.
ed486397-6f2e-5e7e-898e-db4869717ed6.dimensions: 370 x 150 mm (277 x 150 mm), ff. II, II*, 447 folios.
ed486397-6f2e-5e7e-898e-db4869717ed6.method_for_datation: Two colophons: fol. 251a: 1026 AH / 1617 AD; fol. 447a: 1025 AH / 1616 AD
ed486397-6f2e-5e7e-898e-db4869717ed6.method_for_provenance: On fol. 447a, there are two oriental owner's stamps: Muhammad b. Muhammad Hashim (1029 AH / 1619 AD) and Muhammad Nasir (1051 AH / 1641 AD). On fol. 447b, there is an owner's stamp of Joseph von Hammer-Purgstall (1223 AH / 1808-09 AD).
ed486397-6f2e-5e7e-898e-db4869717ed6.obtention: Acquired by the Austrian National Library in 1842.
ed486397-6f2e-5e7e-898e-db4869717ed6.bibliography: Duda, Dorothea, *Islamische Handschriften I. Persische Handschriften, Die illuminierten Handschriften und Inkunabeln der Österreichischen Nationalbibliothek*, vol. 4, Vienna: Verlag der Österreichischen Akademie der Wissenschaften, 1983: 59-63.
ed486397-6f2e-5e7e-898e-db4869717ed6.binding_desc: The brown European leather binding has a neoclassical gold embossing of the Austrian National Library as well as gilt edges. It was likely made in 19th-century Vienna, Austria.
ed486397-6f2e-5e7e-898e-db4869717ed6.author: Theresa Zischkin
keywords: Afrasiyab; Bahram; Div; epic; Faridun; Ferdowsi; Garshasp; Isfandiyar; Iskandar; Rustam; Shahnama; Sam; Simurgh; Zal
materials: Ink, colour and gold on paper. Calligraphic *nasta'liq* script of 25 lines per page.

ed505641-7fab-598f-a27b-c58fb38cc49e.name: Portrait of the Ottoman Sultan Ahmed I.
ed505641-7fab-598f-a27b-c58fb38cc49e.description:
This miniature painting executed in gouache on paper is a portrait of the Ottoman Sultan Ahmed I (AH 1012–26 / AD 1603–17) and once formed part of an album that contained both Ottoman Turkish and Persian miniatures, apparently assembled in the AH 12th / AD 18th century. The youthful ruler, best known as the founder of the Blue Mosque in Istanbul, is seated on a large, richly decorated throne beneath a cusped arch. He is leaning against a decorated bolster wearing a white turban enhanced by two tall plumes issuing from bejewelled sockets. His green and gold-brocade caftan has large, gold globular buttons down the front. The garment is secured by a jewel-studded gold belt, which incorporates three cusped, circular units at the front. A bejeweled dagger handle can be seen protruding from Sultan Ahmed’s belt on the right. He wears a red-orange overcoat with small gold buttons down the front; the coat is lined with ermine. A gold-coloured slipper protrudes from underneath his garments. In his left hand, the fifth finger of which is enhanced by a gold ring with circular stone, Sultan Ahmed holds the *mandil*, a ceremonial handkerchief with gold detailing. In his right hand he holds a volume of poetry bound in the so-called *sefine* format (with the vertically oriented pages bound at the top, narrow end). The gilt binding shows a delicately drawn, central medallion enclosed within an elongated, arched cartouche.  
Above the portrait of the sultan runs a cursive inscription contained within two elongated cusped cartouches, written in white against a blue background and enhanced by white floral detailing, it reads: ‘Hasrat Sultan Ahmad \[Ahmed\] ibn Sultan Muhammad \[Mehmed\] Khan’. A tiny inscription on the lower left-hand side of the work names the painter ‘al-fakir Süleyman’. The portrait is surrounded by a green inner frame and an orange outer frame with additional ruled frames in blue, red, gold and green in between and around the outside of the outer border.
ed505641-7fab-598f-a27b-c58fb38cc49e.short_description: This miniature painting shows the Ottoman Sultan Ahmed I, best known as the founder of the Blue Mosque in Istanbul. It has been suggested that this portrait was executed in the court workshops of the Topkapı Saray in Istanbul during the early AH 11th / AD 17th century.
ed505641-7fab-598f-a27b-c58fb38cc49e.dates: Hegira first half of the 11th century / AD first half of the 17th century
ed505641-7fab-598f-a27b-c58fb38cc49e.dimensions: 29 x 19.9 cm (with frame), 19 x 12.7 cm (without frame).
ed505641-7fab-598f-a27b-c58fb38cc49e.method_for_datation: It is assumed that this portrait was painted during or just after the lifetime of Sultan Ahmed I (r. 1012–26 / 1603–17).
ed505641-7fab-598f-a27b-c58fb38cc49e.method_for_provenance: It has been suggested that this portrait was executed in the Court workshops of the Topkapı Saray in Istanbul during the early 11th / early 17th century.
ed505641-7fab-598f-a27b-c58fb38cc49e.obtention: Purchased from M. Richard, Tehran, in 1888.
ed505641-7fab-598f-a27b-c58fb38cc49e.bibliography:
Scarce, J., *Domestic Culture in the Middle East: An Exploration of the Household Interior*, Edinburgh, 1996, p.87.  
Sourdel-Thomine, J., and Spuler, B., “Die Kunst des Islam”, *Propyläen Kunstgeschichte*; 4, Berlin 1973, Plate 416.

ed505641-7fab-598f-a27b-c58fb38cc49e.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
keywords: Ahmed I; Al-fakir Suleyman
materials: Gouache and gold on paper.

eda80913-f027-5404-9e2e-9aaf84a86ff7.name: Qur’an fragment
eda80913-f027-5404-9e2e-9aaf84a86ff7.short_description: This Qur’an fragment is a single leaf penned in calligraphic angular (*kufic*) script on parchment, and can be stylistically dated back to c. 250–300 AH / c. 850–900 AD within the Near East. It is part of a series of 19 fragments from various manuscripts, referred to as *Codex Mixtus 814*. The horizontal format, the monumental *kufic*, and the overall rich decoration reveal that it belonged to an early Qur’anic manuscript of particularly high quality. The text is written in black-brown ink with coloured dots and strokes for vocalisation and diacritical marks, respectively. These kinds of Qur’an fragments are exceedingly rare due to the poor state of preservation most of such early manuscripts experienced.
eda80913-f027-5404-9e2e-9aaf84a86ff7.obtention: Likely part of the Austrian National Library from 1830 onwards.
eda80913-f027-5404-9e2e-9aaf84a86ff7.bibliography: Duda, Dorothea, *Islamische Handschriften II. Persische Handschriften, Die illuminierten Handschriften und Inkunabeln der Österreichischen Nationalbibliothek*, vol. 5, Vienna: Verlag der Österreichischen Akademie der Wissenschaften, 1992: 194-195.
eda80913-f027-5404-9e2e-9aaf84a86ff7.binding_desc: All fragments were originally kept in a wooden box, possibly from the 19th century. Since 1980, some of them are kept between panes of acrylic glass.
eda80913-f027-5404-9e2e-9aaf84a86ff7.author: Theresa Zischkin
keywords: Calligraphy; illumination; Qur’an; Kufic
materials: Ink, opaque watercolour and gold on paper. *Kufic* script.

edc14340-a97e-5565-a4cb-1ff1d239124a.name: Two pages from the Blue Qur’an.
edc14340-a97e-5565-a4cb-1ff1d239124a.description:
Two pages taken from an unique Qur'an, written in gilt *kufic* script and containing the *sura*s Luqman (31: 34) and al-Sajdah ('Prostration' 32: 1–3).  
Preliminary analyses has established that the indigo used for the dye was imported from Egypt or India, countries with which trade was beginning to develop in the AH 4th / AD 10th century. The gold-leaf was glued to the parchment using egg white.  
The writing is compact and lacks any diacritical signs over the vowels. The letters are not stippled with dots.  
The title of the *sura* is in a gilded strip made up of several small floral motifs. Attached to this strip and toward the left margin of the page is a gilt palm-leaf motif of floral arabesques. Marking the divisions between the verses are silver-gilt flowerets which have turned black from oxidisation.  
Contrary to the views of certain art historians, the various pages of Qur'ans copied onto blue parchment and kept in a number of different museums and collections throughout the world originate neither from Mashhad in Iran nor from Spain. They all belong to the Blue Qur'an from the library of the Great Mosque of Kairouan. This is confirmed by similarities in the measurements, the number of lines, the writing and the gilding.
edc14340-a97e-5565-a4cb-1ff1d239124a.short_description: Two pages belonging to a single Qur'an: the Blue Qur'an, copied in gold *kufic* script. They contain the *suras* Luqman and al-Sajda. Pages from the Blue Qur'an from the Great Mosque of Kairouan, copied onto blue vellum, can now be found in different places throughout the world.
edc14340-a97e-5565-a4cb-1ff1d239124a.method_for_datation: The simple and archaic *kufic* calligraphy is reminiscent of the writing in other Qur'ans of the 4th / 10 century taken from the old library of the Great Mosque of Kairouan. This is corroborated by the palaeographic study carried out by the art historian M. Bloom, who showed that the calligraphy is of Maghrebi origin and can be dated from the 4th / 10th century, and even from the second half of that century.
edc14340-a97e-5565-a4cb-1ff1d239124a.method_for_provenance: From the same studies by the art historian M. Bloom.
edc14340-a97e-5565-a4cb-1ff1d239124a.provenance: Very probably from Kairouan, a great centre for book production at that time.
edc14340-a97e-5565-a4cb-1ff1d239124a.obtention: After the abolition of the *habus* foundation in Tunisia, the National Library obtained this Qur'an in 1967. In 1983 it went back to Kairouan, to the Centre of the Islamic Arts and Civilisation of Raqqada. It has been displayed at the Raqqada Museum of Islamic Art since 1986.
edc14340-a97e-5565-a4cb-1ff1d239124a.bibliography:
*De Kairouan a Carthage* (exhibition catalogue), Tunis, 1995, p.41.  
*Ifriqiya: Thirteen Centuries of Art and Architecture in Tunisia*, pp.159–62, 182–3.
edc14340-a97e-5565-a4cb-1ff1d239124a.author: Mourad Rammah
keywords: Calligraphy; floral decoration; habus; religious manuscript
materials: Parchment dyed with indigo, illuminated.

ee03a75d-9b6a-5031-8a38-a31dc82d9b98.name: Mosque lamp.
ee03a75d-9b6a-5031-8a38-a31dc82d9b98.description: A mosque lamp of typical size and shape for Mamluk lamps, with flaring neck, wide body and high foot. Thick glass loops are attached for the suspension cords. The body is decorated with a large inscription which reads, 'This is what was made a *waqf* by the servant yearning for God the Exalted, hoping for the pardon of his generous Lord, Qijlis, \[officer\] of al-Malik al-Nasir'. The neck carries a verse from the Qur'an (9:18) and three medallions with the Mamluk blazon indicating the owner's rank, in this case a sword telling us that Qijlis was *amir silah* (arms-bearer) to the sultan. The lamp is said to have come from a monastery in Seidnaya, a village near Damascus.
ee03a75d-9b6a-5031-8a38-a31dc82d9b98.short_description: A mosque lamp of typical Mamluk form, with bold inscriptions and three medallions with the patron’s blazon, a sword. The patron was one Amir Qijlis, arms-bearer to the sultan, who commissioned this lamp as a pious donation to an unknown mosque.
ee03a75d-9b6a-5031-8a38-a31dc82d9b98.initial_owner: Sayf al-Din Qijlis al-Nasiri, an officer of the Mamluk Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad between AH 716–31 / AD 1317–31.
ee03a75d-9b6a-5031-8a38-a31dc82d9b98.method_for_datation: The inscription mentions Sayf al-Din Qijlis al-Nasiri, who was promoted to *amir silah* of Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad in 716 / 1317 and died in 731 / 1331.
ee03a75d-9b6a-5031-8a38-a31dc82d9b98.method_for_provenance: Cairo and Damascus were the two most important centres of art production under the Mamluks.
ee03a75d-9b6a-5031-8a38-a31dc82d9b98.bibliography: Lamm, C. J., Mittelalterliche Gläser und Steinschnittarbeiten aus dem Nahen Osten, Berlin, 1930, p.439.
ee03a75d-9b6a-5031-8a38-a31dc82d9b98.author: Barry Wood
keywords: waqf; religious object; Mosque interior decoration; calligraphy; inscription; coat of arms
materials: Enamelled glass with gilding.

ee1f4b01-6ab5-5630-b130-11699979b383.name: Veterinary treatise *Kitâb fî al-inâya bi al-khayli wa sâiri-d-awâbbi al-rukub*.
ee1f4b01-6ab5-5630-b130-11699979b383.description:
This veterinary treatise on horse care consists of three volumes, each one divided into 30 chapters or *bab*, some of which are missing. The texts are written with brown ink in Maghrebi cursive characters and with irregular vocalisation, partial diacritic points and orthoepic marks in the same colour. Each page has 17 lines. Some of the words in the text and the titles are in red. The colophon at the end of the third volume provides the date of the manuscript without mentioning the copyist's name.  
The significance of this manuscript lies in the nine miniatures, some of which are captioned, that illustrate the texts. Each depicts a horse, alone or with a carer, grazing, having its teeth checked, covering, being given medicine with a horn, swimming and having its mouth examined for an illness that prevents it from eating normally. Each miniature appears in a square space filling nearly the whole of the width of the page to the same height as the written area and sometimes framed with a triple red line. The people and the horses as well as their surroundings are depicted with great realism and detail. In the interior scenes, the figures stand out against a plain blue or green background and on a brick-red coloured floor. The miniatures with grazing horses have a background with a graduated sky, going from midnight blue with a hint of purple in the upper part to a pinkish white in the horizon.
ee1f4b01-6ab5-5630-b130-11699979b383.short_description: This work is a veterinary treatise on horse care. The nine miniatures that illustrate the text are its most interesting aspect, each showing a horse on its own or held by a groom. All are drawn with noteworthy realism and attention to detail.
ee1f4b01-6ab5-5630-b130-11699979b383.method_for_datation: Date mentioned on the last page colophon in volume three of the work, the beginning of Dhu 'l-Hijja 1126 / December 1714.
ee1f4b01-6ab5-5630-b130-11699979b383.method_for_provenance: From the origin of the copyist and the writing style.

eeadc3f4-cf85-5e38-bce5-3c6d8631b78c.name: Maghrebi *rab’a*.
eeadc3f4-cf85-5e38-bce5-3c6d8631b78c.description:
A *rab’a*, a Qur'anic manuscript divided into 30 parts, each of which has an independent binding. The *rab’a* was preserved in a square wooden box covered on the outside with leather and embellished by four embossed decorative bands that incorporate geometric patterns outlined with silver thread. In between the four bands are three silver belts which reach from the back to the front of the box to support it. Each belt is decorated with three star-like shapes made from silver and overlaid with blue enamel. In all, the box bears 10 decorative forms in the same style; on the four corners of the box, for example, there are geometric shapes inlaid with mother-of-pearl and red and blue enamel.  
The bindings of all 30 parts are made from embossed red leather, with both the front and back embellished with ornamentation and text, which is identical on all the volumes. On each cover there are four inscription bands that form a square, and which are encircled by silver thread. The text is gilded, and in the middle of each front cover there is a silver-braided circle. Within the circle in gilded text is a Chapter from the Qur'an (14: 52), which tells the story of Ibrahim (Abraham). It reads: “Here is a message for mankind. Let them take warning there from, and let them know that he is (no other than) One God. Let men of understanding take heed”.On the back cover there is another quote from the Qur'an “al-Baqara” (“the Cow”, 2: 181), which reads: “If anyone changes the bequest after hearing it. The guilt shall be on those who make the change. For Allah hears and knows (All things)”.  
Each part of the *rab'a* begins with two identical illuminated panels that differ in design from one volume to the next. Most of the square-shaped panels are surrounded by broad illuminated frames and contain decoration consisting of lines, circles and squares painted in more than one colour, but predominantly in gold. The *rab'a* is written in Maghrebi-style script with black ink, with five lines to each page. Verses are divided from each other by the word “verse” written in gold and surrounded by three circles. The *waqf* charter of the *rab'a,* written in an illuminated *kufic* script within a square that is also illuminated, is on the last two pages of each volume.
eeadc3f4-cf85-5e38-bce5-3c6d8631b78c.short_description: A *rab’a*, a Qur’anic manuscript in 30 parts, preserved in a wooden box covered with leather and decorated with silver bands. The texts are in Maghrebi *kufic* script, written with saffron water on gazelle parchment. The *rab’a* is filled with decorative motifs, colours and illumination. This is one of three *rab’a* written for Mecca, Medina and Jerusalem; only the last copy has come down to us.
eeadc3f4-cf85-5e38-bce5-3c6d8631b78c.holder: Islamic Museum, al-Aqsa Mosque / al-Haram al-Sharif.
eeadc3f4-cf85-5e38-bce5-3c6d8631b78c.initial_owner: Commander of the Faithful, Abu al-Hasan Ali, the first Marinid (ruled in the Maghreb AH 732–49 / AD 1331–48).
eeadc3f4-cf85-5e38-bce5-3c6d8631b78c.dimensions: Length 22 cm, width 20 cm, depth 5 cm.
eeadc3f4-cf85-5e38-bce5-3c6d8631b78c.method_for_datation: The *rab’a* is dated by an inscription.
eeadc3f4-cf85-5e38-bce5-3c6d8631b78c.method_for_provenance: The Maghreb was narrowed down as the place of production for this manuscript based on the *waqf* charter that appears at the end of each volume. For example, the *waqf* in the eighth volume reads: “The eighth volume of this Holy Qur'anic manuscript completes a part of a thirty volume series, all of which have been written in the handwriting of Abd Allah Ali, *amir* of the Muslims, son of the *amir* of the Muslims, Abi Said Uthman, son of the *amir* of the Muslims, Abi Yusuf Ya'qub bin Abd al-Haqq, ruler of the Maghreb, May God bless him, and it has been endowed for recitation in al-Aqsa Mosque.”
eeadc3f4-cf85-5e38-bce5-3c6d8631b78c.obtention: The piece was transferred at an unknown date from al-Aqsa Mosque in Jerusalem to the Islamic Museum.

eeb73625-9b7f-5b6e-bac6-70835ba47781.name: Amulet
eeb73625-9b7f-5b6e-bac6-70835ba47781.short_description: Tear-shaped pendant with a silver openwork border of twisted wire and granulation. It is inscribed on both sides with Arabic repoussé invocations and Qur’anic texts. The invocations in *thuluth* script on the scrolling ground at the centre are surrounded by epigraphic bands with verses in *naskhi* calligraphy: ‘*Ma sha’ Allah!*’ (‘God willing’) is encircled by the verses of Sura CXIII (*Al-Falaq*/ *The Daybreak*) and ‘*Ya Hafiz!*’ (‘O Preserver!’), by the verses of Sura CXIV (*Al-Nas* / *Mankind*). These last two chapters of the Qur’an, very short and intensely evocative, referred to as *al-mu‘awwidhatan* (the two protecting ones), appear quite frequently on amulets.
eeb73625-9b7f-5b6e-bac6-70835ba47781.holder: The National Museum of Art of Romania
eeb73625-9b7f-5b6e-bac6-70835ba47781.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis; Comparison with related objects
eeb73625-9b7f-5b6e-bac6-70835ba47781.obtention: Partial return (1956) of the Romanian treasure sent to Russia for safekeeping during World War I.

ef10164f-a690-53dc-a8c5-b066a2dcb828.name: Folio from the 'Blue Qur'an'
ef10164f-a690-53dc-a8c5-b066a2dcb828.short_description: This folio comes from the Blue Qur'an, so named for the rich hue of its indigo-dyed surface. The dyeing of parchment for use in luxurious manuscripts originated in Byzantine tradition and continued into the early Islamic period. The gold and silver ink of the *kufic* text and circular verse markers add to the opulence of this folio. While many scholars believe this Qur’an to have originated in Qayrawan, Tunisia, details in its verse markers have led others to argue that it may have actually been produced in Umayyad Córdoba. Nevertheless, a description of a manuscript with the same specifications as this one appeared in an inventory of the Mosque of Qayrawan in AH 693 / AD 1293, indicating that it was part of the mosque’s endowment by this time.
ef10164f-a690-53dc-a8c5-b066a2dcb828.dates: Hegira 3rd–4th century / AD second half 9th–mid-10th century

ef6f3f6c-f567-5300-9a2c-887d4b9a516c.name: Anonymous, *Ruznamce-i shemsiyye ve qamariyye* ('Small calendar of solar and lunar years')
ef6f3f6c-f567-5300-9a2c-887d4b9a516c.short_description: The anonymous Arabic treatise titled *Ruznamce-i shemsiyye ve qamariyye* (‘Small Calendar of Solar and Lunar Years’) was compiled for the years 905 AH / 1499 to 1000 AH / 1592. It was possibly written in the 16th-17th centuries in Ottoman Syria. The Latin marginalia *Deo Trino et Uno honor Lausq infinita* on fol. 8a were probably written by a later Christian owner, while the owner’s stamp on fol. 8b is by Joseph von Hammer-Purgstall, from whom the manuscript was purchased by the Austrian National Library in 1842. The extant European half-leather binding corresponds to a possibly Viennese production date in the 19th-century. The calendar itself is composed in a format similar to Ottoman prayer calendar scrolls and their tabular arrangement. Particularly fascinating, however, is the fact that small paintings are pasted in the margins of the manuscript, which is atypical for this manuscript format. These paintings include both zodiac images as well as monthly allegories. The zodiac miniatures are stylistically relatable to Timurid Shiraz of the early 15th century when patrons had great interest in astrology and the natural sciences. It can be hypothesised that these paintings were cut out from an older calendar or astrological treatise and reused in a new context. They are visually integrated into the page layout, as the border is drawn around the images. The monthly allegories, in contrast, are pasted over these borders and hence must have been added later. They display themes from a Christian context mixed with Islamic artistic conventions, the scenes reminiscent of Islamic metalwork. As such, it is possible that the calendar was later owned by a Christian who pasted this second group of illustrations onto the pages.
ef6f3f6c-f567-5300-9a2c-887d4b9a516c.method_for_provenance: On fol. 8a, an owner's stamp by Joseph von Hammer-Purgstall dated to 1223 AH / 1808 AD is visible.

efc1e427-4c81-58f3-a2ae-e846616be1e3.name: Qur’an cabinet.
efc1e427-4c81-58f3-a2ae-e846616be1e3.description:
The body of the cabinet is four-sided and has short legs. The cover is in the shape of a dome. The wood has been decorated with ebony and ivory using the inlay technique.  
  
The side faces of the cabinet's body are organised into rectangular panels. The interiors of these panels have the same designs as those found in bookbinding compositions of the classical Ottoman period. In the corners of the rectangular panels are ivory corner pieces. Cartouches with palmette-shaped lobes are covered with ebony. At the centre of each of the panels are ivory medallions in relief, each with a huge boss at its centre and pendants terminating in rosette and palmette motifs. On either side of the medallions are Chinese cloud-bands; while in the upper and lower areas are four six-sided rosettes. The interiors of the six-sided rosettes are decorated with mosaic-inlay of white and painted ivory and silver wire. Around the rectangular cartouches are inlays of ivory over ebony, as well as undulating designs featuring split-palmette motifs.  
  
Around the bottom border of the cover, separated by lobed cartouches, are ivory cartouches on which is carved Qur'an *sura* 2, verse 255 in *thuluth*\-style calligraphy.  
  
The surface of the dome is covered with broad ebony and ivory plaques, the V-shapes of which make up a zigzag design. The dome comes to a point; its upper section is decorated with ivory inset with the reverse side out, a series of ebony palmettes, and six-sided rosettes filled with mosaics. The finial on top has broken off.  
  
The cabinet was prepared in order to house sections of the Qur'an. It has five interior compartments. The interior of the dome is decorated with medallions made up of compositions of palmette and *rumi* (split-palmette) motifs painted (*kalemişi*) on a background painted cream. The inner border of the cover is decorated with black palmettes and *rumi*s on a red ground.
efc1e427-4c81-58f3-a2ae-e846616be1e3.short_description: This wooden cabinet was produced at the Ottoman palace ateliers to contain chapters of the Qur'an. It is decorated in classical Ottoman style and inlaid with ebony, ivory and silver wires.
efc1e427-4c81-58f3-a2ae-e846616be1e3.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts.
efc1e427-4c81-58f3-a2ae-e846616be1e3.dates: Hegira first half of the 10th century / AD 16th century.
efc1e427-4c81-58f3-a2ae-e846616be1e3.method_for_datation: The enrichment of the surfaces, the shape, the technique, and the balanced use of materials all reflect the attributes of Ottoman woodwork of the first half of the 10th / 16th century.
efc1e427-4c81-58f3-a2ae-e846616be1e3.method_for_provenance: The cabinet shows all the characteristics of the decorative motifs and compositions of the classical Ottoman Period, as formulated in the Ottoman court workshops. It is highly probable that the object was produced in the first half of the 10th / 16th century in one of the Istanbul workshops directed by the court.
efc1e427-4c81-58f3-a2ae-e846616be1e3.obtention: Brought to the Museum in 1914 from the Ayasofya Library, which was built by Sultan Mahmud I (r. 1142–68 / 1730–54).

efc2172a-d635-578e-af49-9d6126ab9b75.name: Part 8 of a 30-part Qur’an
efc2172a-d635-578e-af49-9d6126ab9b75.short_description:
The text contains the *sura* *al-An‘am* (V’), verse 111, to *sura* *al-A‘raf* (VI), verse 87. The main text is in *muhaqqaq*, incidentals are in *kufic* and *naskhi* and there are 3 lines to the page. The text is written in a stately form of *muhaqqaq*, a style that from the rise of the rounded scripts was particularly favoured for fine Qur’ans. The vocalisation in gold is outlined in black. A rectangular band terminating in a large marginal hasp on folio 38a has the heading of *sura* *al-A‘raf*, written in a black-outlined white *kufic* against a superbly illuminated background.  
Both the script and the illumination of this imposing manuscript are related to a seven-part copy of the Qur’an dedicated to Abu’l-Qasim Harun ibn ‘Ali ibn Zafar, the vizier of Özbeg, the last atabeg of Azerbaijan (r. 1210–1225).

efcc7ec3-36f8-59b0-a853-5e760fd7f0b1.name: An obituary listing eight victims of the Nizari Ismaʿili assassins
efcc7ec3-36f8-59b0-a853-5e760fd7f0b1.short_description: This folio, along with two others in the Aga Khan Museum Collection (AKM89 and AKM41), comes from a manuscript assembled at the court of Shahrukh (d. 1447) and disassembled by the art dealer Émile Tabbagh in the 1920s and 30s. The manuscript’s content draws primarily from a world history prepared by Rashid al-Din (d. 1318) for the Mongol Ilkhan Oljeitu in 1307. It is not a simple copy of Rashid al-Din’s work, but rather a hybrid manuscript with a tangled history made even more complex by its dispersal. This folio comes from one of the most heavily illustrated sections of the manuscript, a section that also helps reveal a secret about the work’s origins: Rashid al-Din was probably not its original author.
efcc7ec3-36f8-59b0-a853-5e760fd7f0b1.obtention: Former Prince Saddrudin Aga Khan Collection
keywords: Folio; work-on-paper; works-on-paper; manuscript
materials: Ink, watercolour, and gold pigment on paper

f01728d7-fe74-597e-b37f-12f01e9ac1a3.name: *Rab’a* of Sultan Murad.
f01728d7-fe74-597e-b37f-12f01e9ac1a3.description:
A *rab’a* (Qur'an divided into 30 parts) that has been preserved in two identical wooden cube-shaped boxes, each of which is covered with a level of stucco and painted black. A number of inscription bands form part of the decoration and contain gilded texts written in *thuluth* script. The texts include *hadiths* of the Prophet to encourage study of the Qur'an. The corners of each box are decorated with vegetal designs composed of intertwining plant motifs gathered within a frame of zigzag lines.  
Each volume of the *rab’a* is bound by a two-leaf cover and a library marker. Each leaf of the cover holds a medallion with a helical frame and an illuminated background. The spine is decorated with independent illuminated vegetal motifs. Each medallion is connected at the top and bottom by two suspended ornaments. The two inside covers are decorated with a medallion, divided into illuminated geometric forms on a blue, black, red and green background. The medallion is connected at the top and bottom to a smaller medallion.  
The endowment charter of the entire *rab’a* appears at the beginning of the first volume. On the first page of every volume there is a condensed version of the charter surrounded at both the top and bottom by two decorative bands that are different in size and decorative style from one volume to the next.  
Folio 2b–3a forms the beginning of each volume. The frontispiece consists of two identically decorated pages. Five lines are written on each of the two pages, in alternating gold and black, the text surrounded by a number of bands with extremely beautiful ornamentation in polychrome; specifically red and gold against a background of blue. The text is intercepted with independent vegetal decoration in a variety of different colours.  
Each page of the 30 volumes of the *rab’a* is divided into five horizontal rectangles. In each of the first, third and fifth rectangles, there is a single line of the Qur'an written in a large and illuminated *rayhani* script. In each of the second and fourth rectangles, four lines are written in black *thuluth* script. The second and fourth rectangles are intersected on both sides by two side-bands ornamented with illuminated motifs consisting of intertwining vegetal decoration against a white background.  
The layout of this *rab’a* is reminiscent of the Qur'anic manuscript of Sultan Bayezid.
f01728d7-fe74-597e-b37f-12f01e9ac1a3.short_description: A *rab’a* (Qur’an in 30 parts) in two wooden boxes covered with stucco and painted black with inscriptions and vegetal designs. The *rab’a* was donated by Sultan Murad to al-Aqsa Mosque. Each page is divided into five parts, three in illuminated *rayhani* script and two in *thuluth* script written with black ink. The word ‘Majestic’, chapter names, verse numbers and their area are illuminated.

f01728d7-fe74-597e-b37f-12f01e9ac1a3.method_for_provenance: Turkey was narrowed down as the place of production for this manuscript supported by the text of the *waqf* charter which appears on the third page of the Qur'an. The name of the copyist, illuminator and the place of production does not appear.

f02545d3-2c1e-56ed-999c-fd59a3ff72c3.name: *Shahnama*
f02545d3-2c1e-56ed-999c-fd59a3ff72c3.short_description: This is a fragmentary copy of the *Shahnama* (‘Book of Kings’), the verse epic that tells the story of the pre-Islamic kings and heroes of Iran. The manuscript was probably produced for the Iranian ruler Shah Abbas the Great, sometime after his accession in 1587, and contains sixteen paintings, two of which were added later, in about 1676. The paintings are amongst the finest examples of Persian painting ever produced, each one finely rendered and filled with abundant detail.

f076e01a-b92e-50ef-8e77-6d8f18842351.name: Fragmentary cenotaph cover with Qur'anic calligraphy
f076e01a-b92e-50ef-8e77-6d8f18842351.short_description: This rectangular silk textile exhibits a design of chevron bands containing calligraphic inscriptions in *thuluth* script with verses of the Qur’an, invocations to God, and the *shahada*, or Muslim profession of faith. This type of textile covered important Ottoman tombs, and recalls the *kiswa* fabrics woven in similar designs, but of much larger scale, that were sent annually by the Ottoman sultans to adorn the Ka‘ba in Mecca.

f0a22720-4486-5cd9-b830-526d7c53d494.name: Kettledrum.
f0a22720-4486-5cd9-b830-526d7c53d494.description:
The kettledrum is of hemispherical form and has a flat base. In the plain zone below the upper edge there are four rectangular loops with 16 protuberances in between serving to fix the drumhead, which is now missing. The decorated surface of the kettledrum consists of two zones. Both show medallions alternating with oblong panels on a background of a Y-pattern. The panels of the central zone contain a bold *naskhi* inscription against a background of arabesques. The text consists of nine nouns expressing praise and good wishes, without referring to the owner or mentioning his name. The medallions are filled with arabesques and whirling motifs. The oblong panels in the zone towards the base of the kettledrum show a *kufic* inscription of unknown content. The eagles with heads turned to the left and claws grasping the tips of the wings show the typical form of this bird used as an emblem by the Mamluk amirs. The emblem is repeated twice on the flat base on either side of a rectangular loop.  
This kettledrum was probably used in falconry to call the falcon back to the owner.
f0a22720-4486-5cd9-b830-526d7c53d494.short_description: Kettledrum of hemispherical form and with a flat base. The loops below the upper edge served to fix the drumhead. It is decorated with panels containing an inscription and medallions filled with arabesques and whirling motifs. It was probably used in falconry to call the falcon back to its owner.

f0a22720-4486-5cd9-b830-526d7c53d494.method_for_datation: Lamm (see Bibliography) dated the kettledrum to the first half of the 8th / 14th century.
f0a22720-4486-5cd9-b830-526d7c53d494.method_for_provenance: As a place of manufacture Lamm (see Bibliography) suggests Cairo, but he does not give a reason.
f0a22720-4486-5cd9-b830-526d7c53d494.obtention: The kettledrum was bought from the art collector Carl Robert Lamm by the Royal Armoury in 1922. In 1899, Lamm acquired it from F. R. Martin who had bought the kettledrum in Cairo during his journey through Egypt and Turkey in 1895–6.

f1004103-36c5-5a6a-a73a-16b1705a3c92.short_description: This sculptured master piece is dominated by a lion’s head in whose jaws hangs a combination of a handle and a knocker - a ring embellished with a cock. The *Kufi* inscription on a black niello ground proclaims the Muslim profession of faith: “In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate. I testify that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is the messenger of God.”

f213ba89-7885-5b92-9751-68053497df4b.name: Two  textile fragments
f213ba89-7885-5b92-9751-68053497df4b.short_description:
With its calligraphic frieze, in which letters end in animal heads, its lively lions and griffins rooted in the Sasanian and Byzantine tradition, and its sumptuous, lotus-like flowers on arabesque vines, the textile combines features from the culture of East and West.  
The use of paper for the silver thread points towards China, while the iconography is Western.

f21d4542-13e1-5350-b5fc-fb0fe10ff753.name: Boccia Vase
f21d4542-13e1-5350-b5fc-fb0fe10ff753.short_description: This Boccia vase embodies a crossover of cultures, decorated with floral patterns and Arabic calligraphy in bright colours. Mesmerized by the aesthetic of Arabic calligraphy, Christian artisans attempted to mimic the script to achieve a similar charm. While many ceramic-makers could not read Arabic, only a fragment of the script may be decoded as the Declaration of Islam. The vase is representative of Italy’s proximity to the Islamic world, incorporating elements of Islamic art into the pottery. Manufactured in Tuscany, the artisan drew inspiration from the Ottoman Empire and integrates recognizable characteristics from Hispano-Moresque pottery such as the whimsical shape and star-shaped handles. The picturesque appearance of Arabic calligraphy still enchants global audiences embellishing pottery, garments and jewellery.

f21d4542-13e1-5350-b5fc-fb0fe10ff753.method_for_datation: The date and origin were derived from an examination of material and technique in a research comparison with similar vases.

f2ab9cfb-bbce-54c1-b8c6-caafd9c9b90a.name: Saint Christophorus with the Infant Jesus
f2ab9cfb-bbce-54c1-b8c6-caafd9c9b90a.short_description:
According to Emperor Jahangir's (r. 1014-1037 / AD 1605-1627) inscription, the image of St. Christopher carrying the infant Jesus and accompanied by a dog was painted by the court painter Miskin (a pen name meaning "the humble one"). Miskin contributed to the codification of the Mughal style and played an increasingly important role in the illustration of the chronicles of the Mughal emperors. He is known for his keen observation of humans and animals. For this work, he probably drew inspiration from European engravings with Christian themes, which were brought to India by Jesuits at the end of the 16th century.  
  
The border with the prominent hazelnut branch was originally part of a larger album project completed under the Persian artist Muhammad Baqir (active Hegira late 1160s-1204 / AD late 1750s-1790) between Hegira 1178 / AD 1765 and Hegira 1183 / AD 1770. Parts of the album with Mughal and Safavid miniatures and calligraphies were rebound for the Qajar ruler Fath ʿAli Shah (r. Hegira 1211-1250 / AD 1797-1834) in the Hegira year 1237 (AD 1822). The individual leaves of this album were sold at auction by Drouot in Paris on 23 June 1982. Other leaves that originally belonged to this convolute known as the Drouot or Baqir album are currently scattered. The leaf seen here has another miniature pasted on the reverse.
f2ab9cfb-bbce-54c1-b8c6-caafd9c9b90a.initial_owner: Shahram Pahlavi; 2002-2013: Mehdi Metghalchi, London; 2013-2014: Catharina Dohrn, Münsingen

f30819fe-fb4c-5ec9-a552-17d8231b324a.name: Coat of armour.
f30819fe-fb4c-5ec9-a552-17d8231b324a.description:
A suit of armour made from iron mail that would cover the body from the head to the knees. It has solid metal plates that cover the neck and the stomach – the latter being much larger in size than the former – to provide additional protection. A number of these chain-mail suits survive, often bearing signs of wear and tear from use in battle. One example reveals evidence of injury received on the left sleeve, where the metal chain is torn through.  
The sword shows a curved-edged blade which was popular among Muslim fighters, while the Crusaders preferred straight swords. Decorative features on swords are usually found at the hilt near the handle.  
The protective plates of the amour are decorated with geometric designs, a Mamluk blazon, and Arabic writing executed in gold *thuluth* script. Most of the decoration has worn away and it is possible to read only some of the words. These include: “made for … the exalted … the great … the lord”. From these words it is possible to conclude that this suit belonged to a ruler, military commander, or other high-ranking official.
f30819fe-fb4c-5ec9-a552-17d8231b324a.short_description: Mamluk military suits of armour decorated with gilded emblems, such as this one, were worn in battle against the Crusaders.
f30819fe-fb4c-5ec9-a552-17d8231b324a.method_for_datation: The blazon and phrases mentioned on the abdominal plate of this suit of armour indicate that it is from the Mamluk period.
f30819fe-fb4c-5ec9-a552-17d8231b324a.method_for_provenance: Although this armour is decorated with a Mamluk blazon and was found in Damascus, its provenance is not clear. The Mamluk period saw an increased regional mobility of people and goods, especially military. It was likely produced in Cairo or Damascus, since these were two major regional centres at this time.
f30819fe-fb4c-5ec9-a552-17d8231b324a.provenance: Probably Damascus, Syria or Cairo, Egypt.
f30819fe-fb4c-5ec9-a552-17d8231b324a.bibliography:

f30ef8ba-a67a-55f8-91cb-fa65f19de25e.name: Sword.
f30ef8ba-a67a-55f8-91cb-fa65f19de25e.description:
A sword composed of a steel blade and a hilt made of animal horn. The scabbard is of gilded silver. The blade has decorative cartouches with inscriptions inside them. On the upper part of the blade there is a prominent medallion, which bears the following text: 'The work of al-Hajj Sanqur', and below this medallion is another inscription of the first verse of the chapter 'Mariam' from the Qur'an: 'Kaf Ha Ya Ayn Sad'. This line is followed byanother cartouche bearing the text, 'Sultan Fatih Muhammad Khan'.Below this cartouche are written verses 1 and 2 from the Qur'anic chapter 'al-Ha Mim', and 'Ain Sin Qaf'*.* The inscriptions and decorations that appear on the blade are executed in gold inlay. The scabbard is ornamented with vegetal decoration carved in high relief. The owner of the sword was the Ottoman Sultan Muhammad II Al Fatih ('The Conquerer').  
The Arabs imported swords from Iran and India. Quality swords were produced in Khurasan (Persia, now Iran), Damascus in Syria and Toledo in Spain.
f30ef8ba-a67a-55f8-91cb-fa65f19de25e.short_description: Ottomans excelled in making swords and their decoration rivalled that of the Iranians. In addition to their military use, swords bearing the names of Ottoman sultans were worn on gala celebrations at the court. This sword bears the name of Sultan Mohammad II and the name of its maker.
f30ef8ba-a67a-55f8-91cb-fa65f19de25e.initial_owner: Ottoman Sultan Muhammad II Al-Fatih (‘The Conqueror’); known in Turkey as Fatih Sultan Mehmet or Mehmet II.
f30ef8ba-a67a-55f8-91cb-fa65f19de25e.method_for_datation: The sword is dated based on the fact that the names of Ottoman Sultan Muhammad II and the name of the craftsman are recorded on it. In addition to this, the styles of the inscriptions, as well as the technique of manufacture, closely resemble the techniques that are specific to the Ottoman period.
f30ef8ba-a67a-55f8-91cb-fa65f19de25e.obtention: The sword was donated to the museum by Prince Yusuf Kamal, one of the princes of the family of Muhammad Ali, who was a collector of antiques. He donated a large number of ceramic and wooden objects and textiles to the museum.

f31ff28f-d559-5abc-880d-148f4aa71f67.name: Table (*khwan*) with scenes of princely leisure and inscribed with Persian poetry
f31ff28f-d559-5abc-880d-148f4aa71f67.short_description: This low, rectangular wood table on four legs is extensively ornamented with lacquerwork on the table top. Around the interior rim are painted and gilded floral arabesques surrounding inscriptions in cartouches. On the surface of this table, young men and women repose, feast, and hunt in abundant landscapes, and their style of depiction echoes manuscript illustrations of canonical Persian poetry.

f35b2d0a-540c-52cf-a794-46af21e2ee41.name: Underglass painted calligraphic panel
f35b2d0a-540c-52cf-a794-46af21e2ee41.description:
This underglass-painted panel consists of inscriptions in black *jali thuluth* (calligraphic Arabic script) inside an oval frame of leaves in a chestnut shade of gold. At the top is the word "Allah", below that the word "Muhammad", and in the centre the phrase "Ya aman Ali", all written as symmetric mirror compositions (*müsenna*). Between the two "ya" letters is a picture of a Bektaşi headdress and below it the figure of a submission stone (*teslim taşı*). The lines of the two lams are extended upwards to form two halberds, and the letter "ya" in the word ‘Ali’ forms his double-pointed sword Zülfikar. Around the lower edge of the oval frame appears the signature of the artist written in *riq‘a* script: "Painted by Hafız Ahmed Feyzi from the Demirhan neighbourhood of Bursa." In the lower corners of the panel are medallions formed of leaves painted in chestnut brown tones of gold, and in the upper corners are compositions of leaves and flowers.  
The pictures and scripts under glass are products of folk art. Such works are applied to the back of a piece of glass in reverse. They are dependent on the glass because the work disappears if the glass is broken. Their subjects are mostly illustrations of folkloric myths, stories, beliefs and symbols. Such panels were seen in the homes, small mosques, meeting places of dervishes and tombs in the past.
f35b2d0a-540c-52cf-a794-46af21e2ee41.holder: Vehbi Koç Foundation Sadberk Hanim Museum
f35b2d0a-540c-52cf-a794-46af21e2ee41.method_for_datation: It was determined through publications and expert opinion.

f35b2d0a-540c-52cf-a794-46af21e2ee41.author: Havva Furat Ay

materials: Glass; Underglass painting

f37cfcce-b0a0-5a4d-a76e-e42800b88c6a.name: Ewer
f37cfcce-b0a0-5a4d-a76e-e42800b88c6a.short_description: This jug is a rare example of early Islamic glasswork that carried any form of inscription. It is a rich, deep turquoise, a spectacular colour which was extremely unusual for any glass of this period. Made of mould-blown glass, the ewer is a drop form with a short foot, a thistle mouth and an extruded spout. A simple bent handle links the mouth and the body. A broad band of moulded *kufic* inscription that consists of repetitions of the Arabic word *al-Malk* (ownership) runs around its body divided by palmettes. The technique of moulding *kufic* inscriptions is found on glass vessels from Mesopotamia and from northeast Iran.
f37cfcce-b0a0-5a4d-a76e-e42800b88c6a.bibliography: Walton, Michelle, *Imperfect Perfection - Early Islamic Glass*, Doha: Bloomsbury Qatar Foundation Publishing, 2012: 82.
keywords: Glass; Ewer; Free-blown; Abbasid
materials: Glass; free-blown with applied, impressed and tooled decoration

f38d6e15-e344-5817-ac1d-988aed7ec5c8.name: Qur’an leaf
f38d6e15-e344-5817-ac1d-988aed7ec5c8.short_description: This Qur’an leaf is written in a transitional script that lies between the Hijazi and the *kufic* script styles. This vellum leaf demonstrates a crucial phase in the development of Quranic scripts. Towards the end of the first century Hijra, the Arabic letters started to acquire dots, as shown in this leaf, in the same brown ink used for the writing. Vocalization marks are seen in red and green dots, and the verse dividers are marked by the use of slanting dashes in brown ink.
f38d6e15-e344-5817-ac1d-988aed7ec5c8.bibliography: *Islamic Arts Museum Malaysia, IAMM Guide Book*, Kuala Lumpur: IAMM Publications, 2014: 14.
materials: Hijazi script on parchment

f396e33d-9645-55ac-affd-ff0c3b5c089a.name: Page from a Qur’an.
f396e33d-9645-55ac-affd-ff0c3b5c089a.description:
This Qur'an was written in gilt *kufic* script outlined in brown ink (sepia) on gazelle skin. The verses on the page shown (112: 3– 113: 1) are set in a richly illuminated frame, also gilded and outlined in brown ink. There are no diacritical marks. Vowel marks are shown as red or black dots. The beginning of a new chapter (*sura*) is only indicated by the *basmala* (the formula: 'In the Name of God, the Compassionate, the Merciful'). Three diagonal lines are placed at the end of the verses.  
  
The Qur'an page is framed by a wide border delineated by narrow bands. The rectangles formed by the border bands form joining sections. The large spaces within these rectangles are filled with decoration including spiralling tendrils with leaves and flowers.  
  
Only five leaves remain to us from this Qur'an, which was made in the AH 3rd–4th / AD 9th–10th centuries in or . Written in *kufic* script, gilded and richly illuminated, it must have been made for an important mosque or ruler.
f396e33d-9645-55ac-affd-ff0c3b5c089a.short_description: Calligraphy developed as a result of careful copying of the Holy Qur'an in order to make it accessible to the masses. This page is written in *kufic* script, named after the calligraphic centre in the city of Kufa, and its character is plain and rigid yet striking.
f396e33d-9645-55ac-affd-ff0c3b5c089a.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts.
f396e33d-9645-55ac-affd-ff0c3b5c089a.method_for_datation: The style of writing, the lack of diacritic marks, and the designs used in the illumination all suggest a date of the 3rd–4th / AD 9th–10th centuries.
f396e33d-9645-55ac-affd-ff0c3b5c089a.method_for_provenance: The Abbasid Empire was centred in Baghdad, and one of its most important regions was Syria. For this reason the object is thought to have been produced either in Iraq or in Syria.
f396e33d-9645-55ac-affd-ff0c3b5c089a.obtention: Ismet Bey, the mayor of Istanbul and a member of the board of directors of the Museum of Islamic Foundations (the old name for the Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts), visited the Umayyad Mosque in Damascus while travelling. He had a number of items in the collection at *Qubbat al-Hazine* (Treasury) of the mosque, including this Qur'an, transferred to the Museum where they were registered in the inventory in around 1332 / 1914.
